en: Now, therefore, begins the inquiry into Dharma. Dharma is a beneficial purpose characterized by Vedic injunction. An investigation into its means of proof [is now undertaken].

When there is contact with existing objects, the arising of cognition in a person through the sense organs is perception; it is not a means [for knowing Dharma], because it apprehends only what is already present. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.4) But the relation between a word and its meaning is innate; the knowledge thereof is instruction, which is non-deviating regarding an object not perceived [by other means]. That is the means of valid knowledge, according to Bādarāyaṇa, because of its independence.
(Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.5) Some [hold that the Veda concerns] action, because it is seen to be so in that regard. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.6)
Because it is not possible [for a word to denote a universal];
because [the agent] acts [as indicated] by the word;
and because [the cognition occurs] simultaneously in other beings.
And [the rule applies] to both the archetype and the modification; Jaimini 1.1.10.
And there is an increase [in the number of performers] due to the plurality of agents; Jaimini 1.1.11.
But in that case, the observation is equal; Jaimini 1.1.12.
The non-perception of that which exists is due to the non-arrival of the object [at the senses]. (Jaimini 1.1.13) The non-perception of the performance [of the sacrifice] is likewise.
(Jaimini 1.1.14) Simultaneity is like that of the sun. (Jaimini 1.1.15)

The difference in color is not a modification [of the word]. (Jaimini 1.1.16) It is not for the purpose of increasing the sound. (Jaimini 1.1.17) But it must be eternal, because its manifestation is for the sake of another. (Jaimini 1.1.18)
Because [the action] occurs simultaneously everywhere; because of the absence of number; because of independence. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.19–21)
And because of the absence of any manifestation of yoga;
and because of the observation of indicative marks (Jaimini 1.1.22–23).
Or rather, [the names] would not be expressive at the time of origin, because the purpose does not have that as its cause (Jaimini 1.1.24).
The collection of words denoting existing things is for the sake of action, because the meaning [of the Veda] has that as its cause.

(Jaimini 1.1.25) In the world, there would be a close connection with usage due to the restriction of what exists. (Jaimini 1.1.26) And some maintain that the Vedas have a close connection [with human authors], being designated by the names of men. (Jaimini 1.1.27)
And because of the observation of impermanence.
(Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.28) But it has been stated that [the Veda] is preceded by the Word. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.29) The name [of the Veda] arises from its proclamation. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.30)
"But it is merely a similarity of sound.

(Jaimini 1.1.31) "Or rather, there would be an application [of the word] once [the ritual act] has been performed, because of its connection with the action. (Jaimini 1.1.32) "Since the Veda has action as its purpose, those parts which do not have that as their purpose are useless; therefore, they are said to be non-eternal. (Jaimini 1.2.1)
And because there is no contradiction with the view of the scriptures (Jaimini 1.2.2);
likewise, because of the absence of results [thereby] (Jaimini 1.2.3);
and because other [injunctions] would be rendered purposeless (Jaimini 1.2.4).
And because of the prohibition of those who have no share [in the sacrifice]; Jaimini 1.2.5.
Because of the connection with impermanent things; Jaimini 1.2.6.
But because they form a single syntactical unit with an injunction, they must be for the purpose of praising the injunctions; Jaimini 1.2.7.

And the traditional teaching is the same. (Jaimini 1.2.8) Furthermore, there is no logical impossibility regarding the authoritative source; for if [the Veda] were a human composition, there would be contradiction. However, since the meaning of the word is not something produced by human application, it is therefore logically consistent.
(Jaimini 1.2.9) But it is a figurative statement. (Jaimini 1.2.10)
Because of the form; because of the departure; because of the greater distance; and because of the fault of the performer, there is the seeing of the son.
The desire for what is not immediately present;
[this is] praise of knowledge;
the state of "all-encompassing" pertains to the qualified person.
Because the fruit arises from the completion of the ritual action, there would be a distinction in the fruit according to the magnitude [of the action], as in the world; Jaimini Sūtra 1.2.17.
Regarding the last two [cases], it is as previously stated; Jaimini Sūtra 1.2.18.
Or rather, it must be an injunction because it conveys something not previously known, for a mere statement would be purposeless; Jaimini Sūtra 1.2.19.
If it is argued that this is like the case in common worldly practice (Jaimini 1.2.20),
we say no, because of the priority [of the Vedic text] (Jaimini 1.2.21).
Furthermore, the status of being a supplementary part of a sentence (*vākyaśeṣatva*) has already been explained (Jaimini 1.2.22).

And in some cases an injunction would be purposeless; therefore, praise should be understood [there]. By analogy with that, the same applies to the others. (Jaimini 1.2.23) Since the displacement [of the mantra] is possible within the context, it should not be assumed; for that would render the injunction purposeless toward it. (Jaimini 1.2.24) Furthermore, there would be a split in the sentence if it were an injunction. (Jaimini 1.2.25)
Or it may be the cause [of knowledge], because of its meaningfulness and logical consistency.

(Jaimini 1.2.26) But its stability [as a source] is due to its being preceded by the Word, and because it is not an injunction. (Jaimini 1.2.27) If it is argued that praise is improper when the object is already established, (Jaimini 1.2.28)

But the meaning [of the word] is subordinate to the injunction, as is seen in common worldly usage. (Jaimini 1.2.29) And if it were established that [the word] expresses a reason, because of the specific mention [of a particular case], then there would be a restriction of injunctions based on similarity. (Jaimini 1.2.30) Because there are explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) for that purpose. (Jaimini 1.2.31)
Because of the restriction of the sentence; because of the teaching regarding cognition; because of the mention of what is non-existent. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.2.32–34)
Because of the connection with meaning in that which is insentient;
because of the contradiction of meaning;
because of the statement being like that of one's own Vedic study.

Because they are unintelligible; because of their connection with impermanent things, the mantras would be purposeless (Jaimini 1.2.38–39). But the meaning of the sentence is not distinct [from ordinary speech] (Jaimini 1.2.40).
Furthermore, the repetition is for the sake of a quality (Jaimini 1.2.41);
it is a restrictive enumeration (parisaṃkhyā) (Jaimini 1.2.42); or it is an explanatory praise (arthavāda) (Jaimini 1.2.43).
The subsequent [passage] is not contradictory. Jaimini 1.2.44:
In the case of an injunction, there is no censure of the ritual act because it is a purificatory rite (saṃskāra). Jaimini 1.2.45:
In the case of a naming, it is an explanatory statement (arthavāda). Jaimini 1.2.46.

There would be no prohibition on account of the qualities. (Jaimini 1.2.47) There is no mention of Vidyā because of the lack of connection. (Jaimini 1.2.48) There is subsequent cognition of that which exists. (Jaimini 1.2.49)
And the connection with impermanence has been stated [Jaimini 1.2.50]. And the instruction by means of indicative marks is for that purpose [Jaimini 1.2.51]. There is modification [Jaimini 1.2.52].

And there are words of injunction. (Jaimini 1.2.53) Since dharma has its root in verbal testimony, that which lacks verbal testimony would be unreliable. (Jaimini 1.3.1) Or rather, because the agent is common [to both], inference should be a means of valid knowledge. (Jaimini 1.3.2)
But in case of contradiction, it should be disregarded, for when there is no [contradiction], there is inference (Jaimini 1.3.3).
And because a reason is observed (Jaimini 1.3.4).
If it is argued that "it is not contradicted when there is no subversion by the learned" (Jaimini 1.3.5).
[Objection: It is not so, because of the limited extent of the treatises (Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.6).
[Response: Or rather, when the cause is apprehended, they should be understood as being employed [for that purpose] (Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.7).
Since no contradiction is observed among them, the disagreement would be equal (Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.8).

Or rather, they are based on the Śāstra, because it is the cause of that [knowledge]. (Jaimini 1.3.9) But what is enjoined should be understood as authoritative, since there is no contradiction with a means of valid cognition.
(Jaimini 1.3.10) If it is argued that it is a manual of ritual practice (*prayoga-śāstra*), (Jaimini 1.3.11)
Because there is no restriction regarding non-existence; because there is no supplementary statement (*avākyaśeṣa*);
because it is employed everywhere, and because of the scriptural injunction concerning proximity.

Because it is established by inference, the means of knowledge would be connected with that. (Jaimini 1.3.15) Or rather, all [Vedic] dharma would be [established by it], because the injunction follows that same principle. (Jaimini 1.3.16) There would be application [of the mantra] based on observation. (Jaimini 1.3.17)
And because there is no indicative mark (*liṅga*) for that which is eternal, [Jaimini 1.3.18]. For a name arises from connection with a place, [Jaimini 1.3.19].
If it is argued that [the name] would not exist in other places, [Jaimini 1.3.20].
For it may be designated as "yoga," like that of Mathura (Jaimini 1.3.21);
or rather, it is a property of the ritual action, like the sloping ground (Jaimini 1.3.22);
but it is equal to the property of the agent (Jaimini 1.3.23).
Because there is no scriptural injunction regarding the production [of sounds], there would be no fixed determination with respect to words (Jaimini 1.3.24).
Since sound is produced through effort, it is subject to error (Jaimini 1.3.25).
And it is unreasonable for there to be multiple words [for the same object] (Jaimini 1.3.26).
In that case, the true meaning [of the Veda] would result from a specific application [of reasoning].
(Jaimini 1.3.27) And there is an incapacity [to understand it otherwise], because [the literal sense] is appropriate.
(Jaimini 1.3.28) And because it occupies only one part [of the whole], there would be a change of grammatical case. (Jaimini 1.3.29)
Because there is no injunction for a separate application, there is unity of purpose due to the lack of division; because it is not a word denoting a substance;
and because of the observation of something else. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.30–32)
But the form [is what is denoted], because it serves the purpose of action (Jaimini 1.3.33).
If it is argued that there would be no action, or that there is an injunction regarding a different object, or that it is not a substance (Jaimini 1.3.34), [the reply is:
there is no distinction [between the word and its meaning] because the performance [of the ritual] is for the sake of that [form] (Jaimini 1.3.35).

It has been stated that this [Veda] is for the sake of purposeful action; therefore, everything in it must be for that purpose. (Jaimini 1.4.1) Or rather, it may be a name, because it is something new at its origin and lacks injunctive force.
(Jaimini 1.4.2) In a case where there is an instruction regarding a quality, the connection is primarily with the principal act. (Jaimini 1.4.3)
And there is another scripture that makes [the meaning] known; Jaimini 1.4.4.
And there is the designation of that [meaning]; Jaimini 1.4.5.
If it is argued that because a quality is heard in the name, there must be an injunction [of that quality]; Jaimini 1.4.6.

[The injunctions] do not [apply] because the two actions are equal; (Jaimini 1.4.7). When there is a single word, it is like something intended for another; (Jaimini 1.4.8). But its qualities would be enjoined, since they are not divided from the injunction, provided they are not already taught by another [injunction] regarding the purpose of the injunction; (Jaimini 1.4.9).
In the case of *barhis* and *ājya*, because the words are used even when there is no consecration (*saṃskāra*), they are not [names] based on that [consecration].
(Jaimini 1.4.10) In the case of *prokṣaṇī* waters, it is because of the connection with the purpose (*artha*). (Jaimini 1.4.11) The same applies to the *anirmanthya* fire. (Jaimini 1.4.12)

If it is argued that there is an option regarding the Vaiśvadeva [offering], [the reply is]: No, because of the context and because of the direct injunction; for the context does not pertain to the substance. Furthermore, there is no connection of purpose between them.

Because the subordinate elements (guṇas) exist for the sake of another [Jaimini 1.4.16]. Those [elements] which possess a prior [basis] are not intended as injunctions; their capacity is found in the traditional recitation [of the Veda] [Jaimini 1.4.17].

But when there is an injunction of a subordinate element, its own subordinate qualities would be purposeless in the performance [of the rite], for they have no meaningful function with respect to that [injunction] [Jaimini 1.4.18].
The remainder of that [injunction] is not tenable.
(Jaimini 1.4.19) Because there is no distinction, they would be tenable as having the purpose of praise for the sake of the injunction.
(Jaimini 1.4.20) If it is argued that there must be a cause [for this], (Jaimini 1.4.21)
Because it would be purposeless, it is not the cause; for the causes [of an action] are prescribed for the sake of a quality. Jaimini 1.4.22.
Its accomplishment [is through that]. Jaimini 1.4.23. It is the genus. Jaimini 1.4.24.
On account of similarity;
[the mention of] praise;
[the mention of] abundance.
On account of the inherence of the indicative mark (Jaimini 1.4.28);
in doubtful cases, on account of the remainder of the sentence (Jaimini 1.4.29);
or rather, it is determined by the sense, because it is a part of the same conceptual construction (Jaimini 1.4.30).

Words denoting action have the sense of bringing something into being; from them, the ritual act is understood, for it is this meaning that is enjoined. (Jaimini 2.1.1) If it is argued that all words have the sense of bringing into being as their meaning, (Jaimini 2.1.2) then those words whose form is perceived when they are uttered in their own usage are nouns; therefore, because they denote something already existing in their own usage, there is no further expectation [of an action] from them. (Jaimini 2.1.3)

But those verbal roots for which no application is found when their own meaning arises are called *ākhyāta*s; therefore, the action should be understood from them, because their application is dependent [on something else]. Jaimini 2.1.4. Furthermore, an injunction (*codanā*) is an instigation (*ārambha*). Jaimini 2.1.5.
These are of two kinds, being either subordinate (*guṇa*) or primary (*pradhāna*). Jaimini 2.1.6.

Those [actions] by which a substance is not intended to be produced are primary, because the substance is subordinate to them. But those by which a substance is intended to be produced—therein the action should be understood as subordinate, because the substance is primary to it. However, in the case of a mere *dharma*, the action would be primary, because there is no [other] purpose served, as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings.
Or rather, because the scriptural expression is identical, it should have the same status as the others.

(Jaimini 2.1.10) If it is argued that this is an instruction regarding a substance, (Jaimini 2.1.11) we say no, because it exists for the sake of that [ritual], as is seen in common worldly practice, and because that [substance] is a subordinate element. (Jaimini 2.1.12)

But the consecration of the *stotra* and *śastra* [hymns] is like that of the *yājyā*, because they denote the deity. (Jaimini 2.1.13) However, it should be displaced by the purpose, because there is no injunction regarding the deities, as the purpose is subordinate. (Jaimini 2.1.14) Or rather, it may be for the sake of a quality, as in the case of the barren cow (*vaśā*). (Jaimini 2.1.15)
Not so, because of the inherent connection with the Vedic revelation (Jaimini 2.1.16);
and because of the difference in designation (Jaimini 2.1.17);
furthermore, the quality [of being a seer] would be purposeless (Jaimini 2.1.18).

Likewise [the rule applies] to the *yājyā* and *puroruc* verses; (Jaimini 2.1.19) because in the case of the *vaśā*, there is a connection with the purpose; (Jaimini 2.1.20) or rather, it should apply because of the meaningfulness of the phrase "and that which" (*yac ca*). (Jaimini 2.1.21)
But it is not seen in the case of those [mantras] recited in the traditional texts (Jaimini 2.1.22). It is observed [in the case of others] (Jaimini 2.1.23).
Or rather, because of their connection with the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), the two verbal roots *stauti* and *śaṃsati* should enjoin the production of an action within the context (Jaimini 2.1.24).
And because of the distinctness of the words (Jaimini 2.1.25);
and that statement would be purposeless (Jaimini 2.1.26);
and a different meaning is perceived (Jaimini 2.1.27).
And the designation [of the action] is like that of the ritual act; Jaimini 2.1.28. And there is the accomplishment of the fruit; Jaimini 2.1.29.
There is identity of purpose between the injunction and the mantra because they consist of the same word; Jaimini 2.1.30.
Alternatively, by virtue of its capacity for performance, a mantra should be that which expresses a designation;
the term "mantra" applies to those [texts] that enjoin such [actions]. The word "Brāhmaṇa" applies to the remainder.

Jaimini 2.1.34: That which is not recited [in the Vedic canon] is not a mantra; for there is a distinction among those that are so recited. Jaimini 2.1.35: Among those, it is an *ṛc* where there is a division into quarters (*pāda*) determined by the sense of the meaning.
Jaimini 2.1.36: When these same syllables are set to song, they receive the designation of *sāman*.

In the remainder, the term *yajus* [applies]. (Jaimini 2.1.37) Or rather, the *nigada* should be the fourth [type], because of its distinct ritual characteristic. (Jaimini 2.1.38) And because of its specific designation. (Jaimini 2.1.39)
Or rather, they are *yajus* formulas because of their form; Jaimini 2.1.40.
There is a specific property [of the ritual] due to a direct scriptural statement; Jaimini 2.1.41.
And also because of the purpose; Jaimini 2.1.42.
The designation is for the sake of the quality. (Jaimini 2.1.43) If it is argued that [the term applies] to all [of them], (Jaimini 2.1.44) [we reply:
No, because of the designation "ṛc. (Jaimini 2.1.45)

"Because there is unity of purpose, there is a single sentence, provided that if it were divided, there would be mutual expectancy. (Jaimini 2.1.46) "Or rather, if they are equal [in independence], there would be a split of sentences. (Jaimini 2.1.47) "Or there is *anuṣaṅga* (supplying an elided word), because the completion of the sentence occurs through equal connection with all [the preceding parts]. (Jaimini 2.1.48)
One should not attach [the action] to what has already been separated. Jaimini 2.1.49:
There is a difference of ritual action (*karmabheda*) when there is a different word, because it is connected with a distinct performance. Jaimini 2.2.1:
Thus, for a single [action], a repetition [of the injunction] would be meaningless, as there is no distinction [in the act itself]. Jaimini 2.2.2.
But the context belongs to the Full Moon sacrifice, because its specific form is not mentioned [in the other cases];
and because a distinction is observed, for if all were equal, there would be no application [of the context].
But it is a subordinate quality, because of its connection with the direct scriptural statement.

Or rather, there is a simultaneous injunction of the subordinate elements because of the scriptural teaching; for when that [principal] is enjoined, each of those [subordinates] is taught as being for its sake.
(Jaimini 2.2.6) And the designation is likewise. (Jaimini 2.2.7) And because of the observation of an indicative mark. (Jaimini 2.2.8)
The *upāṃśuyāja* should be like the *paurṇamāsī*,
because it is not a primary injunction (*codanā*) [of a new sacrifice],
due to the connection with a subordinate quality (*guṇa*). (Jaimini Sūtra 2.2.9–11)
And because of the statement in the *prāya* [section];
(Jaimini 2.2.12) the *āghāra-agnihotra* is not a distinct rite because it lacks a specific form;
(Jaimini 2.2.13) because of the connection with a technical name; (Jaimini 2.2.14).
And because it is not the subject under discussion [Jaimini 2.2.15].

On the contrary, it is an injunction, because the meaning of the word constitutes the performance; therefore, due to its proximity, the repetition is for the sake of a subordinate quality [Jaimini 2.2.16].

Because of the connection with a substance, there is an injunction regarding the animal and the Soma; for in the context, the connection with a substance would be purposeless, as it is not for the sake of a subordinate quality [Jaimini 2.2.17].
And the preparatory acts (saṃskāra) are not injunctive [of the primary act].

(Jaimini 2.2.18) Because of that distinction, there is a repetition of the rite; for if there were a distinction based on the separateness of the substance, it would be purposeless, since the distinction [of the act] is subordinate to the substance.
(Jaimini 2.2.19) But the preparatory act would not be distinct, because it exists for the sake of another, as the substance is subordinate to it. (Jaimini 2.2.20)
Because they are established as distinct, there would be a difference in the ritual acts according to their number (Jaimini 2.2.21).
And the name [is distinct] because of its connection with the original injunction (Jaimini 2.2.22).
And the subordinate factors [are distinct] when connected with a new unseen result, because the two sentences are equal in status (Jaimini 2.2.23).
But when the word denotes an action and no quality [is otherwise established], a quality would be understood therein.

(Jaimini 2.2.24) However, because of the mention of a fruit, it must be an action, since a fruit is connected with an action. (Jaimini 2.2.25) But because the two sentences are not equivalent, that [quality] would be understood as a quality [of the action]. (Jaimini 2.2.26)
In the case of [the *saubhara*] being common [to all], it would be connected with the ritual action.

(Jaimini 2.2.27) In the *saubhara*, because of the mention of the person (*puruṣa*), there is a connection with a specific desire regarding the *nidhana*. (Jaimini 2.2.28) Or rather, since every [desire] has already been stated [as the result], the mention of desire (*kāma-śruti*) in that [context] should be for the purpose of the *nidhana*; the repeated mention is for the sake of the *nidhana*. (Jaimini 2.2.29)

But a quality, because of its connection with a sacrifice, should enjoin a different ritual action, since that connection is not subordinate to anything else. (Jaimini 2.3.1) However, for the sake of a specific purpose, it may be stated that there is unity [of the ritual] due to a difference in indicative marks, because the statement concerns a quality. (Jaimini 2.3.2) In the case of the *Aveṣṭi*, because of its connection with the term "sacrifice" (*yajña*), it is said that the sacrifice is the primary element. (Jaimini 2.3.3)
[The fire-installation is] subsidiary to everything, because it is common to all; Jaimini 2.3.4.
In the case of the solstices (ayana), there is a separate injunction, because of the connection with a specific name; Jaimini 2.3.5.
And because no accessory quality is mentioned, it is an injunction for a distinct ritual act; Jaimini 2.3.6.
And the sentence regarding the fruit is completed. Jaimini 2.3.7.
Or rather, it is a modification because of the context. Jaimini 2.3.8.
And because of the observation of an indicative mark. Jaimini 2.3.9.

The application of the name [to the sacrifice] is based on its quality. (Jaimini 2.3.10) The completion [of the rite] is not distinguished [from the model sacrifice]. (Jaimini 2.3.11) And it is a purificatory act (*saṃskāra*), because in the absence of a specific context (*aprakaraṇa*), there is no word denoting a primary action (*akarmaśabdatvāt*). (Jaimini 2.3.12)
As it has been stated: "Because action is rooted in scripture" (Jaimini 2.3.13);
"But the act of sacrificing [is primary], because of the connection with the material, the fruit, and the enjoyer, and because these are connected to the ritual action" (Jaimini 2.3.14);
and "Also because of the observation of indicative marks" (Jaimini 2.3.15).
Because it is commonly observed in that context;
and because the explanatory passage (arthavāda) is thus justified.
But [the word] is connected with the word denoting the purpose, for its meaning is that [purpose], due to its connection with the Vedic text (śruti).
But in the case of the *pātnīvata* offering, there is a restriction because it occurs earlier; [Jaimini 2.3.19].
Because it lacks a material substance, it would be merely a remnant of the ritual action; [Jaimini 2.3.20].
But the fire, on account of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*), should be understood as a term denoting the sacrifice; [Jaimini 2.3.21].
Or it may be a substance, because the injunction has that as its purpose (Jaimini 2.3.22).
Through connection with that [substance], the sacrifice would be named after it; therefore, the prescriptions of ritual duties apply to it (Jaimini 2.3.23).
When there is a different context, there is a difference in purpose (Jaimini 2.3.24).
And the fruit [accrues] when there is no proximity to the action (Jaimini 2.3.25).
But when there is proximity, because there is no division, the repetition is for the sake of the fruit (Jaimini 2.3.26).
Because it is the cause of the Āgneya hymn, it should be understood as being performed through repetition (Jaimini 2.3.27).

But because there is no distinction among the acts, it is not prescribed by the repetition [of the word]; rather, the repeated mention serves another purpose. (Jaimini 2.3.28) Or, the repeated scriptural statement has a different aim.
(Jaimini 2.3.29) The lifelong repetition is a property of the ritual act, because of the context. (Jaimini 2.4.1)
Or rather, it belongs to the agent because of its connection with the Vedic text;

and because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga). For if it were a property of the ritual act, it would be restricted by the commencement [of the rite], and in that case, the other [mention] would be purposeless. Furthermore, it shows the completion [of the act]; and if time were the factor, there would be a division of the ritual acts.

But because of impermanence, it would not be so. (Jaimini 2.4.5) And there is also a contradiction, as before. (Jaimini 2.4.6) But because of the restriction of the agent's duty, the scriptural injunction regarding time would be contingent upon a cause. (Jaimini 2.4.7)

There would be a difference of ritual acts (*karmabheda*) in different recensional branches (*śākhāntara*) on account of differences in name, form, injunction, repetition, censure, incapacity, completion, statement of expiation, and the observation of another purpose.

(Jaimini 2.4.8) Or rather, it is one [act], because there is no difference in connection, form, injunction, and name. (Jaimini 2.4.9) It cannot be [different] by name alone, because a name does not denote an injunction. (Jaimini 2.4.10)
And there would be a single function for all [of them]. (Jaimini 2.4.11) And the designation is artificial. (Jaimini 2.4.12) Even in the case of oneness, it is subordinate. (Jaimini 2.4.13)
The Dharmaśāstra is included within Vidyā;
[this is so] because it is a restatement, like the Agneya sacrifice (Jaimini 2.4.14).
Or rather, there is no repetition, because there is no difference in its connection with the revealed scripture (śruti) (Jaimini 2.4.15–16).
And because of the non-proximity of the purpose;
and one [act] is not enjoined for [only] one person;
and there is a consideration of the completion [of the rite]. Jaimini 2.4.17–19.

Even though [the sacrifice] is one, there are other statements regarding censure, incapacity, and completion. (Jaimini 2.4.20) The expiation is occasioned by a specific cause. (Jaimini 2.4.21) Or rather, it follows from the commencement, because of the mandatory injunction. (Jaimini 2.4.22)

The completion [of the rite] should be understood as before, according to what is known [from the model sacrifice]. (Jaimini 2.4.23) The indicative mark (*liṅga*) is not restricted because it applies as a supplement to all; for there is no injunction of a ritual action (*karmacodanā*) therein. Therefore, the designation of "taking up" (*āhāra*) should apply to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*). (Jaimini 2.4.24) Furthermore, since no specific substances are enjoined, there would be a lack of fixed order among the injunctions. However, due to the specific direction [in the text], the order would be established; therefore, this must be a permanent restatement (*nityānuvāda*). (Jaimini 2.4.25)
Because there is a prohibition of what has been prescribed, there would be an excess in one alternative (Jaimini 2.4.26).
In the case of the Sārasvata sacrifice, because of the conflict, it should be "when" (yadā) [the specific condition occurs] (Jaimini 2.4.27).
In the Upahavya sacrifice, there is no counter-exception (Jaimini 2.4.28).

Or rather, the repetition is for the sake of a quality (guṇārthā). Furthermore, it shows the cognition [of this]. Or else, due to the connection with the sequence, the distinctness of the injunctions would remain established within a single [textual unit].

But because there is no connection with that which is contradictory, when there is a single action, there would be a cognition of all actions as being enjoined due to the connection with that [single action]. Jaimini Sūtra 2.4.32. Now, therefore, follows the definition of the subsidiary (śeṣa). Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.1. A subsidiary is so called because it exists for the sake of another. Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.2.

Bādari [holds that the purpose of the Veda] lies in substances, qualities, and preparatory acts; Jaimini [holds that] even ritual actions [are the purpose], because they are for the sake of the fruit;
and the fruit [is the purpose], because it is for the sake of the person.
And the person [is subordinate] because he exists for the sake of the ritual action; JaiS 3.1.6.
There is a connection between them by virtue of that purpose; JaiS 3.1.7.
But the prescribed duty must apply to all, because there is no distinction in the connection and no distinction in the context; JaiS 3.1.8.

Because the purpose is lost, it would not be an action; [Jaimini 3.1.9]. But the fruit is connected with the effort; the meaning of the word would exist in the absence [of the fruit] when there is separation; [Jaimini 3.1.10].
And the substance, because of its connection with the origination [of the rite], should be enjoined for that very purpose; [Jaimini 3.1.11].

When there is a single purpose, there should be a restriction because the substance and the quality serve a single function (Jaimini 3.1.12). That which is joined with the singular number belongs to one [entity], because of its connection with the direct Vedic statement (śruti) (Jaimini 3.1.13).
Or rather, it applies to all [entities] because they are all characterized; for the characteristic is indeed non-distinct (Jaimini 3.1.14).
Jaimini 3.1.15: Since it is enjoined for the sake of another, it should be understood according to the scriptural text.
Jaimini 3.1.16: Or rather, because it is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*), there would be no restriction regarding the qualities of the voice.
Jaimini 3.1.17: But there is indeed a restriction of the purpose, because of its connection with the scriptural text, since that [scripture] is the authority for the word.
Because it would otherwise be purposeless, [the injunction] applies to its subsidiaries (Jaimini 3.1.18).
But if it were a quality of the agent, there would be a syntactical split because of the lack of connection with the action (Jaimini 3.1.19).
However, it should be a single sentence with an expectancy, for it is not completed by the preceding [word] (Jaimini 3.1.20).
In a case of doubt, there would be a split in the sentence due to intervention; Jaimini 3.1.21.
Furthermore, because subordinate elements exist for the sake of another, there would be no connection [between them] due to their equality; Jaimini 3.1.22.
And because there is no connection of purpose between them mutually; Jaimini 3.1.23.
There is no injunction for the immediate sequence [of subsidiaries],
because the sentences are complete in themselves (Jaimini 3.1.24). Furthermore,
a subsidiary connected with a quality should be understood as common [to all], because there is no mutual connection between those [sentences] (Jaimini 3.1.25–26).

Or rather, because of the connection with the purpose, the mention of a quality (*guṇa-śruti*)—due to the relationship of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) with its meaning—is for the sake of characterization.

(Jaimini 3.1.27) The status of being a subsidiary (*śeṣabhāva*) in mantras would arise from their capacity to express a meaning; therefore, there is a connection with the [primary] purpose at the time of origin (*utpatti-sambandha*), because of the eternal association with that purpose. (Jaimini 3.2.1) It would [be performed] by that which is not specifically enjoined, because it serves as a purificatory rite (*saṃskāraka*). (Jaimini 3.2.2)
"But because of the direct statement, the *aindrī* mantra would be used in a non-literal sense" (Jaimini 3.2.3).
"Or rather, there may be a designation based on a quality, since the relationship [between the mantra and its application] is not based on scriptural injunction" (Jaimini 3.2.4).
"If it is argued that this is also the case for the *āhvāna* (invocation)" (Jaimini 3.2.5).
There is no rule regarding the time [of performance], because it has been enjoined; because of the absence of a subordinate quality; and because of the indicative mark. (Jaimini Sūtra 3.2.6–8)
There would be a contradiction of the injunction in the instruction;
likewise regarding the rising and the dismissal. And in the *sūktavāka*, it is an injunction of time, because it serves another purpose.
Or rather, it is an instruction; for the word *yājyā* does not occur without cause (Jaimini 3.2.12).
It has a deity as its object because of its connection with that [deity] (Jaimini 3.2.13).
If it is argued that it is a mere disposal (*pratipatti*), then, like the *sviṣṭakṛt*, it would be a consecration of both (Jaimini 3.2.14).
Because of the instruction regarding the whole, the term "all" applies to both;
or rather, it is according to the purpose, because it is a refinement of that which has become a subordinate element.
If it is argued [that it is so] because of a specific scriptural statement—Jaimini 3.2.15–17.

Because there is no division of context, the word "entire" applies to both [the morning and evening libations]. (Jaimini 3.2.18) On account of indicative mark, order, and name, that which is recited is connected with the optional rites. (Jaimini 3.2.19) And within the context, there is an injunction for the mantra regarding those not so named, because it is taught as such. (Jaimini 3.2.20)

Or rather, it is designated by that [name] because of both the context and logical consistency (Jaimini 3.2.21). Furthermore, the instruction would be purposeless due to the lack of connection with anything that possesses a fruit; for the *upasthāna* itself does not possess a fruit (Jaimini 3.2.22).
Moreover, because [the act] is taught as belonging to all [of them] (Jaimini 3.2.23).
By means of both indicative mark (*liṅga*) and name (*samākhyāna*), the section [of the *anuvāka*] has the purpose of reciting the *bhakṣa-mantras*.

(Jaimini 3.2.24) There is a displacement (*apakarṣa*) of that [section] from its original place due to its form (*rūpa*) and explicit instruction (*upadeśa*), because the specific meaning [of the mantra] has been enjoined.

(Jaimini 3.2.25) Because it expresses a subordinate quality (*guṇa-abhidhāna*), the mantra beginning with "mandra" should be a single mantra, since those two [the quality and the act] are connected to a single purpose. (Jaimini 3.2.26)
Jaimini 3.2.27: Because of the specification of gender, among those [offerings] subject to the same rule, those not dedicated to Indra are without mantras.
Jaimini 3.2.28: Or rather, they are according to the deity, for it shows that they have that as their archetype.
Jaimini 3.2.29: In the case of the cups that have been refilled, there is a mention of all [deities], because there is a dual distinction.

Or rather, there is no removal of the former because of this [new] injunction; or, on the contrary, there should be a removal because of the specific mention. But in the case of the Pātnīvata cup, it is as before.
Or rather, it would be excluded because of its being grasped; but one should indicate Tvaṣṭṛ because of the drinking. However, this cannot be so because of the inequality.
And there are thirty [verses] because they are for the sake of another; Jaimini 3.2.36.
And the *vaṣaṭ*-call is like the agent; Jaimini 3.2.37. But there is a prohibition of the meters because they apply to all [the priests]; Jaimini 3.2.38.

But in the case of the offering to Indra-Agni, it should be so because of the manifestation of the indicative mark (liṅga). Or rather, it should be so for one [deity] because of the distinction from the other deity, as in the case of the division.
And the metre is like the deity.

Or rather, because [the mantra] exists in all [of them], it belongs to one who has a single *chandas* (Jaimini 3.2.42). Or rather, according to Aitiśāyana, there is a single mantra for all, because of the drinking by way of devotion (*bhakti*), for the qualification for the *savana* [belongs to all]. (Jaimini 3.2.43). On account of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), the qualification should belong to the [entire] class (*jāti*). (Jaimini 3.3.1).
Or rather, it belongs to the Veda, because it is seen primarily there; and because of its indicative mark;
and because of the instruction regarding dharma, for there is no connection with a material substance.

And it is called the "knowledge of the three Vedas" because one who knows them [is so designated]. (Jaimini 3.3.5) If it is argued that [the name applies] according to the literal sense in the sequence of individuals, (Jaimini 3.3.6) [We reply:
No, because it is applied to all [who possess that knowledge]. (Jaimini 3.3.7)

Because of the connection with the Veda, it is not set aside by the context (Jaimini 3.3.8). In the case of a conflict between the subordinate and the principal, the connection with the Veda belongs to the principal, because it exists for its sake (Jaimini 3.3.9). Where both [Vedic texts] are heard, [the decision is made] by the majority (Jaimini 3.3.10).

It is not connected [to the main ritual] because of the context, since there is a requirement for the procedure (*kartavyatā*). (Jaimini 3.3.11) And the order [of subsidiaries] is determined by the commonality of location.
(Jaimini 3.3.12) And the name is likewise [determinative], because it is for that purpose. (Jaimini 3.3.13)

In the case of a conflict between direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyā*), each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding because of its remoteness from the purpose. Jaimini 3.3.14.
Or rather, it is the *ahīna* sacrifice [that applies] due to the context, as [the term] is used in a secondary sense. Jaimini 3.3.15.
But because of the lack of connection with the primary [meaning], it should therefore be displaced. Jaimini 3.3.16.
Or rather, it is joined with duality and plurality because of the injunction regarding it;
if it is argued that this is by way of an alternative for what is produced by the purpose,
[we reply] no, because of the connection with a single performance.
And the tail [is the offering], because it is a single part; Jaimini 3.3.20.
Or rather, it is the injunction [of the whole], because it is something not previously established; Jaimini 3.3.21.
If it is argued that it is only a single part; Jaimini 3.3.22.
Not [is it] from the archetype, because it is not established by the scripture.

(Jaimini 3.3.23) The *santardana* (joining together) should exist in the archetype, like the purchase [of Soma], because there is no loss of purpose. (Jaimini 3.3.24) Or rather, there is a displacement [of the rite], because of the mention of a specific [feature]. (Jaimini 3.3.25)

Or rather, [the distinction] is based on the agent, because he is the cause of that [distinction]. (Jaimini 3.3.26) Or rather, it should be based on the sacrifice, because the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are thus rendered consistent. (Jaimini 3.3.27) And the terminuses (*saṃsthā*) are like the agents, because there is no difference in their purpose regarding the maintenance [of the fire]. (Jaimini 3.3.28)
Because the purpose exists in the Ukthya and other [sacrifices] (Jaimini 3.3.29).
If it is argued that praise is useless because there is no distinction [between them] (Jaimini 3.3.30), [the reply is:
it may be so because of their non-permanence (Jaimini 3.3.31).
That which is associated with a number should belong to the sacrifice because of the context (Jaimini 3.3.32).
Or rather, it is occasional because of its connection with the agent, since the indicative mark has that as its cause (Jaimini 3.3.33).
The pounding for Pūṣan should be understood as belonging to the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), because there is no injunction for it in the archetype (prakṛti) (Jaimini 3.3.34).
Jaimini [holds] that it applies to all [substances] without distinction (Jaimini 3.3.35).

[The opponent argues: "In the case of the *caru*, it is stated for the sake of the purpose; in the case of the *puroḍāśa*, because of the contradiction of the purpose, it would not apply in the case of the animal sacrifice" (Jaimini 3.3.36).
[The opponent continues: "If it is argued that it should also apply in the case of the *caru*" (Jaimini 3.3.37).
Not so, because it is the name of the cooked offering;
(Jaimini 3.3.38) because of the connection with a single [deity] in one case; (Jaimini 3.3.39) and because there is no contradiction regarding the ritual properties. (Jaimini 3.3.40)
Or rather, it should apply when there is a companion, because the deity is the determining factor (Jaimini 3.3.41);
and because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga) (Jaimini 3.3.42).

Due to the explicit statement, there is grinding of all [grains] for that [deity], since the scripture prescribes it for him; however, in the absence of that purpose, there is no grinding in the case of the *vicāra* (the mixed offering) (Jaimini 3.3.43).
In one case, because it is the nature of the object, [the offering] for Indra and Agni would not belong to both, since it is not so enjoined.
(Jaimini 3.3.44) The state of ending in "ad" is merely a reason. (Jaimini 3.3.45) The [other] statement is the final authority. (Jaimini 3.3.46)
"‘Wearing the sacred thread around the neck’ is a duty for humans, because the word has that as its primary meaning" (Jaimini 3.4.1).
"Or rather, it is a descriptive reference, because the matter already exists" (Jaimini 3.4.2). "It must be an injunction, because it conveys something not previously known" (Jaimini 3.4.3).
That [act] would be a duty of ritual action (*karmadharma*),
because it is a supplementary part of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*). That which is connected within that context [belongs to the ritual], because there is no contradiction.
Or rather, [the mention of the other] is equal [to the mention of the primary], because it is enumerated together with that which is primary, since the other exists for the sake of that;
or it is an explanatory passage (arthavāda) because of the context;
and because it forms a single syntactical unit with the injunction. (Jaimini 3.4.7–9)
And likewise, the division of directions [is not a separate act], because the connection has its purpose in the substance; Jaimini 3.4.10.
And similarly regarding what is torn at the joints, what is full, what is ghee, and what is burnt; Jaimini 3.4.11.
That which is not an action, when connected with a sacrifice, would be a permanent restatement (anuvāda) due to that connection; Jaimini 3.4.12.
Or rather, it is an injunction because of a different connection (Jaimini 3.4.13).
It is like the *ahīna* sacrifice; the person [is the object] because it is for his sake (Jaimini 3.4.14).
Or, due to the specific context, it is a consecration of that which is connected [to the rite], just like the sacrificial materials (Jaimini 3.4.15).
It would be excluded because of the specific designation;
and also because of the complete surrender [of oneself] at the Śaṃyu-rite;
and because of the exclusion prior to [the period of] wearing soiled clothes.
And because of the prohibition of food [in that context].

(Jaimini 3.4.19) But in the absence of a specific context, those properties [belong to the sacrifice] because of that distinction. (Jaimini 3.4.20) However, because it lacks a substance, it would be a subsidiary element. (Jaimini 3.4.21)
Because of the connection with the Veda (Jaimini 3.4.22);
and because of the connection with the substance (Jaimini 3.4.23).
Or rather, there may be a connection of this [rite] with the fruit, like the connection [of other rites]; therefore, it is a ritual action—so says Ātiśāyana (Jaimini 3.4.24).
The remaining [offerings] belong to all rites because there is no distinction in the context;
however, the *homās* (libations) are restricted [to specific rites] due to their connection with the *āhavanīya* fire;
and the remainder [belongs to the specific rite] because of its designation (*samākhyāna*).
But because of a defect, there should be an offering in the worldly fire; for according to the scripture, there would be no defect in the Vedic fire.

(Jaimini 3.4.28) Or rather, it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), because [otherwise] it would be illogical; therefore, it should be understood as applying to the sacrifice. (Jaimini 3.4.29) And it is not enjoined, because of the difference in the acts. (Jaimini 3.4.30)
On account of the indicative mark, it should apply to the officiating priest (Jaimini 3.4.31).

And the same applies to the mishap involving the drinking [of Soma] (Jaimini 3.4.32). But because of the fault, it should apply to the Vedic [rite], for since the purpose [is served] by the worldly [method], there would be no fault in that case (Jaimini 3.4.33).
Because there is no distinction in all cases [Jaimini Sūtra 3.4.34];
or rather, it belongs to the master, because it is for his sake [Jaimini Sūtra 3.4.35];
and also because of the observation of indicative marks [Jaimini Sūtra 3.4.36].
The entire oblation is to be offered, because it exists for that purpose (Jaimini 3.4.37).
But there must be a remnant, because of the taking of portions (Jaimini 3.4.38). Or rather, [the offering] is merely a means, because its purpose is that [of the sacrifice] (Jaimini 3.4.39).
But because the action has already been performed, it should occur only once, since the substance is subordinate to it;
and because we observe the remnants [of the action].
Since they are not the motivators, the actions should be performed from a single [substance], because the remnant is subordinate.
And because it is a *saṃskāra* (consecration);
[Jaimini 3.4.43] "Or rather, it belongs to all [the priests], because there is no distinction in the reason, since the consecration is for their sake";
[Jaimini 3.4.44] "And because of the observation of an indicative mark" [Jaimini 3.4.45].
If [the option] were from one [of the two], it would be according to preference, because there is no distinction;
or rather, it is from the primary [one], because of its prior occurrence. Since there is no mention of eating, the word "giving" refers to a purchase.
And because of its association with that [Jaimini Sūtra 3.4.49];
or rather, it is for the purpose of consumption, since the substance is common [to both] (Jaimini Sūtra 3.4.50);
[and] because of the specific assignment, there is a praise of the gift (Jaimini Sūtra 3.4.51).
And because of the ghee and because of all connections; Jaimini 3.5.1;
and because of the cause; Jaimini 3.5.2;
and because of the word *samavatta* (cut-off portion) in the case of one [victim]; Jaimini 3.5.3.

And because it is seen [in the case] of the clarified butter (*ājya*), this [offering] serves the purpose of the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice. (Jaimini 3.5.4) But because there is no remainder, it would not be so; for there is no remainder due to the taking of the whole. (Jaimini 3.5.5) It would not apply to the *dhruvā* vessel because of its commonality. (Jaimini 3.5.6)
"And because it has been cut off [into the *juhu*], and because that [cut portion] is connected with the oblation;

if it be argued that this is 'like the *camasa*' [vessels]. (Jaimini 3.5.7) "No, because of the contradiction with the injunction and because it is merely a preparation of the sacrificial offering. (Jaimini 3.5.8–9)
Because the context concerns what has already arisen, the word "all" applies only when [the object] exists.
(Jaimini 3.5.10) It refers to the subsequent [act] because of the distinction in genus. (Jaimini 3.5.11) The final [act] is for the purpose of removing the debt. (Jaimini 3.5.12)
In the Sākamprasthāyya sacrifice, the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *iḍā* are likewise;
so too in the *sautrāmaṇī* regarding the cups (*graha*).
And the mention of the "remnant" (*śeṣa*) is similar to that.

If there is oneness of substance, then because of the difference in actions, the acts should be performed for each action; (Jaimini 3.5.16) and because the remnant is undivided, it is not distinguished with respect to all [the recipients]. (Jaimini 3.5.17) But in the case of the cup for Indra and Vāyu, because of a specific scriptural statement, the consumption should take place for each action. (Jaimini 3.5.18)
"Because of the scriptural statement, there is no eating [of the remnants];
or rather, it should exist because another purpose is observed;
but since the statements are based on something previously unknown (*apūrva*), they should be according to the instruction."
Because of the designation [of the cups] as *camasa*s, the connection [of the action] is based on that [designation].

(Jaimini 3.5.22) The single [priest] [drinks] from the *udgātṛ-camasa*, because of the connection with the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). (Jaimini 3.5.23) Or rather, all [the priests drink], because of the connection with all [the cups]. (Jaimini 3.5.24)
Or rather, it belongs to those who perform the hymns because of their connection with them and because of the great learning [required]; (Jaimini 3.5.25).
But all [the priests] [participate] because of their connection with the Veda; on account of this reason, it should apply to one part [of the ritual]; (Jaimini 3.5.26).
There is no portion for the Grāvastut priest, because it is not prescribed [for him]; (Jaimini 3.5.27).
[The *hāriyojana* cup belongs] either to all [the priests], because of the connection with the whole;
or [it belongs] to the *camasins*, because of their proximity.
But since it is a rule for all, the mention of the *camasins* is for that purpose.
And one should consume [the portion] from the *vaṣaṭ*-call;
and also from the oblation and the pressing.
Because of the explicit instruction regarding the cups (*camasa*), the rule for the remainder is not clearly defined.

Or rather, there may be no designation [of the cup] because it is a cause; for the word refers to the maker [of the cups]. (Jaimini 3.5.34) And because another [person] is seen in connection with the cup. (Jaimini 3.5.35) In the case of a single vessel, the Adhvaryu should drink first according to the sequence. (Jaimini 3.5.36)
Or rather, it is the *hotṛ* [priest], because of the wording of the mantra (Jaimini 3.5.37), because of a direct statement (Jaimini 3.5.38),
and because of the sequence of the causes (Jaimini 3.5.39).

The eating [of the portion] is permitted by means of a verbal command. (Jaimini 3.5.40) One should request permission by means of the formula "It has been invited; invite [me]," because of the indicative mark [in the text]. (Jaimini 3.5.41) In that case, the response follows from the sense of the matter. (Jaimini 3.5.42)
Because of the combination of those who are entitled to a single portion;

Jai. 3.5.43. The consumption [of the remnant] is removed by the removal of the *yājyā*, just like the *pravara*; Jai. 3.5.44. Or rather, it belongs to the sacrificer because the cause for it has arrived; Jai. 3.5.45.

Because it has already commenced, there is no removal of the *pravara*; [Jaimini Sūtra 3.5.46]. The *phalacamas* is an occasional modification of the consumption [of soma], because of its connection with the scriptural text; [Jaimini Sūtra 3.5.47].
Or rather, it is a modification of the sacrifice, because the consecration is for the sake of that [sacrifice]; [Jaimini Sūtra 3.5.48].
Because of the *homa*;
because of the simultaneity with the cups;
and because of the observation of an indicative mark.
Because they follow along by virtue of being common [to all]; or rather, because the word is identical to that of the *brahman* priest;
that [rite] is for the sake of all [priests], as it is not within a specific context.
Or rather, it belongs to the archetype (prakṛti), because it is not repeated [in the ectype]. But that [archetypal rule] is excluded when there is a specific scriptural injunction.
If it is argued that this is so "because of observation" [of the practice], [we reply: no. Jaimini Sūtra 3.6.2–4.

Not so, because of the unity of purpose of the injunction. (Jaimini 3.6.5) If it is argued that this refers to the originative injunction, (Jaimini 3.6.6) we say no, because of the equality [of the two]. (Jaimini 3.6.7)
But because the purpose of the injunction is complete [in the archetype], and because there is a primary contradiction, it refers to the meaning of the base form (prakṛti).

(Jaimini 3.6.8) However, due to the specific context, it would be contradictory in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti). (Jaimini 3.6.9) But the occasional (naimittika) rule applies to the archetype; it is a modification thereof, because of a specific connection. (Jaimini 3.6.10)

The establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya) is for the sake of the desired sacrifice, because of the context; [Jaimini 3.6.11]. Or rather, it is not so, because those [fires] are for that purpose; [Jaimini 3.6.12].
And because of the observation of an indicative mark; [Jaimini 3.6.13].

That [fire] is for the sake of the archetype, just like other uncontextualized injunctions (anārabhyavāda); [it serves] all purposes because the establishment of the fire has its own specific time. Therefore, by virtue of the archetype, the fire should belong to those [offerings] just as the *prayāja* offerings do.
Or rather, it does not apply to them, because they are for that purpose [Jaimini 3.6.17].
The injunction regarding the animal sacrifice is equal for all, because there is no distinction in the context [Jaimini 3.6.18].
And because of its position, it belongs to the preceding [Jaimini 3.6.19].
"But for some, the prior mention there is for the sake of a subordinate element.
(Jaimini 3.6.20) "If it is argued that, by this, there is an injunction of time for that which has been displaced," (Jaimini 3.6.21) "No, because it is a part [of the whole]. (Jaimini 3.6.22)

If it is argued that [the order] is determined by the purpose (*artha*), [we reply]: No, because that would contradict the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). Rather, it is due to the position (*sthāna*) of the preceding preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*), since its purpose is for that [subsequent rite].

And because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga). Jaimini 3.6.26. It is not an injunction for the sake of a subordinate element (guṇa). Jaimini 3.6.27. Due to the difference in time between the two milkings, the boiled milk (śṛta) would be unconnected [to the rite]. Jaimini 3.6.28.

Or rather, because of the division of the context, the rule regarding time applies to that which is connected with it. (Jaimini 3.6.29) Likewise, there is the scriptural injunction for the cups at another pressing. (Jaimini 3.6.30) And the girdle [is prescribed] because of the observation of an indicative mark. (Jaimini 3.6.31)
The remnant is distant from and unconnected with the others because of its proximity [to the primary].
Or rather, it is connected, because the remnant exists for that purpose and is caused by it. It would be restricted by specific designation.
The subsidiary of the fire-altar is likewise [to be performed] when it is not in its proper context (Jaimini 3.6.35).
The occasional rite should belong to those who do not share the same *viṭhāna*, because of their inequality (Jaimini 3.6.36).
And there is a substitute (Jaimini 3.6.37).
Likewise, because the purpose is one;
and because it is not characterized by the scriptures;
the mention of the quality is for the sake of a restrictive rule.
But the *saṃsthās* (termini) have the same injunctions, because there is no distinction in their context; JaiS 3.6.41. And the designation is likewise equal; JaiS 3.6.42.
But there is an option when there is a connection with a specific desire, because of the equality of the obligatory [rite]; JaiS 3.6.43.
Or rather, they will belong to the archetype because of being restated;
however, there is a combination because of the scriptural statement;
and also because of the prohibition of the previous gender-markers.
The designation of one [action] is due to a distinction in quality (Jaimini 3.6.47).
Because of the distinction in context, that which is not connected [to a specific subsidiary] belongs to the primary [rite] (Jaimini 3.7.1).
Or rather, it belongs to all [the primaries], because the status of being a subsidiary is not prompted by that [specific context] (Jaimini 3.7.2).
If it is argued that [the injunction] is from afar, [we reply]:
No, for that is not a syntactical unit (vākya), because it serves that purpose;
and also because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga).
But because of the connection with the result, [the accessory] belongs to the primary act when it is connected with its master; JaiSū 3.7.6.
And because of the connection with the desire to perform; JaiSū 3.7.7.
Likewise, because of the designation; JaiSū 3.7.8.
But when that [rite] is joined [with others], there is a scriptural declaration of the fruit; therefore, there should be a desire to perform all [the rites].
(Jaimini 3.7.9) Because of the mention of the accessory, the mention [of the fruit] pertains to all [the rites].
(Jaimini 3.7.10) However, the initiation and the sacrificial fee belong to the principal [rite] because of a specific scriptural statement. (Jaimini 3.7.11)
And because cessation is observed [in the case of the post].

(Jaimini 3.7.12) Likewise, the altar belongs to the sacrificial post. (Jaimini 3.7.13) Or rather, it is merely a location, because it forms a single syntactical unit with what follows. (Jaimini 3.7.14)
"Regarding the statement, 'They recite the Sāmidhenī verses after that,' [it refers to] the Sāmidhenīs because of the mention of the two *havirdhāna* carts [in the context]; Jaimini 3.7.15.
Or rather, it refers to the location alone, for the purposeful act (*arthakarma*) of the Soma is directly perceived; Jaimini 3.7.16.
And the designation (*samākhyāna*) is likewise. Jaimini 3.7.17.

The fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer, because that is its characteristic; therefore, it should be performed by oneself. (Jaimini 3.7.18) But in the case of the relinquishment (*utsarga*), since the principal act is primary, the one who performs the subsidiary acts is the one who performs the principal; therefore, it may be done either by another or by oneself. (Jaimini 3.7.19) Or rather, it should be done by another, because of the scriptural injunction regarding hiring (*parikraya*); for there is a contradiction [if one were to perform it] in relation to one's own self. (Jaimini 3.7.20)
In that case, the number of performers would be determined by the sense [of the context], as there would be no restriction due to the absence of a specific distinction (Jaimini Sūtra 3.7.21).
Or rather, because of the difference in the scriptural texts, there should be one for each name (Jaimini Sūtra 3.7.22).
If it is argued that this is because of the difference in the ritual acts for a single person (Jaimini Sūtra 3.7.23).
For regarding the origin [of the office]:
Jaimini 3.7.24 states that the *camasādhvaryus* are also [separate priests] because they are designated by them;
however, Jaimini 3.7.26 states that it is so at the origin because of the scriptural mention of the plural.
The state of being ten [is established] because of the observation of indicative marks (liṅga) [Jaimini Sūtra 3.7.27];
and the *śamitṛ* [is distinct] because of the difference in verbal expression [Jaimini Sūtra 3.7.28];
or rather, it is due to the context, since there is no connection with the original injunction [Jaimini Sūtra 3.7.29].
And the *upagā*s [are priests] because of the observation of their characteristic marks (Jaimini 3.7.30).
But the seller is different, because he is not enjoined for the ritual act (Jaimini 3.7.31).
All [the assistants] have the status of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) because of their performance of the ritual work, as there is no distinction [between them] (Jaimini 3.7.32).
Or rather, it is not so, because of the enumeration [of specific individuals].
(Jaimini 3.7.33) If it is argued that it applies to one side [of the two alternatives], (Jaimini 3.7.34) then there is no entitlement for all. (Jaimini 3.7.35)
But the restriction [regarding the number] is by means of the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), because of the connection with the Vedic revelation (śruti) [Jaimini 3.7.36];
and because, having declared their status as sacrificers (yajamāna), their initiation (dīkṣā) is prescribed [Jaimini 3.7.37];
[thus] they have the master as the seventeenth, due to the commonality of the ritual action [Jaimini 3.7.38].

All those purposes are accomplished because they have been applied; and the fires [are established] because of their own specific time. (Jaimini 3.7.39) There should be a restriction of the ritual action due to its connection with that [fire], because the connection is purposeful. (Jaimini 3.7.40) Its specification is made through direct instruction and designation. (Jaimini 3.7.41)
And likewise, there is the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga):

"The recitation of the *praiṣa* and *anuvacana* belongs to the Maitrāvaruṇa because of the direct instruction" (Jaimini 3.7.42); "Or rather, it is the *puro'nuvākyā* that is his duty, because of its proximity to the *praiṣa*" (Jaimini 3.7.43).
And because the Hotṛ is seen [performing it] during the morning recitation (prātar-anuvāka) [Jaimini Sūtra 3.7.45];
the Camasādhvaryus [should offer] the cups because of their designation [by that title] [Jaimini Sūtra 3.7.46];
or rather, the Adhvaryu [should do so], because that is the logical rule [Jaimini Sūtra 3.7.47].
And because another [usage] is seen in the case of the *camasa* cup;
they should be understood as such when there is incapacity.
Because of the instruction in the Veda, as in the previous case, when there is a difference from the Veda, they should be according to that instruction.

Or rather, his own duty (svadharma) would arise from that quality, because of the force of the qualification; [the sacrifice] is unmanifest with its subsidiaries in the remainder. (Jaimini 3.7.51) The hiring of the master’s labor is for the sake of the ritual, because the ritual has that as its purpose. (Jaimini 3.8.1) It would apply to the others because of a specific scriptural statement. (Jaimini 3.8.2)
But the preparatory rites (saṃskāra) would be restricted according to the Veda, based on the capacity of the person, like the ritual acts themselves.

(Jaimini 3.8.3) But they belong to the sacrificer, because he is the principal agent, as in the case of the ritual acts. (Jaimini 3.8.4) And because of the designation [of the sacrificer]. (Jaimini 3.8.5)

Its designation is as a quality (guṇatva), because it exists with respect to the injunction (codanā); and because they are not equal, they would have different rules of application (asamānavidhāna). Jaimini Sūtra 3.8.6–8.
And austerity [is required] because of the attainment of the fruit, as in the case of worldly practice; Jaimini 3.8.9. And the supplementary statement is likewise; Jaimini 3.8.10.
For the others, it would be so because of a direct scriptural injunction; Jaimini 3.8.11.
And because it is a quality, there would be no fixed restriction by means of the Veda (Jaimini 3.8.12).
Likewise, desire [serves as a restrictive factor] due to its connection with a purpose (Jaimini 3.8.13). There may be [restriction] for the others on account of specific designation (Jaimini 3.8.14).

And likewise, the mantras do not perform the ritual action; [this is so] because they are seen to be employed even when [the primary act] is absent (Jaimini 3.8.15). Furthermore, in the case of those [mantras] recited twice, both [versions] are used, because the twofold recitation serves a purpose (Jaimini 3.8.17).
And when [the person] is known [to be qualified], there is the recitation; for one who is ignorant is not prescribed [for such duties].

(Jaimini 3.8.18) Because of the designation (*samākhyāna*) in the section on the sacrificer's acts, the rituals should belong to the sacrificer. (Jaimini 3.8.19) Or rather, the Adhvaryu [should perform them], for he is intended for that purpose; the designation follows the prior logical principle. (Jaimini 3.8.20)
In case of conflict, the instrument [is determined] by a specific connection; the other is different from them, since there would be a distinction based on that.
(Jaimini 3.8.21) And in the case of directions, because of the authority over another.
(Jaimini 3.8.22) But the Adhvaryu [is the director], because of the scriptural indication. (Jaimini 3.8.23)
Or rather, it is figurative because of the commonality of the action (Jaimini 3.8.24).

The fruit belongs to the officiating priest because he is the instrument, as that is his purpose (Jaimini 3.8.25). Or rather, it belongs to the master, because the rite is for his sake (Jaimini 3.8.26).
And because of the observation of indicative marks (Jaimini 3.8.27);
the fruit belongs to the ritual action for the sake of the master, because it serves a purpose with respect to him (Jaimini 3.8.28);
and because of the designation (Jaimini 3.8.29).
The preparation of the substance pertains to all rites because there is no distinction in the context (Jaimini 3.8.30).
However, due to specific instruction, there is no application of that which is not previously established in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) (Jaimini 3.8.31).
And in case of conflict, because of the specific scriptural statement, it remains unmanifest in the remainder (Jaimini 3.8.32).

But there is a removal of a single part because of its connection with what is already present. (Jaimini 3.8.33) In the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the remainder serves all purposes, just as in the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*).
(Jaimini 3.8.34) Or rather, it serves the primary purpose, because the subsidiary is not enjoined. (Jaimini 3.8.35)
Because there is no distinction in proximity, it would be impossible for those things that are not its auxiliary parts [to be included].
If it is argued that the same applies to the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) rite, we say no;
because it is not within the context (*aprakaraṇa*), and because an auxiliary part does not have that [the *ādhāna*] as its cause.
Or [the application] is at that time, because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga) [Jaimini Sūtra 3.8.39];
or rather, it applies to all [the priests], because there is no distinction [Jaimini Sūtra 3.8.40];
the observation of the indicative mark occurs when the logical principle has been stated [Jaimini Sūtra 3.8.41].

But the flesh belongs to the *savanīya* offerings because of the specific injunction; [Jaimini 3.8.42]. If it is argued that a figurative application (*bhakti*) is improper when the primary substance is not present, [Jaimini 3.8.43], [we reply] it would be so, on account of the indicative mark of the archetype, just as in the case of the *vairāja* chant; [Jaimini 3.8.44].

Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into that which is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and that which is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). (Jaimini 4.1.1) When there is pleasure for a person, there is a desire for that [result], because it is characterized by the object [of desire] and is not [otherwise] distinguished. (Jaimini 4.1.2) Upon the abandonment of that [desire], the ritual acts are for the sake of the person, because the scripture is beyond doubt. Furthermore, the substance is not intended to be processed; since it is connected with that purpose, the mention of the person in relation to the action [indicates it is for his benefit]. (Jaimini 4.1.3)

But because the scripture makes no distinction, the results should follow exactly as they are stated [in the texts]. (Jaimini 4.1.4) Or rather, when no specific cause is perceived, the purpose is not connected to that [general rule], because the purpose is not linked to it. (Jaimini 4.1.5) And so it is with those things that are like worldly objects. (Jaimini 4.1.6)
Substances, however, should be offered without distinction, because otherwise they would be purposeless.

(Jaimini 4.1.7) But there is no connection of substances with their own [specific] purpose, because substances serve distinct purposes; therefore, they should be used according to the scriptural injunction. (Jaimini 4.1.8) And they are enjoined in the case of purposeful acts. (Jaimini 4.1.9)

And because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga). Jaimini 4.1.10. In that case, singularity is not a subordinate element of the sacrifice, because the object is subordinate. Jaimini 4.1.11. And because of the singular number in the scriptural expression. Jaimini 4.1.12.

If it is argued that [the meaning] is understood [from the word], [we reply: No, for that is not based on the word, because its authority is like that of the previous [case]. Rather, it is perceived as being like the word itself; for when that [word] occurs, it is observed, since the cognition of it is just like that of other [objects]. Jaimini Sūtra 4.1.13–15.
And likewise there is the observation of an indicative mark; Jaimini 4.1.16.
And similarly there is an indicative mark; Jaimini 4.1.17.
In the case of the dependent [rites], the existence [of the result] would be understood as the purpose without distinction; Jaimini 4.1.18.

But in the case of an injunction (*codanā*), there is no undertaking [of a subordinate action] because it is not distinct; for it is not enjoined by another. (Jaimini 4.1.19) Or rather, when there is a desire to prepare a substance, there would be the state of being a primary action (*bhāva*); and in the case of the purpose (*artha*), there is a state of subordination (*guṇabhūtatā*) because of its dependence [on that purpose]. (Jaimini 4.1.20) For substances and actions are unequal in their relation to the purpose. (Jaimini 4.1.21)

Because they are produced as one, all [the substances] would be equal [in status]. (Jaimini 4.1.22) Or rather, the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) would be the primary [substance], because it is produced through the process of coagulation (*saṃsarga*). (Jaimini 4.1.23) And because it is praised by means of the primary term [for the sacrifice]. (Jaimini 4.1.24)
The ritual action of anointing the feet is not the motive for the leading [of the animal], because that leading serves another purpose.

(Jaimini 4.1.25) And it is an action intended to express the meaning, because its connection with what is yet to come is caused by that; for it is ordained for that purpose. (Jaimini 4.1.26) In the case of the animal sacrifice, since there is no seizing [of the blood], the red blood and the dung are not part of the ritual action. (Jaimini 4.1.27)

And [the substance] is a part [of the whole], because at the time of its production it is conjoined with that which is being sacrificed. (Jaimini 4.1.28) If it is argued that another [substance] is required for that [act] because of the specific mention [in the text], [we reply:
no, because of the proximity of the remnant. (Jaimini 4.1.29–30)

Because of the performance of the ritual action; and because of the observation of an indicative mark (Jaimini 4.1.31–32). In the case of the sprinkling [of clarified butter], there should be a distinction of vessels due to the separation [of the acts], as in the case of the after-offerings (anūyāja) (Jaimini 4.1.33).
Or rather, there is no loss of eligibility because of [the presence of] a portion, since it is a part;
and because the joint performance is the cause;
and because of the observation of its absence. Jaimini 4.1.34–36.
If it exists, there is the statement with a specific purpose; Jaimini 4.1.37.
If it is argued that it does not belong to that [person], Jaimini 4.1.38;
[we reply] it would belong to him, because he is the primary [subject]; Jaimini 4.1.39.
But the bringing together [of the butter] should be primary, because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga);
for in the case of a direct statement (vacana), there is no capacity for a reason (hetu).
In that case, the originative injunction would be undivided.
In that context, the mention of the *jauhava* [clarified butter] is for the purpose of prohibiting the *anūyāja* offerings.

(Jaimini 4.1.43) If it is argued that the same applies to the *aupabhṛta* [clarified butter], (Jaimini 4.1.44) [we reply: it would be so; however, because of the prohibition regarding the *juhū*, it is a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*). (Jaimini 4.1.45)
In that case, the number is eight because of the scriptural statement;
and because of the favoring of the *jauhava* [clarified butter].
But for the two [offerings], there is both the capacity of the reason and the scriptural statement regarding the bringing together (*samānayana*).
But the *svaru* is not produced by multiple [actions], because its own word denotes its specific function; Jaimini 4.2.1.
And one might suspect it is so because of its difference in genus; Jaimini 4.2.2.
Or rather, it is a part of that [wood], because the state of being a *svaru* is caused by that; Jaimini 4.2.3.
And because of the scriptural mention of "pieces" (Jaim_4.2.4);
and because it is seen [to be done] for each sacrificial post (Jaim_4.2.5);
and because the word "makes" (karoti) is used in reference to the taking up [of the wood] (Jaim_4.2.6).
Because that [the branch] is the primary object in the case of the branch; Jaimini 4.2.7.
Because that [the branch] is the primary object in the case of the branch, there would be a separation by means of the *upaveṣa*; that is the difference. Jaimini 4.2.8.
And because of the departure from the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). Jaimini 4.2.9.
Regarding the act of taking away, however, it is an *offering* (*juhoti*) because of the commonality of the application and because substances are subordinate to a purpose.
(Jaimini 4.2.10) Or rather, it is a disposal (*pratipatti*), because the word has that as its primary meaning.
(Jaimini 4.2.11) And even if there is a purpose [for the substance], [it remains a disposal]. (Jaimini 4.2.12)
Not so, because he lacks the qualification [for that act] and because the purpose has already been accomplished.
(Jaimini 4.2.13) Because there is no connection with the production [of the water], there should be a distribution of the *praṇītā* waters like the clarified butter (*ājya*).
(Jaimini 4.2.14) Or rather, there is a disposal of those intended for the mixing [of the dough], because the others have that as their primary purpose. (Jaimini 4.2.15)
The handing over of the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa priest is like the throwing [of the grass-bundle], because its purpose has already been fulfilled;
[however, it is] rather a ritual act (arthakarma) because of its connection with the agent, like the wearing of a garland;
and because it is seen to be connected with the performance of the rite.

In the case of its production, that which is connected [to a substance] is for the sake of that [substance], because it is the cause for the scriptural mention of it; therefore, when that [substance] goes toward another purpose, there should be a disposal (*pratipatti*) because it has become a subordinate element (*śeṣa*). And in the *saumika* [sacrifice], this is so because its purpose has already been fulfilled.
Or rather, it is a primary act (*arthakarman*), because of its connection with the designation [of the substance]. Jaimini 4.2.19–21.
Or rather, it is a performance [of the sacrifice], because that is the logical principle; thus the scriptural mention of the place is like the *avabhṛtha* bath.

(Jaimini 4.2.22) There is no injunction regarding the agent, the place, and the time, because they are eternally inherent in the performance. (Jaimini 4.2.23) Or rather, the scriptural statement is for the purpose of restriction. (Jaimini 4.2.24)

Likewise, the mention of qualities (*guṇa*) with respect to substances (*dravya*) is because of their connection with the originative injunction; and in the case of a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*), it is because that [substance] is the primary element.

Regarding the injunction "he sacrifices" (*yajati*), it refers to the action involving substance and deity, because its purpose is fulfilled in the aggregate [of these elements]. (Jaimini Sūtra 4.2.25–27)

Because it is heard as stated in that [context], the *juhoti* should be [the same] as the *āsecana* (pouring). (Jaimini Sūtra 4.2.28) Since an injunction concludes with the performance of the action, there would be an extension of the injunction to another purpose.

(Jaimini Sūtra 4.2.29) Or rather, because of the connection at the time of origin, the relationship of the purpose among those things not distinguished [from one another] would be the cause for the unity of the performance. (Jaimini Sūtra 4.2.30)

In the case of substances, preparatory acts, and rituals, because they exist for the sake of another, the mention of a fruit must be an explanatory praise (arthavāda). (Jaimini 4.3.1) And because the originative injunction does not have that [fruit] as its primary purpose. (Jaimini 4.3.2) But the fruit belongs to that which has that [injunction] as its primary purpose. (Jaimini 4.3.3)
In the case of an occasional rite, because it is a modification, another [rite] would be the primary element of the sacrifice (Jaimini 4.3.4).
