But when one thing has both [functions], there is a distinctness of connection (saṃyogapṛthaktva) (Jaimini 4.3.5).
If it is argued that it is merely a subsidiary (śeṣa) (Jaimini 4.3.6).
It is not so, because there is no difference in purpose (Jaimini Sūtra 4.3.7).
However, for substances intended for action, the consecration belongs to the ritual duty (Jaimini Sūtra 4.3.8).
Because of their distinctness, it would remain restricted [to each] (Jaimini Sūtra 4.3.9).
Because no fruit is mentioned in the injunction, only the ritual act would be enjoined, for that which is not expressed by the word is not understood [as part of the injunction].

Or rather, by the force of the scriptural recitation, it should be understood through the purpose of the injunction; for the statements of these matters are perceived as being for the sake of a purpose. Since there is no connection between things that lack a common purpose even when they are in immediate sequence, that [phrase] is merely a portion of the direct Vedic statement (śruti).
And the meaning of the sentence is like the meaning of the subordinate element.
(Jaimini 4.3.12) That [rite] serves all purposes, because there is no specific instruction. (Jaimini 4.3.13) Or rather, it is one, because the injunction is a single unit. (Jaimini 4.3.14)
That [heaven] would be [the result] for all, because it is not distinguished [from one person to another]; and because of the cognition [of it as such].
(Jaimini 4.3.15) And because of the conviction [thereof].
(Jaimini 4.3.16) Kārṣṇājini [holds that] in the case of a sacrifice, the statement of the fruit is like an auxiliary [element]. (Jaimini 4.3.17)
Ātreya [holds that] the fruit [is mentioned] because of its specific instruction; for where it is not heard, there must be inference.
(Jaimini 4.3.18) In the case of subsidiary elements (*aṅga*), the praise is for the sake of another, because they serve a different purpose.

(Jaimini 4.3.19) In the case of an optional rite (*kāmya-karman*), heaven is the constant result, just as in the case of a rite-constituent (*yajñāṅga*), it serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). (Jaimini 4.3.20)

And when the cause has ceased, [the result follows] by necessity. (Jaimini 4.3.21) Or rather, it is desire that is enjoined through its connection with that. (Jaimini 4.3.22) In the case of the subsidiaries, there is praise because they exist for the sake of another. (Jaimini 4.3.23)
And when [the desire has] ceased, there is a restriction for that purpose.

(Jaimini 4.3.24) It is desired by all because of the desires for the subsidiaries, due to the context. (Jaimini 4.3.25) Or rather, it is the instruction of the fruit, because of its connection with the word denoting the primary act. (Jaimini 4.3.26)
In that case, all [are included] because there is no distinction (Jaimini Sūtra 4.3.27).
Or rather, there is the accomplishment through connection, because the purpose is not connected with the origin (Jaimini Sūtra 4.3.28).
Because, in the case of a combination, the connection with the injunction is purposeful (Jaimini Sūtra 4.3.29).
If it is argued that "time" [is the subject] because it is heard in connection with time, [we reply:
No, because it does not connect with the purpose.
If it is argued that it serves both purposes, [we reply: No. Jaimini Sūtra 4.3.30–32.
Not so, because of the unity of the word.
(Jaimini 4.3.33) If it is argued that it is due to the context, (Jaimini 4.3.34) we say no, because of the connection with the originative injunction. (Jaimini 4.3.35)

But in the case of non-origination, there would be a time [for the rite], because of its connection with a purpose (Jaimini Sūtra 4.3.36). Regarding the doubt as to whether it is a time for origination, it would indeed be a time, because the sentence has that as its primary focus (Jaimini Sūtra 4.3.37). However, if it were not enjoined, there would be no connection with the fruit, because it would not be an integral part of the whole (Jaimini Sūtra 4.3.38).

The connection with the impairment of the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) is for the purpose of providing a causal occasion (*nimitta*). (Jaimini 4.3.39) Because they are connected with the primary act (*pradhāna*), the auxiliary parts share the same time as the principal. (Jaimini 4.3.40) But when [the primary] has been completed, the injunction [for the auxiliaries] should apply at its own proper time, because it shares that commonality. (Jaimini 4.3.41)
And in the absence of a specific context, both [alternatives] would indeed be contradictory; JaiS 4.4.1.
Or rather, they should be subsidiary acts not involving sacrifice, because of that distinction; JaiS 4.4.2.
That which stands in the middle belongs to that [which is in the middle]; JaiS 4.4.3.

Or rather, because all [the offerings] are equal, it should be [understood] from the injunction; for its context is not stated for the purpose of indicating location in the middle. (Jaimini 4.4.4) And since there is no division of the context, both [options] would be contradictory. (Jaimini 4.4.5) Or rather, it should be merely a matter of time, because no specific distinction is observed. (Jaimini 4.4.6)

Because the stated reason possesses a result, the other [the *dadhi-graha*] would be primary. (Jaimini 4.4.7) The *dadhi-graha* is occasional (*naimittika*), because of its connection with a scriptural injunction. (Jaimini 4.4.8) And it is constant (*nitya*), because of the word "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*). (Jaimini 4.4.9)
And because it possesses all forms [Jaimini 4.4.10].
Or rather, it should be a permanent explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), because those two have no connection with the ritual action and because an interruption is transitory [Jaimini 4.4.11].
And the Vaiśvānara [offering] should be permanent, because its number is equal to that of the permanent [offerings] [Jaimini 4.4.12].
Or rather, [the sixfold altar is established] because of the connection with what has already arisen; Jaimini 4.4.13.
The sixfold altar is so called because it follows the previous [pattern]; Jaimini 4.4.14.
And because it is enumerated as having the same number as those [six layers]; Jaimini 4.4.15.
And because the explanatory passage (arthavāda) is thus rendered logical; Jaimini 4.4.16.
Or rather, there should be a single layer (ekaciti), for it is enjoined by a specific occasion once [the others] have been excluded; Jaimini 4.4.17.
Due to the contradiction, there is equality of number with them; Jaimini 4.4.18.
The ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña) should not be a subordinate part [of the New Moon sacrifice] because it has its own specific time;
likewise, because it is enumerated as being equal [to the other parts];
and because it is seen [as such] even when [the main sacrifice] is prohibited. (Jaimini 4.4.19–21)
The rope (*raśanā*) should be an accessory of the animal, because its injunction occurs upon the arrival of that [animal] (Jaimini Sūtra 4.4.22).

Or rather, it is an accessory of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), because it serves as a consecratory act for it (Jaimini Sūtra 4.4.23). And the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is meaningful in that sense (Jaimini Sūtra 4.4.24).
And the *svaru* [is part of the animal] because it is a single constituent; Jaimini 4.4.25.
And its purchase is like that of its subsidiary parts; Jaimini 4.4.26.
Or rather, it is a part of the animal because it serves a purposeful ritual function; Jaimini 4.4.27.
The statement regarding a ransom-offering would be based on devotion.
(Jaimini 4.4.28) In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, all the offerings are primary because there is no distinction.
(Jaimini 4.4.29) Or rather, some are subsidiary parts, for they are praised as being such; indeed, the praise is general. (Jaimini 4.4.30)
And likewise, there is the observation of another purpose [Jaimini Sūtra 4.4.31].
But the remaining reason is because the subordinate element exists within the primary elements [Jaimini Sūtra 4.4.32].
There is no observation of another purpose when it has not been stated, because it is for the sake of another [Jaimini Sūtra 4.4.33].

The application of the two designations [of the primary and the subsidiary] occurs according to their distinctness, based on direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and formal designation (*vyapadeśa*). Furthermore, that which possesses fruitfulness is the primary [act];

in its proximity, that which is not otherwise connected should be a subsidiary (*aṅga*), because it shares in the cause and because no connection with another is heard. (Jaimini 4.4.34) And qualities (*guṇa*) are enjoined in connection with names; they do not apply to the subsidiaries. (Jaimini 4.4.35)
The scriptural mention of the cause is equal [to other cases], and there is a relationship between the subsidiary and the principal.

(Jaimini 4.4.36) Since the connection exists at the time of origination, there should therefore be an instruction regarding the subsidiaries. (Jaimini 4.4.37) And likewise, there is the observation of another purpose. (Jaimini 4.4.38)

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the [elements] are equal, for the cause is undifferentiated. (Jaimini 4.4.39) But because the qualities are connected with the originative injunction, there is a scriptural statement of the cause; therefore, Soma should be the primary element. (Jaimini 4.4.40) And likewise, there is the observation of another purpose. (Jaimini 4.4.41)
The sequence is characterized by direct Vedic statement (śruti), because that is its authority; Jaimini 5.1.1.
And it is also [determined] by the sense (artha); Jaimini 5.1.2.
In other cases, there is no fixed rule (aniyama); Jaimini 5.1.3.
Or rather, it should be restricted according to the sequence, because when there is unity of the sacrifice, that [sequence] is subordinate to it.
(Jaimini 5.1.4) If it is argued that this is not based on the Vedic word, [we reply] that it would indeed be so, because the word "sentence" (*vākya*) is used here.

(Jaimini 5.1.5) Or rather, there would be an inference based on the purpose, since when there is unity of the sacrifice, [the sequence] serves another's purpose; however, its connection is with its own specific meaning, and therefore it is expressed by its own term. (Jaimini 5.1.6)
And likewise, there is the observation of another purpose:
"Because of the commencement of those qualities that are simultaneous with the activity.
[Objection: "If it is argued that everything [is thus]. Jaimini 5.1.8–9.

[The opponent argues: "No, because it has not been performed; [it would be] like another sacrifice," [Jaimini 5.1.10]. [The author replies: "No, because of the lack of connection," [Jaimini 5.1.11]. [The opponent argues again: "Because of the lack of inherent connection," [Jaimini 5.1.12].

And because of the connection with their place of origin; or rather, by the order of the principal acts, since the subsidiaries are for the sake of those [principals]. But in the archetype, because of the explicit scriptural statement, the sequence should be understood according to its own [textual] order.
But in case of a conflict, it should be according to the mantra, because of the capacity of its form in the performance; therefore, that is the place of origin.

(Jaimini 5.1.16) Because of that statement, in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), it should be as in the primary (pradhāna). (Jaimini 5.1.17) Or, in case of disagreement, because of the connection with the archetype (prakṛti), it should be as in the archetype. (Jaimini 5.1.18)
Jaimini 5.1.19: "The modification (vikṛti) should take place at that same time [as the archetype], because it possesses the nature of the archetype, just as is taught by the learned.

Jaimini 5.1.20: "Or rather, being connected with a specific sequence and time, it should be performed immediately; in that case, there would be an omission of the archetypal characteristics due to the inference of a different injunction. Jaimini 5.1.21: "If it is argued that there is a displacement of the time [of the performance]."
Not so, because of the connection [with the principal].

(Jaimini 5.1.22) Since the subsidiaries have the same time as the principal, there would be a displacement (utkarṣa) as previously stated. (Jaimini 5.1.23) Or rather, because of the connection starting from that [point], there would be a displacement downward (apakarṣa) ending at that point. (Jaimini 5.1.24)
For those whose time is determined by the sequence of performance;
and because of the contradiction with the scriptural word.
But because there is no connection, the modified [rite] itself would be drawn forward.

And one should not postpone that which is incidental, because there is no connection [with the primary rite]; likewise for what is unprecedented (apūrva). However, the Sāntapanīyā [offering] should postpone the Agnihotra, just like the Savana [offerings], because otherwise there would be a deficiency (vaiguṇya).
And because of the mention of another [deity], Jaimini [says] 5.1.31; but one should not transfer [the rite] because of the lack of connection, Jaimini [says] 5.1.32;
and because of the occurrence of the occasion [for the rite], Jaimini [says] 5.1.33.
The *savana* is a principal act because of its connection [with the sacrifice]; Jaimini 5.1.34.
And the *ṣoḍaśī* [cup] is so because of its conjunction with the *ukthya*; Jaimini 5.1.35.
When there is a simultaneous occurrence, the subsidiary acts should be performed for each of the principal acts individually; Jaimini 5.2.1.
For all [acts], there is a single performance because they have been arranged in a fixed sequence (Jaimini 5.2.2).
Repetition occurs for a specific reason (Jaimini 5.2.3).
And in the cases of the handfuls, the potsherds, the cuttings, the collyrium, the anointing, the shaving, and the purifying, it is done by one person (Jaimini 5.2.4).

But all [the acts] have a single purpose because they possess that quality [of being subordinate to the main act]. (Jaimini 5.2.5) However, when [an act] is connected [to the main act], it should be a subsidiary part of that [main act] due to the commencement [of the procedure], because the other [acts] are for the sake of that [main act]. (Jaimini 5.2.6) But by virtue of the explicit scriptural statement, the acts beginning with anointing (*añjana*) should extend up to the encircling (*parivyāṇa*). (Jaimini 5.2.7)
Or rather, there would be an increase [of the sacrificial vessels] because of the cause,

just as there is an increase of the vessels; [but] it is not so, because it is brought about by the scriptural word, whereas the other [increase] is merely logical and results from the purpose, as in the case of the increase of the vessels.
In the case of a herd of animals, one should perform the ritual for each individual animal because the animal is a single unit (Jaimini 5.2.10);
because there is a unity of action with the deities (Jaimini 5.2.11);
and because the mantra must be meaningful (Jaimini 5.2.12).
Jaimini 5.2.13: There should be one mortar for various seeds because of its capacity [to handle them all].
Jaimini 5.2.14: Or rather, there should be an increase [in the number of mortars], because of the restriction on the sequence, since that sequence serves that purpose.
Jaimini 5.2.15: Or rather, there should be only one [mortar], because of the state of being rice-grains, since the act of threshing is for that purpose.

In the case of a modification, however, there should be a separation of vessels for the *anūyāja* offerings because of the difference in purpose. (Jaimini 5.2.16) Since the archetype has already been previously mentioned, the new element should occur at the end; for there is no mention of a remnant for that which has not been enjoined. (Jaimini 5.2.17) Ātreya [holds] that it follows immediately after the principal [offering], because it shares the same scriptural status; since there is no scriptural authority for the archetypal elements, there would be an interruption. (Jaimini 5.2.18)

But Bādarāyaṇa holds that they [belong] to the former, because those [terms] are the primary words for them; likewise, there is a scriptural indication of another purpose. However, because their place has already been established, that place should belong to the former ones; therefore, due to the direct connection with the place, the other is merely a figurative application.
And whatever [is mentioned] prior to the subject at hand;
if there is a conjunction, it should be as stated at the end.
There is an increase due to the distinction of the rites, just like the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya), which would be prescribed for each respective [rite].
Alternatively, because they are all enumerated together, they should be understood as a modification [of the original number].
However, they should increase from their own respective positions because their sequence has already been established.
The *dhāyyā* verses should be inserted between the *samidhyamānavatī* and the *samiddhavatī* verses, for it is appropriate that they occupy the space between heaven and earth.

Or rather, the word "that" [refers to the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* verses], because they are seen at the end of the *uṣṇih-kakubh* [chant]. (Jaimini 5.3.5) When there is an increase in the *stoma*, the additional verses (*āgantu*) should be inserted before the *paryāsa* in the *vahiṣpavamāna*, for it is so observed in the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice. (Jaimini 5.3.6–7)

And the term "paryāsa" is a designation for the end; or rather, it is so called because it occurs at the end. However, in the case of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), it is so by virtue of a specific scriptural statement.
And it is not a modification of that [Jaimini 5.3.11]. Even when there is a modification of that, because it is an unprecedented [rule] (apūrva) [Jaimini 5.3.12].
But at the end, one should place [the offering] for the two subsequent [deities] [Jaimini 5.3.13].

Or rather, by virtue of the explicit statement, [the *graha-iṣṭaka*] should pertain to the *gāyatrī*, *bṛhatī*, and *anuṣṭubh* meters; the section concerning the bricks (*aupānuvākya*) would be a subsidiary part of the *savana* and the *citi*. Or rather, they are subsidiaries of the sacrifice and the fire-altar because they are specifically enjoined, whereas there is no injunction for the sequential order.
They should be at the beginning because there is no intervention;
and because of the observation of an indicative mark (Jaimini 5.3.17).
But they belong to the middle [offering] because of a direct statement, as in the case of the Brāhmaṇavatī [verses] (Jaimini 5.3.19).

Prior to the *lokaṃpṛṇā* [brick], because it is for the purpose of completing that [altar]; Jaimini 5.3.20. The ritual action is performed upon the consecrated [object], because the consecrations are for its sake; Jaimini 5.3.21. Immediately after [the consecration] comes the vow, because it has become that [state]; Jaimini 5.3.22.
And because there is a prior observation of an indicative mark (Jaimini 5.3.23);
or rather, it is an explanatory supplement (arthavāda) because the matter already exists (Jaimini 5.3.24);
and because of the contradiction with logical principle (nyāya) (Jaimini 5.3.25).
However, for one who has piled the fire-altar (*agni-cit*), it is appropriate [to perform the rite] because the occasion (*nimitta*) has been reached; (Jaimini 5.3.26).
Or rather, [it should be performed] at the conclusion of the sacrifice (*kratu*), because there is no statement regarding its performance [at that time]; (Jaimini 5.3.27).
Because the fire-altar (*agni*) is designated as the object (*karman*) [of the action]. (Jaimini 5.3.28).
One becomes initiated (dīkṣita) through the announcement made by another, because the initiation is connected with all [the officiants];
or rather, it occurs at the end of the *iṣṭi*, for that is its purpose, since it is connected with a general purpose. And the designation (*samākhyāna*) is likewise.
The sequence of sacrifices is like that of the constituent parts [of a sacrifice], according to Jaimini 5.3.32;
or rather it is not so, because there is no connection [between them], according to Jaimini 5.3.33;
and also because they are performed for the sake of specific desires, according to Jaimini 5.3.34.
If it is argued that [the rite] is not [for the sake of knowledge] because it would be purposeless, [we reply:
it may indeed be for the sake of knowledge, as in the case of others [such as the *sarvasvāra* sacrifice], according to Jaimini 5.3.36.
[Furthermore,] by the phrase "he who with this," the *agniṣṭoma* is [indicated] due to the context, according to Jaimini 5.3.37.
And because of the indicative mark (liṅga). Jaimini 5.3.38.
Or rather, "by another" [is meant] because of the proximity of the *saṃsthās*. Jaimini 5.3.39.
Or, because of that original form (*prakṛti*), the occurrence and modification (*apattivihārau*) are not possible among equals. Jaimini 5.3.40.
And it is a praise because there is no other way to perform [the rite];
or rather, it is due to the presence of an injunctive suffix, for a praise would not occur without cause. Or it refers to the single-stoma [rite], because of its connection with the sacrifice.

Or rather, because of the specific injunction, there is praise for all the *stomas*. (Jaimini 5.3.44) The sequence is determined by both the meaning and the words, due to a specific scriptural statement and because the purpose is primary. (Jaimini 5.4.1) In the acts of cutting portions (*avadāna*), sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*), and placing (*āsādana*), the order should follow the sequence of performance. (Jaimini 5.4.2)
Or rather, it is the giving of the *yathārha* (as is fitting), because that is its purpose;
and because of the observation of indicative marks;
and because of the scriptural statement, the *iṣṭi* comes first.

And for some, Soma [is the subsequent rite] because of the statement regarding the transgression of the season and the lunar mansion for the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya); for otherwise, that [statement] would be meaningless at its conclusion.

(Jaimini 5.4.6) And because of the statement of its purpose, it does not have that [purpose] by virtue of being non-specific. (Jaimini 5.4.7) Furthermore, since there is a specification of time for the Pavamāna oblations for one who is not intending to sacrifice, a doubt might arise regarding their immediate succession. (Jaimini 5.4.8)
The *iṣṭi* belongs to one who is not intending to perform the Soma sacrifice; therefore, there is no requirement for the Soma sacrifice to precede it.

(Jaimini 5.4.9) Because of its displacement, the Soma sacrifice should belong to the Brāhmaṇa. (Jaimini 5.4.10) Or rather, it should be the Full Moon sacrifice, because of its connection with the scriptural injunction. (Jaimini 5.4.11)
"Or rather, because everything has a single function, there should be an injunction for that purpose. "But on account of the context, it should be a time."

It should take place at its own time, because there is no prohibition [to that effect]. (Jaimini 5.4.15) Or rather, there is a displacement of the *āghāra* libation, because it may be performed at any time. (Jaimini 5.4.16) For a Brāhmaṇa, it occurs after the *Soma* sacrifice on the full moon day, according to the scriptural statement. (Jaimini 5.4.17)
Either one [offering] is prescribed first by the force of the word; Jaimini 5.4.18.
But the cake (puroḍāśa) [is prescribed] when there is no specific mention, because in that case there is no deity associated with it; Jaimini 5.4.19.
"The clarified butter (ājya) also [is prescribed]," if this is argued; Jaimini 5.4.20.

It is not [the case that the sacrifice belongs] to mixed deities, as in the case of the offering to Indra and Agni (aindrāgna), because the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) follows the time of the archetype (prakṛti); therefore, the subsequent modified sacrifice is of the same-day performance (sadyaskāla), since its timing is directly enjoined for both. However, in the case of a two-day performance, it is according to the rule.
From the scriptural statement, there would be simultaneity.

(Jaimini 5.4.24) The modifications of the *sannāyya* and the *agnīṣomīya* [offerings] occur after the *soma* sacrifice, just like the archetype. (Jaimini 5.4.25) Likewise, the modifications of the *soma* sacrifice [occur] after the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. (Jaimini 5.4.26)

When substances are connected with an action, they are related to it as subordinate factors (guṇa). (Jaimini 6.1.1) But [the substance] is not the means of accomplishment because it exists for the sake of that [action]. (Jaimini 6.1.2) And because there is a connection with each respective object, the relationship is indeed through the action; therefore, there should be an instruction regarding the action. (Jaimini 6.1.3)

Since action is for the sake of a result, the scripture must apply to all qualified persons. (Jaimini 6.1.4) Or rather, because of the connection with the Vedic text, the injunction is understood to apply to the agent in its entirety.
(Jaimini 6.1.5) Aitishayana [holds] that it is connected only to males, because of the mention of a specific gender. (Jaimini 6.1.6)
And because it is stated as such, the mention of a fault applies when [the person] is not understood [as being of that class].

(Jaimini 6.1.7) But Bādarāyaṇa holds that it refers to the genus, because there is no distinction; therefore, a woman also should be understood [as eligible], since the meaning of the genus is not different. (Jaimini 6.1.8) Because she is enjoined, it should be according to the scriptural text. (Jaimini 6.1.9)

But because men possess property, they should have that which is connected with property through buying and selling; women, however, lack property, because they share a common status with property itself. (Jaimini 6.1.10) And likewise, there is a scriptural observation to this effect. (Jaimini 6.1.11) Because it is for that purpose, the ritual act is for that purpose. (Jaimini 6.1.12)
But because there is no distinction in the enthusiasm for the fruit [of the action],
and because it is connected with the purpose,
the purchase is merely a ritual duty.
He also shows that they possess their own [means]:
"But because of the statement regarding those who possess [their own means], there should be a single performance;
and because of the observation of an indicative mark. (Jaimini Sūtra 6.1.16–18)
"But because he has been purchased, his status as owner is spoken of figuratively" (Jaimini 6.1.19).
"But because of the desire for the fruit, there is a connection [to the rite] by way of ownership" (Jaimini 6.1.20).
"And it shows that he possesses the fruit" (Jaimini 6.1.21).
And there is a dual establishment [of the fires], as in the case of the two sacrifices;

however, because it is an injunction of an accessory, the word "second" (*dvitīya*) refers to the wife. For her, there is only that which is prescribed: the blessing and the state of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), because of the inequality [between the husband and wife].
The four castes [are entitled] because there is no distinction.

Or rather, on account of the specific mention, it should belong to the three [higher castes]; there would be no connection for the *āhitāgni* (one who has established the sacred fires) with the sacrifices, because the *Brāhmaṇa* is heard [as the subject], so says Ātreya. Bādari, however, holds that it is for the sake of a cause; therefore, there should be entitlement for all.
Or rather, because of the observation of another purpose, it should be understood according to the scriptural text. (Jaimini 6.1.28) But because of the specific direction, it would apply optionally.
(Jaimini 6.1.29) If it is argued that it is not so because of a deficiency [in the ritual], (Jaimini 6.1.30)
Not so, because it is optional (Jaimini 6.1.31);
and because in the case of a purificatory rite, that [the person] is the primary factor (Jaimini 6.1.32).
Or rather, because of the mention of the Veda, it should be understood as applying to those other than Śūdras (Jaimini 6.1.33).
If it is argued that [the person] is not [the object of the injunction] because of the desire for qualities (guṇārthitva), [we reply:

No, because the refinement (saṃskāra) is for that purpose; the mention of the "person" (puruṣa-śruti) occurs in relation to knowledge (vidyā). If it is argued that [the person is not the object] because of the specific designation of knowledge (vidyā-nirdeśāt), [we reply: No. Jaimini 6.1.34–36.
Due to a lack of knowledge, there would be an absence of qualification for the ritual action (Jaimini 6.1.37).
Likewise, there is a scriptural indication to that effect (Jaimini 6.1.38).
Among the three [types of persons], only one who possesses the requisite substance is qualified for the ritual action, because the action is accomplished through the substance (Jaimini 6.1.39).

But because of impermanence, it would not be so; for the connection with the substance follows from the purpose [of the rite]. (Jaimini 6.1.40) And one who is deficient in limbs possesses that same status, because of the permanent connection at the time of birth. (Jaimini 6.1.41) Because of the permanent connection at the time of origination. (Jaimini 6.1.42)
There would be the exclusion of one who lacks a lineage of seers (Atryārṣeya) [from the *ādhāna*],

because of the scriptural statement regarding the *rathakāra*’s *ādhāna*, since that [statement] is subsidiary to all [the rules]. Or rather, it is proper [to include him] because of his connection with the ritual act, since the *śūdra* is prohibited [from such acts].
But because it is not an action, this would not be so (Jaimini 6.1.46). And there would be purposelessness due to the connection (Jaimini 6.1.47).
If it is argued that it is for the sake of a subordinate element (guṇa) (Jaimini 6.1.48).

The state of being without a specific mark has been stated. (Jaimini Sūtra 6.1.49) But the Saudhanvanas should be understood [as the performers] because of their inferiority and because of the wording of the mantra. (Jaimini Sūtra 6.1.50) The chariot-lord should be a Niṣāda, due to the force of the word. (Jaimini Sūtra 6.1.51)
And because of the observation of indicative marks (liṅga). Jaimini 6.1.52.

Because the accomplishment of the human goal is one, there should be the entitlement for each [individual]. Jaimini 6.2.1. Moreover, just as there is a connection with the origin [of the rite], such as the eating of food by the Sattrins, so too would there be a division [of the fruit] in the case of its distribution. Jaimini 6.2.2.

Because the word "person" (puruṣa) is heard in connection with the performance [of the rite], one may act according to one's desire regarding the performance. (Jaimini 6.2.3) If it is argued that the word is used for each individual purpose, (Jaimini 6.2.4) [we reply:
there is no status as a subordinate factor (guṇa) because the person exists for the sake of that [rite]; since no other purpose is stated, the agent is the primary element. (Jaimini 6.2.5)

Or rather, in connection with a desire, [the mantra] should be taught for the sake of performance because of its syntactical relation; for the scriptural injunction is directed toward each specific purpose, as in the case of the "horn.
If it is argued that it might belong to something else, [we reply:
there is a connection with another purpose. Jaimini 6.2.6–8.
If it is argued that the sign is for the sake of a result,
[we reply] no, because of its obligatory nature. If it is argued that the ritual act is likewise [for the sake of a result], [we reply] no.
Not because of inherence (Jaimini 6.2.12).
Rather, it should be restricted by the context, because the commencement is the cause for the performance (Jaimini 6.2.13).
Or, there is no restriction because of the desire for the fruit, as in the case of what has not been commenced (Jaimini 6.2.14).

Or rather, because it is caused by that [knowledge], the restriction would be the cause of the agent’s action. (Jaimini 6.2.15) In the world, actions are like those in the Veda; from that arises knowledge concerning persons. (Jaimini 6.2.16) And even in the case of a transgression, there is instruction by means of them. (Jaimini 6.2.17)

But attainment [of the result] occurs through what is not the scripture; the scripture would not be the originator [of the action]. Therefore, since it is not otherwise obtained, the scripture must be understood by means of its purpose; thus, when there is no prior attainment, the scripture is meaningful. (Jaimini 6.2.18) In prohibitions, because they are not actions [in themselves], there must be an action [as the object of negation], since prohibited things are distinct from non-actions.
(Jaimini 6.2.19) However, because the scriptures possess meaning, the human goal is enjoined; for those two [the scripture and the human goal], [the former serves the latter]. (Jaimini 6.2.20)

Because it is not an inherent constituent, there is a transgression of the injunction regarding its purpose (Jaimini 6.2.20). But in that case, the [rites] being taught would proceed by way of production (Jaimini 6.2.21).
Or rather, because they are equal to the Veda, they would proceed by way of means (upāya) (Jaimini 6.2.22).

Practice is enjoined as a human goal because it is not a subsidiary part of the ritual action; since that [human goal] is impossible [to achieve] through that [practice], it follows from the sense of the text that [the times] are not taught for the sake of time. Jaimini 6.2.23–25.

The determination of time is based on the observation of the signs of time. (Jaimini 6.2.26) Since these [signs] are innate, one should proceed by means of traditional scripture (āgama). (Jaimini 6.2.27) For there is indeed the observation of such signs. (Jaimini 6.2.28)

Likewise, those acts enjoined for the internal sacrifice [should be performed]; when they are being observed according to traditional practice (*ācāra*), it should be so because they serve the purpose of the person. However, for the Brāhmaṇa, there is the obligation regarding Soma, Vedic study, and progeny, because of their connection with the statement concerning debts (*ṛṇavākya*).

The performance [of the entire ritual] would apply to one who possesses all the capacities, because the instruction is of that nature. Or rather, it may apply even to one who possesses only a portion [of the capacities], for the accomplishment of the purpose resides in the principal act; the rest is merely an auxiliary, as it exists for the sake of that principal. Furthermore, there is a fault in the non-performance of that [auxiliary]; therefore, there should be a distinction based on that, due to its connection with the principal.

Jaimini, however, maintains that there is no difference in the ritual action, because the injunction for performance is one; thus, there should be instruction for all [the subsidiaries]. (Jaim_6.3.4) Because the purpose is distinct, it may occur even when only one [subsidiary] is performed, as in the case of other sacrifices. (Jaim_6.3.5) And because we observe the completion [of the rite] even when there is a transgression of the rule. (Jaim_6.3.6)
And because of the prescription of expiatory rites (Jaimini 6.3.7);
and likewise in the case of optional rites, because of the presence of desire (Jaimini 6.3.8).
But this would not be so in the case of [the obligatory], because of the lack of connection; for the injunction has the Vedic word as its sole authority (Jaimini 6.3.9).
And because there is no transgression in the non-performance [of the action], [the sacrifice is not established by the name].
(Jaimini 6.3.10) Since actions depend [on substances], there would be a distinction [between them] when the substance is different.

(Jaimini 6.3.11) Or rather, because there is no difference and because the form and the word are inseparable, there should be a single action, like the universal "cowness" (*gotva*); and the name [of the sacrifice] should be like a substance. (Jaimini 6.3.12)

Because the Veda is the authoritative means of knowledge, there is no transmission of [the ritual] from one who is not cultured, since such a person lacks the status of being cultured; Jaimini 6.3.13.
And because it is prescribed in certain cases; Jaimini 6.3.14.
Or rather, there is transmission, because there is no difference in the purpose of the injunction; Jaimini 6.3.15.

In some cases, an injunction serves a restrictive purpose; for that [act] is constant, as it is the desire to perform it. The deity, the fire, the word, and the action are not [restricted], because they are connected with another purpose.
And because the deity exists for that purpose [Jaimini 6.3.19];
and because it is prohibited without distinction, for there is a scriptural statement to that effect [Jaimini 6.3.20];
likewise, because the fruit accrues to the owner, since the fruit is connected with the ritual action [Jaimini 6.3.21].
But when many [priests] are engaged, one may bring another, because there is no deficiency [in the rite].
(Jaimini 6.3.22) He would be the owner [of the fee], because of the connection [with the sacrifice]. (Jaimini 6.3.23) Or he is merely a laborer, because he is paid. (Jaimini 6.3.24)
And because the fruit is seen in that [context]; Jai. 6.3.25.
That [person] would possess those properties because of the connection with the ritual action; Jai. 6.3.26.
For there is a desire to perform that which is common; Jai. 6.3.27.
"But since it proceeds from an explanatory statement regarding an option, [it is] non-scriptural," if this is argued;
[the reply is: "No, because it is not a subordinate element. Jaimini 6.3.28–30.
And because of the scriptural statement, it is improper [to substitute] in the case of absence; there is a substitute for that [original] by virtue of its similarity, since the other is absent.

(Jaimini 6.3.31) There is no substitute, because of equality. (Jaimini 6.3.32) It may exist in the case of what is characterized by direct Vedic statement, because of its fixed nature. (Jaimini 6.3.33)

For there is no desire for that [substitute], because when the primary is obtained, the primary is used; for the scriptural injunction applies to that [primary] alone, as it is absent [in the case of the substitute].
If it is argued that [the rule applies] even when [the rite] has already commenced: Jaimini 6.3.36.
Not so, because it would be purposeless.
(Jaimini 6.3.37) In a conflict between a substance and a refinement, the substance prevails, because the refinement is for the sake of that substance.

(Jaimini 6.3.38) In a conflict between the purpose and the substance, the purpose prevails; because when the substance is absent, the purpose arises [through a substitute], since substances are subordinate to the purpose. (Jaimini 6.3.39)

The injunction might also apply to a single part [of the substance]. Or rather, because the purpose can be accomplished by means of a single part, the rite may be completed with that part alone; for purposes are indivisible, and the other [parts] are merely subordinate qualities since they exist for the sake of that purpose.
In the event of the loss of the two portions [of the offering], the rite should proceed from what remains, because that which remains serves the same purpose.
Or rather, one should understand it as something else because of the specific instruction (Jaimini 6.4.2).
Or rather, it should belong to those who partake in the remnants, because of a specific cause (Jaimini 6.4.3).
Because of the specific instruction, the consumption of the remnants is performed by others, just like the primary offerings (Jaimini 6.4.4).

Or rather, it should apply to all because of their collective association (Jaimini 6.4.5). The specific mention is for the purpose of indicating a subordinate quality (guṇa) (Jaimini 6.4.6). In the case of the primary element, there is the characteristic of direct scriptural statement (śruti) (Jaimini 6.4.7).

If it is argued that [the term] has a meaning, [we reply]: No, because it would contradict the injunction (codanā). Since the purpose is inherent [in the act], the expiation applies even when only a portion [of the substance] is affected.
But it does not apply when there is no deficiency [in the primary], because it is for that purpose; for it is for the sake of that [primary].

(Jaimini 6.4.11) Or rather, it should apply because its occasion has been reached; it is not a property of that [primary] because of its constant connection, for what is beneficial is not for the sake of a subordinate quality, as it would be non-eternal. (Jaimini 6.4.12) And because subordinate elements exist for the sake of another, there should be reliance on the explicit scriptural statement. (Jaimini 6.4.13)
"Regarding the phrase 'for the sake of distinction' (Jaim_6.4.14):
[it is] not so, because it is a subordinate element (Jaim_6.4.15);
furthermore, it would be purposeless if there were a total destruction [of the substance] (Jaim_6.4.16)."
But in the case of emaciation, there would be a total burning [of the offering], because it is impossible to avoid [the burning] of even a single part.

(Jaimini 6.4.17) It should occur in a single part, because such is seen [in the texts]. (Jaimini 6.4.18) Or rather, it should be by means of another [substance], for the application of the cause is established by the scriptural injunction. (Jaimini 6.4.19)

If it is argued that [the term *havis*] does not apply because of the word *havis*, [we reply: it should apply, because it is improper [otherwise]; the word *havis* refers to the sacrifice (*ijyā*) due to its connection with its characteristic mark (*liṅga*). If it is argued that it must be according to the literal scriptural statement (*yathāśruti*), [we reply: no.
It is not so, because that is its characteristic; for the descent [into the womb] is the cause. (Jaimini 6.4.23) And likewise, the offering, the pressing, and the consuming [are causes].
(Jaimini 6.4.24) Or rather, it is by both [the father and the mother], for there is no scriptural injunction regarding those two. (Jaimini 6.4.25)
It should be re-established like cooked rice (odana), according to Jaimini 6.4.26;
or it may pertain to both because of the production of the substance, according to Jaimini 6.4.27;
however, the five-platter offering (pañcaśarāva) should be a substitute because of the scriptural mention of the substance, according to Jaimini 6.4.28.
Or rather, it is an injunction (*codanā*) regarding the substance and the deity, for [the original] is inexpressible; Jaimini 6.4.29.
That [injunction] would be repeated because of the position [of the original]; Jaimini 6.4.30.
Or rather, it is an injunction of a subsidiary (*aṅga*), because of its connection with a specific occasion (*nimitta*); Jaimini 6.4.31.
In the Viśvajit sacrifice, when it has not commenced, there would be the performance of the ritual act;
[this is so] because of the statement regarding its redemption.
And in connection with the calf, there would be an injunction for the vow.
Or rather, it is time [that is indicated], because of its connection with what has arisen, as previously stated (Jaimini 6.4.35);
and because of the lack of a fixed measure of the purpose (Jaimini 6.4.36).
But the calf, because of its connection with the direct Vedic statement, should be a subordinate part of that [rite] (Jaimini 6.4.37).
But it would be [a matter of] time, because there is no injunction;
and it would be purposeless when connected with the ritual act;
and because there is no mention of its own word. (Jaimini 6.4.38–40)
If it is time, then [the rule] applies to the *sannayya* group because of the connection with its characteristic mark (Jaimini 6.4.41); or rather,
because it serves the purpose of indicating time, it would apply to both,
just as the branch is supported upon the sacrificial grass-bundle (prastara) (Jaimini 6.4.42–43).
Or rather, it is a rule regarding time, because both [the fire and the sacrifice] exist;
and because it does not have the purpose of consecrating that [fire];
and therefore it would apply even in their separation. (Jaimini 6.4.44–46)

And the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick) would be optional according to one view. (Jaimini 6.4.47) In the case of the *abhyudaya* (transference of oblations), there should be an injunction for a sacrifice due to the lapse of the proper time, as in the case of the five-platter offering.
(Jaimini 6.5.1) Or rather, it is a removal [of the original offering], because of the difference in the nature of the knowledge. (Jaimini 6.5.2)
And because words have that nature;
because the repeated practice of curdling is observed;
and because it is something not previously established, there must be an injunction.
"Because of the defect in the milk, the other [rice] in the five-plate offering is not defective.

(Jaimini 6.5.6) "If it is argued that the *sānnāyya* offering is likewise [not defective]," (Jaimini 6.5.7) "No, because that [milk] is not defective; for the cause [of the offering's status] is not different. (Jaimini 6.5.8)
The scriptural mention [of the deities] is for the purpose of indicating their characteristics.

(Jaimini 6.5.9) In the *upāṃśuyāja*, because there is no specific statement, it is according to the archetype. (Jaimini 6.5.10) Or rather, there is a displacement [of the deities] due to the application [of the procedure], as in the case of the others. (Jaimini 6.5.11)
It should take place when [the rice] has been poured out, because of its connection with that;
or rather, when [the rite] has commenced, because the occasion for it has arrived;
the other [statement] is merely a defining characteristic. (Jaimini 6.5.12–14)
And likewise, there is the observation of another scriptural fact:

*Jaim_6.5.15* "When the moon has risen while the oblation has not yet been poured out, one should pour it out for the original deities," so says Āśmarathya, because of the removal [of the deities] once the rice grains have been prepared.
*Jaim_6.5.16* But Ālekhana says it should be for those entitled to the subsequent portions, because the removal of the deities is caused by that [rising of the moon]. *Jaim_6.5.17*
When [the grain] has been poured out, there is no removal of the handfuls, because they have become subordinate to that [act].
(Jaimini 6.5.18) For there is a connection with what is non-archetypal, because it occupies its place. (Jaimini 6.5.19) And it would be so because of the absence of the other. (Jaimini 6.5.20)
On account of the connection with the *sānnāyya*, it should not belong to one who has not performed the *sānnāyya* sacrifice; Jai. 6.5.21.
Or rather, on account of the connection with the vegetable offering (*auṣadha*), it belongs to both; Jai. 6.5.22.
If it is argued that this is not so because of a deficiency [in the ritual]; Jai. 6.5.23.
Not so, because it is not a refinement of that [sacrifice].

(Jaimini 6.5.24) In the case of rising together, the Viśvajit occurs when the purchase has been made, because of the connection with distribution. (Jaimini 6.5.25) Or rather, it occurs when the rite has commenced, because the occasion for it has arrived. (Jaimini 6.5.26)

The other scriptural statement is for the purpose of an injunction. (Jaimini 6.5.27) Regarding the duration of initiation, there is freedom of choice due to the absence of a specific rule. (Jaimini 6.5.28) However, it should be twelve days on account of an indicative mark. (Jaimini 6.5.29)

On the full moon day, there is no restriction because there is no specific distinction [stated]. (Jaimini 6.5.30) But it should be the Caitrī [full moon] due to immediate sequence. (Jaimini 6.5.31) Or rather, it is the Māghī [full moon] because of the scriptural mention of the Ekāṣṭakā. (Jaimini 6.5.32)
If it is argued that others [also] do so, [we reply]:
No, because this is figurative; for in common usage, [the term is used] thus. Also because of the favor shown when there is a failure regarding the consecration (dīkṣā).
And because it grows up from what has been raised;
and in this [view], all the indicative marks [are consistent].
(Jaimini 6.5.36) Because the time for initiation has been prescribed, there is no postponement of the fixed rites when that time is exceeded, since their own proper time has arrived. (Jaimini 6.5.38)

Or rather, there is no distinction because of the state of being initiated; for the cause is the same. In that case, no compensatory oblation (*pratihoma*) exists, as was the case with the previous [sacrifices].
And this is because of the primacy of the time.
And because of the prohibition, [the sacrifice] is prescribed after the *avabhṛtha* bath; Jaimini 6.5.42.

If there is a *pratihoma*, the *agnihotra* and subsequent offerings should be performed in the evening; Jaimini 6.5.43. But in the case of the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice, they are performed in the morning; Jaimini 6.5.44.
The expiation applies to the entire scope [of the ritual], because the fault is common to all;
or rather, it applies to the specific context, because the word is the basis [for its application];
and furthermore, there is an extension beyond that.

If that which is unfit for the Aryas to eat has entered into water from something that has become putrid, that [impurity] should be understood [to apply]. (Jaimini 6.5.48) Since there is a scriptural injunction for partitioning, no expiation exists when [the impurities] occur simultaneously.
(Jaimini 6.5.49) Or rather, it should exist because the cause has been reached; [in such a case], there is only a single time [for the rite]. (Jaimini 6.5.50)

In that case, there would be an option due to the contradiction; or rather, there would be the acceptance of both in a different performance. And it is not so, because of the connection with a single [rite].

In a sequence of prior and subsequent [acts], the former is weaker, as in the case of the original nature. (Jaimini 6.5.54) If the Udgātṛ should be the last [to break the connection], one should give away all one's possessions (*sarvavedasa*) at the repeated sacrifice, just as in the other case. (Jaimini 6.5.55) In a multi-day sacrificial session (*ahargaṇa*), that day on which the disconnection occurs should be repeated, because the ritual acts are distinct. (Jaimini 6.5.56)
In the case of a combination [of defects], those of equal status should perform the sacrifice according to their natural capacity due to the deficiency; Jaimini 6.6.1.
Or rather, it should be like the Aśirā [offering] because of a specific scriptural statement; Jaimini 6.6.2.
Not so, because it is a general injunction not addressed to a specific context; Jaimini 6.6.3.

Or rather, it should be so because it serves the purpose of the sacrifice, like the *audumbarī* post; (Jaimini 6.6.4) no, because that [the post] is not the primary element; (Jaimini 6.6.5) since the *audumbarī* exists for the sake of another, like the potsherds. (Jaimini 6.6.6)
If it is argued that [the result] may be achieved by another [means], [we reply]:
No, because of its unity, because that [other person] lacks the qualification, and because the word [denoting the rite] is indivisible.

However, there would be an obstruction of the cause due to the conjunction [of factors], as in the case of the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans], since they are taught as distinct [alternatives] to be performed by Vasiṣṭha.

Alternatively, there would be no obstruction [to the performance] because of the connection with the whole, due to the relationship [of the two Sāmans] as owners. (Jaimini 6.6.10) In the case of the two Sāmans, since they are connected with a portion through the increase of the ritual action, there is a relationship as subordinate factors; therefore, in that case, there would be an obstruction. (Jaimini 6.6.11) But because of the scriptural statement, there is a dual connection; therefore, it belongs to one [singer], like the hand. (Jaimini 6.6.12)

But because there is no purpose [in that case], it could not be so. (Jaimini 6.6.13) And because the purposes are distinct, there is no connection with what is heard therein. (Jaimini 6.6.14) Because the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) exist as subordinate members of the body, their lack of connection would be understood. (Jaimini 6.6.15)
The *satra* sacrifices belong to all social classes (*varṇa*) without distinction (Jaimini 6.6.16);

and because of the observation of indicative marks (Jaimini 6.6.17); or rather, they belong to Brāhmaṇas alone, because the other two [classes] lack the status of officiating priests (Jaimini 6.6.18).
If it is argued that [the ownership] is due to the scriptural statement, [we reply:
no, for ownership is not what is being enjoined. Or rather, both [the *gārhapatya* and *āhavanīya* fires] may belong to the master, as there is no contradiction.
Or rather, it is not so, because of the contradiction with the ritual manual (kalpa). [Sūtra 22:
Because the others possess the status of masters, there is the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga) regarding the Ahīna sacrifice. [Sūtra 23:
Or because of the restriction that the Vasiṣṭhas alone perform the office of the Brahman priest. [Sūtra 24: Jaimini 6.6.24.
Or rather, it applies to all [Bhṛgus] because of a counter-exception;

[however], due to the restriction on the office of the *hautra* priest for Viśvāmitra, those of the Bhṛgu, Śunaka, and Vasiṣṭha lineages are ineligible. Because of the sovereignty of the sacrificial enclosure (*vihāra*), the rite may belong even to those who do not maintain the sacred fires.
And because it is seen in the case of the Sārasvata [sacrifice] (Jaimini 6.6.28),
and because of the prescription of an expiation (Jaimini 6.6.29),
and because for those who possess the sacred fires, the *iṣṭi* must precede [the Soma sacrifice] (Jaimini 6.6.30).
And because it is employed for its own purpose; Jaimini 6.6.31.
And it indicates the pouring together [of the offerings]; Jaimini 6.6.32.
Since the *juhū* and other vessels are not specifically enjoined, there being doubt, one should understand that there is freedom of choice. Jaimini 6.6.33.
Alternatively, they may use other vessels as common property, because of the prohibition established by the author of the scripture (Jaim_6.6.34).
There should be an expiation in times of distress (Jaim_6.6.35).

In the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), there should be a restriction regarding the performers according to the specific person [prescribed], because the sacrifice has that as its quality; in the absence of such a person, there would be entitlement for others individually (Jaim_6.6.36).

If it is argued that [the rule applies] because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), as in the case of a specific sacrifice (*ijyāviśeṣavat*)—[we reply: No, because of the distinctness of the connection (*saṃyogapṛthaktvāt*). Since the accessory (*guṇa*) has the sacrifice as its primary element, the injunction is indeed unconnected [to the other]. Because it is subordinate to the sacrifice, one would restrict it specifically to that sacrifice.

In the case of one's own gift, everything [is included] because there is no distinction; or rather, only that over which one has mastery, because anything else is impossible to give. Land, however, cannot be given away, because it is common to all and thus lacks such a specific distinction.
Furthermore, because it is not something that can be produced, there would be a distinction [between the Veda and other texts] on that account; Jaimini Sūtra 6.7.4.

And because of its eternity, there is no connection between it and things that are non-eternal; Jaimini Sūtra 6.7.5. And a Śūdra [is excluded] because he is not qualified for the treatises on Dharma; Jaimini Sūtra 6.7.6.
At the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), that which belongs to oneself should be understood as what is to be given, because of its connection with the act of giving.
(Jaimini 6.7.7) Because there is no remainder, it would end there, since the ritual action is established by means of the substance.
(Jaimini 6.7.8) Alternatively, there should be a remaining ritual action, because it is directly enjoined for the sake of the sacrifice. (Jaimini 6.7.9)

And likewise, there is the observation of another purpose [in the scripture]. (Jaimini 6.7.10) "But the remainder [of the ritual] would be a residual act through the taking of what is appropriate in its entirety.
(Jaimini 6.7.11) "Not so, because the taking is not permanent. (Jaimini 6.7.12)
Because of the specific instruction regarding the initiations (*dīkṣā*), there is a connection with that which is not for the sake of the sacrifice; therefore, there would be no contradiction.

(Jaimini 6.7.13) And in the multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*), that duty should apply to all [days] because there is no distinction. (Jaimini 6.7.14) Or rather, it should be one hundred and twelve, as in the archetype (*prakṛti*). (Jaimini 6.7.15)
It would not be so because it does not possess those qualities; Jaimini 6.7.16. And because of the observation of an indicative mark; Jaimini 6.7.17.
Being a modification, it is [the same] on both sides due to the absence of distinction; Jaimini 6.7.18.
Or rather, it is more [than one], because of the counter-exception;
and because of the favor, like the foot [of a verse].
Regarding the "unlimited," there is a prohibition of number for what remains, because that is what is heard in the scripture.
Or rather, another ritual procedure (*kalpa*) [should be used], because they are enumerated as being equivalent (Jaimini 6.7.22).
There is no fixed rule, because there is no distinction (Jaimini 6.7.23).
Or rather, there should be an addition, because the others have multiple purposes due to their proximity (Jaimini 6.7.24).
And the explanatory passage (arthavāda) is for that purpose [of praising the injunction].

(Jaimini 6.7.25) And the "performance by another" (parakṛti) and the "ancient event" (purākalpa) would be a duty of man, for they are recited for a specific purpose. (Jaimini 6.7.26) And because there is a prohibition regarding that which is connected with them. (Jaimini 6.7.27)
Or, because of the specific instruction, it would have that property, like the five-fold portioning (Jaimini 6.7.28).

But in the case of an injunction, because of its connection with the Veda, it would be a direct teaching (Jaimini 6.7.29). Or rather, it is an explanatory passage (arthavāda) because it is supplementary to an injunction; therefore, it must be a constant restatement (nityānuvāda) (Jaimini 6.7.30).

Because a lifespan of a thousand years is impossible among humans, [the rule] does not apply to them. Or rather, it may be a duty for humans because they are the ones entitled to it; no, it cannot be so, because of incapacity.
Because no connection [to a specific individual] is observed,

Jaimini [holds that] it would be a *kulakalpa* (a family tradition), according to Kārṣṇājini, because [the application] is impossible in a single case. Or rather, because of the connection with the whole, there should be the performance of only one [text].
Lāvukāyana says that because of the contradiction, it must be one of the two qualities;
[the year] is the *saṃvatsara* because it is subject to variation. That would be the archetype (*prakṛti*) because of its authoritative application.
Or rather, it refers to the days, because they are specifically enumerated (Jaimini 6.7.40).

Since it is preceded by an *iṣṭi*, the *homa* is not a subsidiary of a *kratu*; it should take place in consecrated fires, even though it precedes the *ādhāna*, because the latter is a subsidiary to everything (Jaimini 6.8.1). However, if it were an *iṣṭi*, there would be no mention [of it]; moreover, the *caturhotṛ* formulas indicate that [the *homa*] occurs in unconsecrated fires (Jaimini 6.8.2).
But the instruction [applies] because it is something not previously known (apūrvatva). Jaimini 6.8.3.

It applies to all [sacrificers] because there is no distinction. Jaimini 6.8.4. Or rather, because of the absence of the sacrifice, for one who has not established the sacred fires (anāhitāgni), there is an instruction regarding the entirety of beings. Jaimini 6.8.5.

Or rather, it is a recitation (*japa*), because it is not connected with fire. (Jaimini 6.8.6) It should be a *homa* because it is praised as being an *iṣṭi*, since it is not connected with fire in a general rule (*anārabhya-vidhi*), and because the others cannot be so designated.
(Jaimini 6.8.7) It belongs to both [the sacrificer and the priests], like the *pitṛyajña*. (Jaimini 6.8.8)

The instruction applies even to one who has not established the sacred fires, because there is no connection with the fires mentioned in the general context; Jaimini 6.8.9. In the case of the Pitṛyajña, there is a restatement of what is already connected [to the fires]; Jaimini 6.8.10.
One should establish the fires while initiating the student, because of the connection with the oblation; Jaimini 6.8.11.

The fire-installation (*ādhāna*) is performed either according to the *Sthapati-Īṣṭi* or in the common (*laukika*) manner, because it follows the sequence of learning and ritual action; furthermore, the installation is connected with a wife. And there is no ritual action subsequent to the installation, for its connection is indeed with the [subsequent] rites.
If it is argued that it is like the *śrāddha* [rite], [we reply]:
no, because of the contradiction with the Vedic revelation (Jaimini 6.8.15);
and because it serves all purposes, one should not perform it for the sake of a son alone (Jaimini 6.8.17).
But because of the drinking of Soma, there is the attainment of the second [fire]; therefore, one should marry [after that].

(Jaimini 6.8.18) However, because it is observed in the Pitṛyajña, it should be understood as occurring prior to the formal establishment of the fires (Ādhāna). (Jaimini 6.8.19) The Sthapati-iṣṭi, like the Prayājas, should cause the Ādhāna to be performed; and because it serves that purpose, it should conclude [the requirement for the fires]. (Jaimini 6.8.20)

Alternatively, it may take place in a common (worldly) fire, because the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires) is not subsidiary to all [rites]. (Jaimini 6.8.21) And the animal sacrifice for one who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*) is likewise, because the *ādhāna* has not yet been performed at that time. (Jaimini 6.8.22) Rites dedicated to the gods (*daiva*) are prescribed for the northern course of the sun, the bright fortnight, and auspicious days; these are based on Smṛti, as is seen from the purpose [of the texts]. (Jaimini 6.8.23)
And on the day [of the full moon], there is the completion of the ritual acts; Jaimini 6.8.24. But on other days, the rites are those pertaining to the ancestors (pitrya); Jaimini 6.8.25.
Begging and purchasing [the sacrificial materials] occur when they are not available, as is common in the world; Jaimini 6.8.26.
It must necessarily be meaningful, because it possesses purpose;
likewise, [the injunctions regarding] the consumption, the command, the covering, the naming, the offering, and the aversion [are meaningful].
However, that which is purposeless would be non-eternal.
In the injunction regarding the sacrificial animal, there is no restriction because there is no specific qualification [Jaimini 6.8.30].
Or rather, it is a goat, on account of the wording of the mantra [Jaimini 6.8.31].
Not so, because that would contradict the injunction [Jaimini 6.8.32].

If it is argued that [the formula] is like that of the *ārṣeya*, [we reply]: No, because there is no injunction for that. Indeed, there is a restriction because of the unity of purpose; otherwise, there would be a distinction due to the difference in purpose, as they are designated separately.
There is no restriction, because it is a different matter due to the difference in the words "otherness" (*anyatva*) and "distinction" (*vyatireka*).
[This is established] from the form and from the indicative mark.
In the case of the goat, there is no mention of the ritual action, due to the form and the indicative mark.

Because of the difference in form, it would not be a word denoting a genus (jāti). (Jaimini 6.8.39) It is a modification because it is not innate. (Jaimini 6.8.40) It is contingent because the quality of the animal has not been enjoined. (Jaimini 6.8.41)

Or rather, [the term applies] to the genus, because it expresses that which is predominant and because it possesses meaning. (Jaimini 6.8.42) Because the remaining [subsidiaries] have the revealed scripture (*śruti*) as their authority, when there is a difference in the primary [rite], their application should occur according to their respective eligibility.
(Jaimini 7.1.1) Or rather, because there is no division in the purpose of their origination, there should be a single commonality of property, just as in the case of living beings. (Jaimini 7.1.2)
Or rather, they would be restricted by the remainder of the injunction, because of its differentiation, since the origin [of the action] is subordinate; Jaimini 7.1.3.
If it exists, it should be understood as universal because of its connection with the defining characteristic; Jaimini 7.1.4.
But because there is no distinction, this would not be so; Jaimini 7.1.5.

And it is contradictory for [a single act] to have two purposes. (Jaimini 7.1.6) Or rather, because there is no injunction regarding its origin, the application would occur through the original impulsion; consequently, there would be a distinction between the acts.
(Jaimini 7.1.7) Or else, as in the case of the naming, the entire ritual property would apply on the basis of similarity. (Jaimini 7.1.8)

But because the purpose is indivisible, it would be so in the case of the designations; since the performance is as before, and because the action is to be brought about by the word, there would be no application of the remaining [details] due to their division. (Jaimini 7.1.9) If it is argued that this is based on Smṛti, (Jaimini 7.1.10) we say no, because it is as before. (Jaimini 7.1.11)
Since the purpose is to be accomplished through the word, its existence elsewhere would have to be based solely on the word due to the context (Jaimini 7.1.12).
Because it is similar and possesses the prior state, there should be an entitlement for that which has already arisen (Jaimini 7.1.13).
"If it is argued that it belongs to the Śyena" (Jaimini 7.1.14).
Not so, because of proximity.

(Jaimini 7.1.15) Or rather, since it is something new (*apūrva*), the other [term] would be for the sake of a different qualification; if it were expressive of that [new element], it would be identical to the injunction pertaining to the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.
(Jaimini 7.1.16) In the case of the five transferences (*pañcasañcara*), there is an extension of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) due to proximity. (Jaimini 7.1.17)
Because everything has a single designation;
and because of the observation of indicative marks. If it is argued that this is not so because of the recitation of what has already been prescribed.
Because it does not have another purpose. (Jaimini 7.1.21) And the same applies to the single-pot-sherd offering for Indra-Agni.

(Jaimini 7.1.22) For the Vaiśvadeva single-pot-sherd offering is the archetype for those in the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, because we observe that the entire oblation is not carried over, and because there is a scriptural injunction for a single double-portioning at the *avabhṛtha* bath. (Jaimini 7.1.23)
The application [of the word] *sāman* should occur by means of its denotative term according to the usage of the learned (Jaimini 7.2.1).
However, because words enjoin a meaning, there would be no application to another meaning, since the connection is with the action as a distinct entity (Jaimini 7.2.2).
Or rather, it should apply to its own primary sense; the purpose of the action is that they should be taught as being subordinate members (*aṅga*) of that action (Jaimini 7.2.3).
If it is argued that [the Veda] is merely sound, [we reply:
no, because it is not innate;
and furthermore, the scripture would thus be rendered purposeless.

If it is argued that this refers to the accent (*svara*), [we reply]: No, because there is no such meaning; thus there is no connection with the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). However, the accent would apply to the original productions [of words], because they are not differentiated by quantity or phoneme.

And because of the observation of indicative marks (liṅga). Jaimini 7.2.10. But because there is no mention of a modification in the subsequent [verses], they should be used according to the scriptural text (yathāśruti). Jaimini 7.2.11. And there would be an inconsistency of the words. Jaimini 7.2.12.
Rather, the word *karman* should have "being" (*bhāva*) as its meaning, because it refers to what is well-known; for [if it meant] a modification, it would be indistinguishable from other [meanings].
(Jaimini 7.2.13) Furthermore, it is observed to denote that which is not a substance.

(Jaimini 7.2.14) And its action is for the purpose of grasping [it], because they take different forms regarding various objects; for their meaning is non-worldly (*alaukika*) due to being prescribed [by scripture]. (Jaimini 7.2.15)
In that case, there would be specific designations due to the distinctness of the modifications (Jaimini 7.2.16).
And those [mantras] belonging to the womb are enjoined as equal to the others (Jaimini 7.2.17).
Furthermore, even in what is not a womb, that which is not of such a womb is seen (Jaimini 7.2.18).
If it is argued that there is no dissimilarity when there is a single meaning (Jaimini 7.2.19), [we reply:
it would exist because other meanings are not accomplished, as in the case of cooking (Jaimini 7.2.20);
and there is consistency among words (Jaimini 7.2.21).
It has been stated that the designation of the action [is based on the name]; therefore, upon hearing it elsewhere, there should be an extension of the injunction (vidhipradeśa).
Or rather, it applies even to the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), because it shares in its nature.
But [this is not so] because the name is innate (*autpattika*). Jaimini 7.3.1–3.
From the direct connection with the qualities, there would be the designation of the action; in the absence of that, it would be unestablished.

Or rather, in the case of the *sattra* sacrifice, this scriptural statement would be for the sake of the qualities. In the *Viśvajit* sacrifice where all *pṛṣṭhas* are employed, because they are preceded by that [model], the *pṛṣṭhas* belonging to the *Jyotiṣṭoma* apply, and the term *pṛṣṭha* exists [therein].
Or rather, it is from the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*), for there is an injunction to that effect;
and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
The *Jyotiṣṭoma* has its application established [prior to this]. (Jaimini 7.3.7–9)
If it is argued that the injunction applies to both,
[the reply is] no, because the word "all" would then be rendered meaningless. Likewise, the *avabhṛtha* rite follows from the Soma sacrifice.
If it is argued that [the term refers to] the material cause (*prakṛti*), [we reply]: No, because it is used figuratively; and also because of the observation of indicative marks.

In the case of a specific substance being prescribed, that very substance [is used] because of its connection with the Vedic text; however, when no substance is prescribed, the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is used because it is the original material for that rite. (Jaimini 7.3.16) But a subsidiary injunction (*guṇavidhi*) would not take hold [of the cake], because of their equal status. (Jaimini 7.3.17) And the same applies in the cases of the *nirmanthya* fire and others. (Jaimini 7.3.18)
But the leading forward [of the fire] belongs to the Soma sacrifice, for the other is not mentioned;
Jaimini 7.3.19. And the prohibition of the *uttaravedi* is likewise; Jaimini 7.3.20.
Or rather, it is the archetypal one, because there is no specific name [for it]; Jaimini 7.3.21.
The mention [of the first and last days] is for the purpose of exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*), or it is a commendatory statement (*guṇārthavāda*) regarding the quality [of those days].
(Jaimini 7.3.22) The carrying forward of the fire occurs on the first and last days because of the prohibition of the *uttaravedi* altar.
(Jaimini 7.3.23) Or rather, it occurs on the two middle days because of the commendatory statement regarding their movement. (Jaimini 7.3.24)
The prohibition regarding the *auttaravedika* [altar] is a general statement (*anārabhyavāda*).
(Jaimini 7.3.25) Furthermore, the *svarasāman*, the *ekakapāla*, and the *āmikṣā* are [prohibited] because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*).
(Jaimini 7.3.26) Or rather, it is because of the commonality of the injunction (*codanā-sāmānya*). (Jaimini 7.3.27)
In the case of that which arises from ritual action (*karmaja*), the action [is the means], like a sacrificial post (*yūpa*); [Jaimini 7.3.28].

Or rather, it is the form [of the object], because it has not yet become a residual by-product (*aśeṣabhūtatvāt*); [Jaimini 7.3.29]. In a case of doubt, it should be understood as worldly (*laukika*), because it serves all purposes (*sarvārthatvāt*); [Jaimini 7.3.30].
It is not Vedic because its meaning is specified [by human agency];
likewise, the origin of the others is similar because they are equal [in that regard]. It should be considered refined (saṃskṛta), because it possesses that word.
Or rather, because they are subordinate to the sacrifice through devotion (*bhakti*), and because the qualities are denotative [of the rite],
the word *pṛṣṭha* should apply to the ritual action, since it is taught as being of such a nature. Or else,
because of the teaching of denotation and due to the contradiction [otherwise], the word *pṛṣṭha* should apply to the substances.

The procedure for the act of sacrificing follows the previous model due to the injunction regarding what is to be done. (Jaimini 7.4.1) That [procedure] would be worldly, because its application is based on what is perceived.
(Jaimini 7.4.2) But by virtue of a specific scriptural statement, it is different from that. (Jaimini 7.4.3)
Or rather, it should be restricted by the indicative mark (*liṅga*), because that mark is subordinate to it (Jaimini Sūtra 7.4.4).

Or else, because it is preceded by what is not logical, those passages would be eternal restatements (*nityānuvāda*) (Jaimini Sūtra 7.4.5). And because of mutual contradiction among the subordinate qualities (*guṇa*), there should be an adjustment according to their respective purposes (Jaimini Sūtra 7.4.6).
But it should be restricted because of its being a share, since qualities are denotative; due to the connection, it is like the denotation [of a quality], as in the case of "a milch-cow with a calf.

Or rather, because the originations are equal, the application should be according to the respective qualification. Furthermore, the mention of both the origination and the subsidiary detail in one [text] would be contradictory.

Jaimini 7.4.10: Or rather, the end of the injunction (*vidhyanta*) should proceed according to the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*) when there is a scriptural injunction (*codanā*), for such is the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*).
Jaimini 7.4.11: Because the indicative mark is the cause [of determination], in the absence of such a mark, the procedure would be worldly (*laukika*).

Jaimini 7.4.12: Since the indicative mark possesses the character of being established by prior usage, it may be determined even by a single instance due to the commonality of the word of the injunction, just as [the quality of all rice in a pot is known] by a single grain of rice (*sthālīpulāka*).

In a multi-day sacrifice (ahargaṇa), the [rite] belonging to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) [should apply], because it is its archetype; however, due to the arrival of additional [elements], it should be designated by that [additional] name, just like a one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*), on account of the indicative mark (*liṅga*). But this is not so, because the additional elements are not denoted by the word, as they do not designate the sacrifice itself.

The *liṅga* (indicative mark) would be a property of the composite (*saṃghāta*), because it serves that purpose, just like a substance (*dravya*). (Jaimini 7.4.16) Or rather, it is not so, because the property belongs to the object; for the composite is subordinate (*guṇa*). (Jaimini 7.4.17) Through the force of the requirement (*arthāpatti*), the acquisition of the property would apply to the substances. (Jaimini 7.4.18)

The observation of a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) pertains to that which is restricted by the context of application (*pravṛtti*). (Jaimini 7.4.19) The observation of the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) pertains to that which is specifically qualified, because the *anārabhyavāda* (unattached statements) pertain to the archetype (*prakṛti*).
(Jaimini 7.4.20) Now follows the definition of specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*). (Jaimini 8.1.1)
Its indicative mark [is established] through connection with the purpose, just like the name;
because it is an activity, there should be an application of the *iṣṭi* at the *soma* sacrifice;
and because of the observation of its indicative mark.
Or rather, it is an original injunction (apūrva) because of the prescription of the whole;
and because of the perpetual restatement (nityānuvāda) of the absence of sprinkling on the ladle.
If it is argued that it is an injunction... [Jaimini 8.1.5–7]
Not so, because it is a supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa) [Jaimini 8.1.8];
and [the objection] is raised because of the lack of fasting [Jaimini 8.1.9];
there would be the observation of the [rites] belonging to the Darśa sacrifice [Jaimini 8.1.10].

In the *iṣṭis*, there should be the application of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* [rites]; likewise in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*). And for the consecration sacrifice (*daikṣa*), it applies to the others.
Because of the observation of the two-fold chariot-yoke belonging to the Soma-day among the Aikādaśinas,
its procedure should apply to the groups [of animals]; because of the observation of a separate sacrificial post for each animal,
however, it applies to the Soma-sacrifice in cases where the details are unmanifested.

In the case of the *gaṇas*, the procedure of the *dvādaśāha* applies; likewise, that of the *gavya* applies to those beginning with it. Furthermore, among the *nikāyas*, the procedure of the preceding one should prevail in the subsequent ones.
But because the ritual action does not persist, there is no continuity of the collection of agents who determine the fruit, since that [collection] is bound to it; Jaimini 8.1.20.
And even if it were to persist, it would be for that purpose alone; Jaimini 8.1.21.
And because it is not so stated in the scripture; Jaimini 8.1.22.
Activity would occur because of dependence on desires for [specific] qualities; Jaimini 8.1.23.
Or rather, there would be cessation because of the distinction between ritual acts; Jaimini 8.1.24.
Or again, activity would occur because they are modifications of that [original sacrifice] and because they serve the purpose of the rite; Jaimini 8.1.25.
Regarding a single action, there is an option because there is no distinction, since the injunction is one (Jaimini 8.1.26).
There would be an option because the indicative mark is common (Jaimini 8.1.27).
Or rather, it should be restricted because of the unity of purpose; for it is a modification, as in the previous case (Jaimini 8.1.28).
