If it is argued that this is not so because it is not mentioned in the scripture,
[we reply] that it must be so because of the existence of indicative marks;
and likewise, there is a scriptural passage showing another purpose.
In the case of conflicting [indications], the ritual act should be regulated by the oblation, because the act is designated by that;
and because it is connected with the ritual through that [oblation];
for the mention of the deity is subordinate [to the oblation]. (Jaimini 8.1.32–34)
Gold has the properties of clarified butter because of its brilliance (Jaimini 8.1.35) and because it favors the ritual requirements (Jaimini 8.1.36);
or rather, it is a vegetable substance because of its clarity (Jaimini 8.1.37).
And because of the word *caru*;
and because cooking (*śrapaṇa*) is prescribed for it;
and because honey and water, by virtue of their commonality as substances, would be a modification of milk.
Or rather, it is clarified butter (*ājya*), because of the similarity of color;
and because of the favoring of the ritual rule (*dharma*);
and because the previous [rule] is not distinguished [from this].
In the Vājina offering, Soma comes first; and in the Sautrāmaṇī, it is so for the cups because they bear that name (Jaimini 8.2.1);
also because of the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-call (Jaimini 8.2.2);
and because of the consumption after having invited one another (Jaimini 8.2.3).
The purchasing, cooking, *puroruc* hymn, taking up the *upayāma*, placing, dwelling, and binding [of the Soma] are likewise [restricted].

(Jaimini 8.2.4) Or rather, it should be restricted by the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), because it is a modification thereof. (Jaimini 8.2.5) The word "Soma" is a commendatory expression (*praśaṃsā*). (Jaimini 8.2.6)
There are other statements as well; Jaimini 8.2.7.
And the designation is likewise; Jaimini 8.2.8.
And there is the observation of an indicative mark regarding the animal-cake offering; Jaimini 8.2.9.
The animal victim should be a modification of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), because of the identity of the deity;
and also because of the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa); and also because of the carrying of fire around it (paryagnikaraṇa).
It is indeed the *sānnāyya* (the milk offering), because it originates from that;
and because its vessel is seen [in the ritual context].
It should be curd, because of the commonality of its solid form.
Or rather, it is milk, because of the commonality of time;
because of the immediate sequence following the animal sacrifice;
and because its fluidity is not distinguished [from that of the other substances].

Because the *āmikṣā* is produced from both [milk and curds], it would be a modification of both; (Jaimini 8.2.19). Or rather, it is one [modification] because the injunction is single; (Jaimini 8.2.20).
Because of the commonality of being a solidification of curds; (Jaimini 8.2.21).
Or rather, it is milk, because that is the primary element, as in common worldly practice, since the curd is for its sake;
and also because of the favoring of the ritual rules (Jaimini 8.2.22).
And the twelve-day rite is both a *sattra* and an *ahīna*; its application is in both ways because of the unity of the action (Jaimini 8.2.23–24).

Alternatively, because of the hearing of the term *yajati* (he sacrifices), there should be the application [of the name] "Ahīna" to those [sacrifices] beginning with the Dvirātra, since they have the same verbal form as the archetype (*prakṛti*). Jaimini 8.2.25.
The sacrifices from the Dvirātra up to the Ekādaśarātra are Ahīnas, because they are enjoined by the word *yajati*. Jaimini 8.2.26.
In those beginning with the Trayodaśarātra, they are of the nature of a *satra*, because they are enjoined by the words *āsana* (sitting) and *upāyi* (approaching). Jaimini 8.2.27.
And because of an indicative mark (liṅga):

[Jaimini 8.2.28] because one side [of the Pañcadaśarātra] is an Atirātra, the Pañcadaśarātra is an Ahīna; and because the status of being an Ahīna is seen in those [days] that have become part of the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana.
[Jaimini 8.2.29] And because there is a statement using the term "Ahīna. [Jaimini 8.2.30]
Or rather, it is a *sattra* because of the injunction regarding the means (*upāya*).

(Jaimini 8.2.31) And it shows the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of a *sattra*. (Jaimini 8.2.32) In a group of oblations (*havirgaṇa*), the latter [is connected] with the former because of the commonality of location. (Jaimini 8.3.1)
Or rather, [the procedure] should be restricted by the deity, because of the explicit mention of the word, since there is no such mention for the other.
(Jaimini 8.3.2) In the case of an injunction for a group, the repetition of that which possesses the indicative mark should be understood, as in the case of the Āgneya sacrifice.
(Jaimini 8.3.3) Or rather, they are distinct days, because they form a collection and are enjoined by means of an indicative mark of performance. (Jaimini 8.3.4)
And likewise, there is the observation of another purpose [Jaimini Sūtra 8.3.5].
Bādari [holds that] there is repetition of the time as well, because of the difference in the acts [Jaimini Sūtra 8.3.6].
But Jaimini [maintains] the repetition of those days, because their number is not directly perceived [Jaimini Sūtra 8.3.7].
In the case of groups [of deities], that practice should be understood [to apply] because of the inclusion of those characterized as such.
Or rather, due to the governing context, the archetype (prakṛti) would be qualified by that, since the designation is based on that.
From the group comes an increase, because it has that as its archetype.
Or rather, it should be on a single day because of their equality; [Jaimini 8.3.11].

In the case of the *gāyatrī* verses, there is an exclusion of the original ones because of the context of the archetype, due to the nature of the number, and because, like the *agniṣṭoma*, there is no distinction, they receive that name; [Jaimini 8.3.12]. And that is stated as a permanent rule even when the verses exist separately; [Jaimini 8.3.13].
If it is argued that "ten" is not [included] within "twenty," then there would be only a single number. Or rather,
the word for the substance [would apply] by way of a quality, because it does not have all things as its scope.
And the possession [of the quality] is like the genus "cow-ness" (Jaimini 8.3.17);
and because number is a property of the word (Jaimini 8.3.18);
and because the other is not heard in the text (Jaimini 8.3.19).
Because it is not applied to another substance, it would be distinguished by the omission of the *ukthya* cups; and because it is not characterized by scriptural injunction (*aśāstralakṣaṇatvāt*).
Since it is a name [given] at the time of origin (*utpattināmadheyatvāt*), it would exist separately through its own application (*bhaktayā*) among those that are distinct.

If it is argued that this is merely a statement [of what is already known], then it is only as much as has been said [in the sūtra]. (Jaimini 8.3.23) Furthermore, there would be an option regarding the *apūrva* if there were an injunction of number. (Jaimini 8.3.24–25)
If it is argued that [the *ṛc*] is not [the primary factor] because it possesses the quality (*guṇa*) of being a verse, [we reply:
so too would it be in the case of the preceding [rule]. Furthermore, the application of qualities occurs everywhere.
If it is argued that [the rule does not apply] because of the mention of what is already accomplished (*niṣpanna*),

then the same would apply here as well. Or rather, if the restriction applies even where there is no doubt because of its connection with the archetype (*prakṛti*), then it would be established for the *śara* reeds as well.
If it is argued that the application [of the rule] has been observed [in the case of the *śara* grass],
then it applies likewise to the *śara* grasses as well. If it is argued that it is because of the word "bhaktyā" (by way of figurative usage), [then the same objection applies].
Likewise in the other case; Jaimini 8.3.35.
And because the purpose is not fully accomplished, it would not apply to a mere portion of them; Jaimini 8.3.36.
The *darvihoma* is a designation for a sacrifice because of its connection with the term *homa*; Jaimini 8.4.1.

It would belong to the worldly [performers], because that is the designation for the agent; (Jaimini 8.4.2) or rather, it belongs to all [the officiants] because it is seen [so] in the case of the *vāstu-homa*;
(Jaimini 8.4.3) or because of the connection with those [acts] enjoined by the term *juhoti*. (Jaimini 8.4.4)
Or rather, there may be a mention of qualities because of the instruction regarding the substance;
[this is so] because worldly practices are not adopted [as authoritative], and because words [used in such contexts] are prescribed for other purposes;
and because another vessel is observed [in the ritual].

Likewise, [the rule applies] to the fire and the oblation. (Jaimini 8.4.8) And the connection of the meaning has already been stated. (Jaimini 8.4.9) In that case, the Soma [rite] should proceed, because [the details] are not explicitly manifest. (Jaimini 8.4.10)

Or rather, [the *svāhākāra*] does not [apply], because of its connection with the *svāhākāra* and because of the specific mention of the *vaṣaṭkāra*; because of the contradiction with the *tantra* [method];
because it is a different word; and because of the observation of indicative marks. (Jaimini 8.4.11–13)

But the *svāhākāra* is for the sake of the subsequent [rite], just as the number seventeen [is for the subsequent]; there, the recurrence is not prohibited because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*), as in the case of the animal sacrifice. (Jaimini 8.4.14) Or rather, it is not for the sake of the subsequent [rite], because it possesses its own purpose; for if it were otherwise, the archetypal [element] would be obstructed due to its pointlessness. (Jaimini 8.4.15) If it is argued that this is not even the case in the archetype, (Jaimini 8.4.16)

It has been stated that in a combination [of texts], there is relative weakness [of the later]. (Jaimini 8.4.17) That [text] should be an injunction because it initiates the *veṣṭi* sacrifice through its own impulsion.
(Jaimini 8.4.18) And also because of the power of the word itself. (Jaimini 8.4.19)
And because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga). Jaimini 8.4.20.
In that case, since non-existence is the cause [of the inference], there would be a non-observation for the sake of a subordinate purpose (guṇa). Jaimini 8.4.21.
If it is argued that it is an injunction (vidhi), Jaimini 8.4.22.

It is not so, because it is a supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa); and a resolution for the sake of a subordinate element (guṇa) is not possible through multiplicity. (Jaimini 8.4.23) Or rather, for those for whom there is gold in the latter two [sacrifices], it would apply because there is no contradiction. (Jaimini 8.4.24) In that case, medicinal herbs are enjoined; they should be understood by means of their position (sthāna). (Jaimini 8.4.25)

Or rather, on account of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), [the rule applies] to the remaining two oblations (*śeṣahoma*). But those two are acts of disposal (*pratipatti*); therefore, there is no modification [of the original procedure]. (Jaimini 8.4.26) In the case of a conflict between concurrent rules, the non-application [of one] should be understood, because the injunctions are established separately and the purpose cannot be altered. However, by virtue of a specific scriptural statement (*vacana*), there shall be an extension [of the rule] (*atideśa*). (Jaimini 8.4.18)

The sacrificial act is primary, for it is that which is enjoined; its preparation (*saṃskāra*) pertains to the materials, as it is prompted by them, because they are for its sake. (Jaimini 9.1.1) Since those things employed in a preparation are for the sake of that [preparation], the prompting must belong to it. (Jaimini 9.1.2) However, because the sacrifice is connected with that purpose, there is a connection with the ritual duty (*dharma*); therefore, it should be prompted by the sacrifice, since the preparation is for the sake of that [sacrifice]. (Jaimini 9.1.3)
And [the same applies] to the fruit and the deity. (Jaimini 9.1.4) For their quality [of being subordinate] does not follow from the injunction.
(Jaimini 9.1.5) Or rather, the deity should be the motivator, as in the case of a guest, because the act of eating is for its sake. (Jaimini 9.1.6)
And by implication (arthāpatti) [the deity is understood].
Therefore, there is a connection with that [deity] (Jaimini 9.1.8).
Or rather, because it is preceded by the word [of the Veda], the sacrificial act should be primary; the mention of the deity is subordinate (Jaimini 9.1.9).
In the case of a guest, that [hospitality] is primary; there would be an absence of ritual action because his satisfaction is the primary concern.

(Jaimini 9.1.10) Or rather, it refers to the collection of substance, number, cause, and aggregate, due to its connection with the Vedic text. (Jaimini 9.1.11) And since the substance is brought about for a specific purpose, there would be no fixed restriction by means of the substance. (Jaimini 9.1.12)
Or rather, the purpose (*artha*) would be the motive for the others, because they are not enjoined [independently] and because that [purpose] is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*). Jaimini 9.1.13.

There would be a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) because of its being something not previously established (*apūrvatva*). Jaimini 9.1.14. And if the *dharma* were prompted by that [purpose], it would have a universal scope (*sarvaviṣayatva*). Jaimini 9.1.15.
"If it is argued that [the rule applies] to one who is connected with that [sacrifice]," [we reply:
"No, because it is not so stated in the scripture" (Jaimini 9.1.17).
"If it is argued that it is due to the context," [we reply: "No" (Jaimini 9.1.18).

There can be no entitlement [to the low-voiced recitation] among those who are equal, for the connection is not enjoined; rather, there is a connection of separate entities with the purpose of the sacrifice, and therefore the sacrifice is the motive. (Jaimini 9.1.19) The low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*) should belong to those [mantras] bound to a specific place, because of the direct scriptural injunction (*śruti*), and because that [recitation] does not exist [elsewhere] in that context. (Jaimini 9.1.20) Or rather, it belongs to the sacrifice itself, because of its connection with that. (Jaimini 9.1.21)
And the restatement (anuvāda) has that same meaning.

(Jaimini 9.1.22) If it is argued that the *praṇītā* water and so forth are likewise [restatements], (Jaimini 9.1.23) [we reply] no, because the sacrifice is not heard [in that context]. (Jaimini 9.1.24)

Or rather, because the injunction pertains to those regions or to their aggregate; [Jaimini 9.1.25] the ritual property of the fire-altar applies to each individual brick because of the nature of the aggregate, as in the case of the Full Moon sacrifice;
[Jaimini 9.1.26] or rather, it should belong to the fire-altar as a whole because the substance is one, while the others exist for its sake; [Jaimini 9.1.27]
But because of the collection of injunctions, it would be so at the Paurṇamāsī sacrifice;
[the rule] that all [rites] end with the Patnīsaṃyājas applies because there is no distinction. Or rather, on account of an indicative mark, [the rule applies] prior to the final [Patnīsaṃyāja].

Or rather, the consecration (*dīkṣā*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*), just as [the time] for concluding at night [is a restatement]; for it would be so because it is prescribed without reference to a specific context (*anārabhya-vidhāna*), and because there is a contradiction with the indicative mark (*liṅga*) at the end. (Jaimini 9.1.31) Or rather, the repetition of the *sāmidhenī* verses would be a property of the position (*sthāna-dharma*) due to its being first; (Jaimini 9.1.32–33) for it is a property of the position because of its primacy. (Jaimini 9.1.33)

In the repetition of an *iṣṭi*, the *ārambhaṇīyā* should be repeated like the *prayājas*. (Jaimini 9.1.34) Or rather, it should be performed only once, because of its connection with the single act of commencement; for there is only one commencement throughout the lifelong performance.

(Jaimini 9.1.35) In the case of mantras, there is the status of being subsidiary (*śeṣabhāva*) due to their connection with the expression of a purpose; therein, that which is not enjoined is not obtained, because [the mantra] expresses what has been enjoined. (Jaimini 9.1.36)
And therefore, their non-utterance is employed for the sake of the other;
if it is argued that it is so because it is a word denoting a quality (guṇaśabda), we say no, because of the lack of inherence (asamavāya).

But when it is enjoined, because it is for the sake of another, there should be no modification according to the rule; JaiS 9.1.40. There would be modification where that [other] is the primary purpose; JaiS 9.1.41.
Because of the lack of connection with those things intended for that purpose, one should understand it as qualified by that; JaiS 9.1.42.
If it is argued that [the rule] is thus because of the absence of ritual action (karma), [we reply]:

no, because it is for the sake of another (parārthatva). Because of the mention of a specific gender-mark (liṅga-viśeṣa), the Sarasvatī [offering] is not applicable among those of equal injunctions, due to its femininity.

Or rather, because it denotes an animal, that [term] indeed constitutes the injunction; furthermore, the state of being an animal pertains to the person. (Jaimini 9.1.46) Or there is a distinction, because of the specification of its purpose. (Jaimini 9.1.47) And the state of being an animal [is denoted] by the same word. (Jaimini 9.1.48)

Or as it has been stated: because of proximity [Jaimini 9.1.49]. "In the case of a ritual application, there should be a modification based on a statement other than what is traditionally recited" [Jaimini 9.1.50].
"Alternatively, there would be a twofold [option], because the grounds are equal; due to their commonality, there should be an option" [Jaimini 9.1.51].

And because of the instruction regarding the *sāman*, there is a restriction [to its specific application] due to the particularity of the scriptural statement; otherwise, it would be like the number seventeen (*sāptadaśya*).
Because of the absence of chanting (*apragāṇa*), when there is a difference in the word, there would be an instruction for that which has become such [i.e., a non-chanted form].
Whether it be in its proper place or sung there, because the primary focus is on the alteration of the words;
and because of the connection with singing. If it is argued that this is merely a scriptural statement (vacana), [we reply: no. Jaimini 9.1.55–57.

Not so, because that [the Sāman] is the primary factor. (Jaimini 9.1.58) Some maintain that the Sāmans are mantras, based on both traditional recollection and explicit instruction. (Jaimini 9.2.1) That [view] is subject to the aforementioned defect. (Jaimini 9.2.2)
Or rather, the action is characterized by the injunction;
such a substance [is required] because of the scriptural statement, as in the case of the *pākayajña*.
In that regard, there is no contradiction regarding the distinction and the application [of the rite] when another substance is used.
But this cannot be so because they are the meanings of words; JaiS 9.2.6. And because words exist for the sake of others; JaiS 9.2.7.
Furthermore, there is no connection between the two words and the ritual action, because their referents are distinct; JaiS 9.2.8.
And the *saṃskāra* (consecration) would be like fire even when not part of the specific context, because it has been employed [as a general term]; Jaimini 9.2.9.
And because words do not denote something to be produced (*akāryatva*), their non-employment would be understood; Jaimini 9.2.10.
And because it is dependent; Jaimini 9.2.11.
If it is argued that it is employed [for a specific purpose],
it would be employed for the sake of grasping (Jaimini 9.2.12).
It should apply to a triplet of verses (tṛca), because of the direct scriptural indication (Jaimini 9.2.13–14).
Because the modification pertains to the meaning of the word;
and [the scripture] also shows this.
But because the sentences are distinct, there should be a completion for each word, since the consecration is for the sake of that [word].
And likewise, there is the observation of another purpose [Jaimini 9.2.18];
and the instruction regarding non-repetition is similar [Jaimini 9.2.19];
the other scriptural statement is due to repetition [Jaimini 9.2.20].
The repetition of that [mantra] should take place during the equal [days],
because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga) [Jaimini 9.2.21];
and because the status of being subsequent is understood as contingent (naimittika), due to its immediate sequence [Jaimini 9.2.22–23].
And because of the unity of purpose, there is the repetition of that; [the *pragātha*], however, is [used] in its own [context]; and in its own [place]. (Jaimini 9.2.24–26)

And [this applies] also in the case of the *pragātha*, because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*) and because there is no difference [in their function]. (Jaimini 9.2.27) There would be an option (*vikalpa*) because the purpose is one and the same. (Jaimini 9.2.29)

Jaimini 9.2.30: There should be an option between the *ṛc* and the *sāman* because they serve a single purpose, since both are intended for that same end. Jaimini 9.2.31: The application [of the *sāman*] should be by virtue of a specific scriptural injunction.
Jaimini 9.2.32: In the case of a portion of the *sāman*, there should be a modification depending on that [injunction], because it is established by scripture.
But Bādari [holds that] it is according to the material, because of the distinction between the materials;

(Jaimini 9.2.33). Some [hold that] there is a cessation of the *stobha* when the material is different, as in the case of the *ṛc*; (Jaimini 9.2.34). But rather, there is an extension of everything because of the commonality; thus there would be a modification, as in the world; (Jaimini 9.2.35).

And it also shows the connection: "Or there is cessation because of the loss of purpose" (Jaimini 9.2.36); "Or the connection would be an explanatory eulogy" (Jaimini 9.2.37); "Or the connection would be an explanatory eulogy" (Jaimini 9.2.38).

Jaimini [holds that] there is an addition and a change of color, because it is a *stobha* sound. (Jaim_9.2.39) Since dharma is produced by purpose, when there is a prohibition against the modification or transgression of substances and qualities, there is a connection with the injunction due to their inherent association. (Jaim_9.2.40) However, because of its origination from that, there should be a cessation, since it is produced by that. (Jaim_9.2.41)
Or rather, they should enter [the modified sacrifice], because it possesses purpose, since the refinement is for that purpose.
(Jaimini 9.2.42) And likewise, the name [of the rite] would apply to the modification because of that entry, owing to its being a new instance.
(Jaimini 9.2.43) But the commonality of purpose exists through the purpose of another, since the refinement is for that purpose. (Jaimini 9.2.44)
Or they should be performed for the sake of accomplishing the purpose;
because they share a single purpose, there would be no division. Or, due to specific instruction, they would remain restricted.
In the case of non-archetypal [sāmans], they should remain as they are because of their modification and contradiction;

likewise in the case of a *ubhayasāman*, because it results in a single purpose. Or rather, there should be a fixed allocation because they serve their own specific purposes, just as in the archetype.
But there is no application [of the *pārvaṇa-homas*] in the two *pārvaṇa* sacrifices, because they are connected with the purpose of the whole [sacrifice], for it is the worship of that [whole].
(Jaimini 9.2.51) If it is argued that [the *pārvaṇa-homas* apply] to the time, (Jaimini 9.2.52) [we reply:
No, because it is not within the context. (Jaimini 9.2.53)
And because of the wording of the mantra (Jaimini 9.2.54).
If it is argued that in the absence of that [mantra], it is like the case of the fire (Jaimini 9.2.55),
we say no, because of the status of being the qualified agent (adhikāraka) (Jaimini 9.2.56).

Because there is no distinction between the two [Jaimini 9.2.57]; "Or rather, they pertain to that which is the object of the sacrifice" [Jaimini 9.2.58]; "If it be argued that this applies even to the *prayāja* [Jaimini 9.2.59]."
Because there is no injunction [to the contrary].

(Jaimini 9.2.60) Just as in the archetype (*prakṛti*) there is a statement regarding the production of the ritual elements, so it is in the subsequent modification (*vikṛti*), because that is its archetype and because the purpose is not something to be produced [by further action]. (Jaimini 9.3.1) And because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*). (Jaimini 9.3.2)
The birth-based [designation] is according to the respective place;
some say there is no modification because it is not of Vedic origin,
and because of the observation of gender markers.
The modification is caused by the wind;
[this is] the indicative mark for the purpose of performing the mantra (Jaimini 9.3.6).
Or rather, there is a restriction because both parts are involved (Jaimini 9.3.7–8).

Jaimini 9.3.9: For in the case of worldly [rites], since [the original] is set aside due to its connection with defects, it is enjoined by means of a specific cause; it would apply to the archetype because there is no [other] share. Jaimini 9.3.10:
But it is improper that it should apply without modification, because it would obstruct what is seen and because there is no distinction [between the two cases].
Jaimini 9.3.11: Or rather, there is a modification, because it is for that purpose.
But rather, because of the connection with what is not the rule, it should apply to the subsequent cases as well, just as in the original;
for the non-rule applies according to the purpose, since it is not enjoined [as a fixed rule].
However, in the Veda (chandas), it is according to how it is observed.

In the case of a conflict, there would be an option, because that [quality] exists; however, in the case of a subordinate element (*guṇa*), there is an unjustified assumption because it is only a partial [application].
(Jaimini 9.3.15) And because of the distinction of context. (Jaimini 9.3.16) But because of the absence of purpose, it cannot be so; the other is merely a subordinate quality. (Jaimini 9.3.17)
If it is argued that [the rule applies] to *dyāv-*, [we reply]:
No, because it is a word denoting the origin [of the sacrifice].
However, in the case of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), there would be no modification, as it is understood from the fact that it is not a substitute.
And because of that statement, it applies even in the case of a modification; (Jaimini 9.3.21).
The *adhrigu* formula applies to the *savanīya* offerings in the same manner, provided they are subject to the same injunction; (Jaimini 9.3.22).
And because there is no modification in the case of a substitute; (Jaimini 9.3.23).

Because it is not mentioned [in the texts], it would lack scriptural authority; or, because the other [the *sāman*] is absent, it would be so. Or rather, because it is for that purpose, it should bear that name, since it is not distinguished from the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*).
And its true nature has already been stated. (Jaimini Sūtra 9.3.24–26)
And because the quantity of the substance in the combined offerings is not fixed;
and because of the observation of indicative marks (Jaimini 9.3.27);
and because of the connection with the word "once" (*ekadha*), there should be a designation by means of repetition [of the mantra] (Jaimini 9.3.29).
Or rather, there is no modification, as in the case of a single action performed by many (Jaimini 9.3.30).

Furthermore, there would be simultaneity and unity, because of the oneness of the skin; since that is the intended material cause, it would be designated even when increased through repetition in subsequent instances (Jaimini 9.3.31).

Regarding the status of being the "lord of the sacrifice" (*medhapati*), because it is connected to both the sacrificer and the deity and is employed everywhere, and because it is not a formulaic recitation (*anigada*) in its own right, there should be no modification in any case (Jaimini 9.3.32).

Alternatively, when there is a combination of two [terms] despite a difference in meaning, their application would be according to their respective order (Jaimini 9.3.33). Or rather, because of the single word for the master, there should be an elevation [of the term] to the deity; the second word would apply to the wife (Jaimini 9.3.34). But the deity [is expressed by the first word] because it is the object of the blessing; since [the status of] master is already established, [the second word] would be purposeless with respect to the master (Jaimini 9.3.35).
And because of the general rule and out of devotion, there would be lordship over that [deity].

(Jaimini 9.3.36) That which is connected with one [deity] should be displaced, because it is possible for two deities [to share it]. (Jaimini 9.3.37) But it belongs to one alone, because of the association, since that is its defining characteristic. (Jaimini 9.3.38)

And because of its association with that [deity], there would therefore be a modification; (Jaimini 9.3.39) even in the case of unity, because the quality does not depart; (Jaimini 9.3.40) the restriction [applies] when there are many deities, for it would be a modification. (Jaimini 9.3.41)
Or rather, there is an option, as in the case of the original form.

(Jaimini 9.3.42) In another case, there would be a modification because of the distinctness of the deities, since they converge upon a single [animal]. (Jaimini 9.3.43) In a group of animals, there are twenty-six [recitations] through repetition, because that is the nature of the group and because the group is divided; for if there were no modification, their connection would not be complete, and due to the modification, there would be no compound because of the lack of conjunction. (Jaimini 9.3.44)

And [the rule applies] with all [of them]. (Jaimini 9.4.1) If it is argued that the same applies even in the case of repetition, (Jaimini 9.4.2) we say no, because it is due to a subordinate quality and because it is performed for a specific purpose. (Jaimini 9.4.3)
If it is argued that the same applies even in the case of a compound,
[the reply is] no, because of impossibility. And the statement regarding one's own [deities] in the archetype would likewise apply here.

However, because the ribs are the primary element, there should be a designation by means of a collective compound; for the *adhrigu* formula has them as its purpose, and they are mentioned in their entirety. But rather, because it is not a direct auxiliary (*asannipāti*), there should be a designation by means of what is traditionally recited, just as in the case of the wife.
But there is modification because it is a specific portion, as in the case of the sacrificer (Jaimini 9.4.10);
likewise with the wife because of her being previously unmentioned (Jaimini 9.4.11);
but there is no modification in the case of numbers not explicitly mentioned, because they apply to all (Jaimini 9.4.12).
But rather, by way of calculation, the *pradhāna* (the primary act) would be thus; however, the *vaṅkrayaḥ* (the ribs) are the *pradhāna*.
For there would be a mention of what is not recited in the text, since the indication of the ribs would occur through non-utterance.
Or rather, there should be repetition because there is no modification.
But the animal itself would be the primary element because it is the cause of the repetition; therefore, there should be a compound word [denoting the total].

(Jaimini 9.4.16) There are thirty-four [limbs] of the horse; because of that specific statement, it is exceptional. (Jaimini 9.4.17) Having prohibited that, the archetype is enjoined, since it is that which is expressed by the number thirty-four. (Jaimini 9.4.18)
It should be the *ṛc* because it is so prescribed in the tradition, and it is logical that there should be no option [between the two].

However, in that case, by virtue of the specific statement, there should be a modification of the word "airavat. Or rather, there should be a prohibition of all [words], because the connection is with the word itself.
Because of the proximity of the *vaniṣṭhu*, the term "urūka" refers to the omentum (*vapā*).
[Jaimini 9.4.22] It is a designation by way of praise. [Jaimini 9.4.23] Or rather, it is a praise of the arms. [Jaimini 9.4.24]

In the cases of the *śyena*, *śalā*, *kaśyapa*, *kavaṣa*, *astra*, and *ekaparṇa*, there is a designation based on form because of the proximity of well-known [objects]. (Jaimini 9.4.25) Or rather, it should be understood as denoting the whole, because it exists in that manner. (Jaimini 9.4.26) And this applies to the *adhrigu* formula as well, because it serves that same purpose. (Jaimini 9.4.27)

In the case of incidental [acts], no expiation exists because they are for the sake of another; for an expiation is prescribed only for that [act] itself. (Jaimini 9.4.28) And because the holding [of the fire] is for the sake of another. (Jaimini 9.4.29) In the case of the others, there should be a ritual act, because they are for the purpose of action. (Jaimini 9.4.30)

But it does not apply when [the substance] has already been produced, because the injunction pertains to the time [of its acquisition]. (Jaimini 9.4.31) The observation of the offering (*pradāna*) occurs during the cooking (*śrapaṇa*), because that [cooking] is for the purpose of preparing the food for the ritual duty, and because of the mixing [of ingredients], like honey and water. (Jaimini 9.4.32) And the prohibition of purification (*saṃskāra*) is likewise. (Jaimini 9.4.33)

And because such [an act] is excluded when that [act] is prohibited; (Jaimini 9.4.34) it is non-dharma because it is not an offering, since it is prescribed for the purpose of the *praṇītā* water, and because of its inequality, there is no connection. (Jaimini 9.4.35) The latter would be a permanent restatement (*nityānuvāda*). (Jaimini 9.4.36)

Or rather, it is a prohibition of what has been prescribed. (Jaimini 9.4.37) Because it is subordinate in the act of avoidance, and because there is a prohibition of what was stated [as the primary], there should be eating of only [the pure substance] for that reason. (Jaimini 9.4.38) And because it is a duty of the vow, like the case of the smearings. (Jaimini 9.4.39)

Or rather, there is a prohibition of the *rasa* (milk) because it is a property of the person; [Jaimini 9.4.40]. At the *abhyudaya* sacrifice, the removal of the milking should retain its own characteristics because it has already commenced; [Jaimini 9.4.41].
And because of the instruction regarding the boiled milk (*śṛta*). [Jaimini 9.4.42].
The removal [of the milk] is for the sake of enjoining another substance, as in the case of the *caru* and the *payaḥ*;
the mention of "boiled" (*śṛta*) is for the purpose of characterization.
However, because the various mixings (*śrayaṇa*) are unprecedented, their injunction must be for the purpose of offering (*pradāna*).
Or rather, it is a subordinate factor (guṇa), because its purpose is to serve as a support;
and because there is no specific designation [of it as primary]; and because the Vedic text (śruti) indicates that it is subordinate to that.

And it is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) because its purpose is that [purpose]; and because it exists for the sake of a consecration (*saṃskāra*), for this reason also it is not primary. Regarding the discarding of those animals over which the fire has been carried around (*paryagnikṛta*), its purpose is for that [consecration], just like the placing of bricks (*upadhāna*).
Or rather, there is a prohibition of the remainder because of the absence of the purpose, as in the case of [the *iḍā*] ending;
and because of the priority of the word, the expression "he concludes" is appropriate only when [the sacrifice] has not yet commenced.

(Jaimini 9.4.52–53) Because the commencement is the cause of the sacrifice, in the event of a prohibition, there would be no performance of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), since they are brought about by that [commencement], just as when the *prayāja* offerings are prohibited, the taking up of the clarified butter (*ājya*) is likewise suspended. (Jaimini 9.4.54)
Or it would be a ritual action because of its delimitation; otherwise, there would be the abandonment of everything.
(Jaimini 9.4.55) It would be a substitute for the *ājyasaṃsthā* because of the relinquishing of the substance. (Jaimini 9.4.56) Because of the statement regarding completion. (Jaimini 9.4.57)
Or rather, there would be an injunction [for the offering] because it is not distinguished from other acts that involve the relinquishing of the substance; Jaimini 9.4.58.
And he shows by means of a well-known conclusion that the *vanaspati* [offering] is not a sacrifice; Jaimini 9.4.59.
It should be a formal conclusion (*saṃsthā*) because it has that same deity; Jaimini 9.4.60.
Because of the extension [of the rule] to another context, the entire ritual procedure would apply.
Or rather, the naming, the consecration, and the substance should be performed for that specific purpose, because they are intended for that purpose;
for those [elements] are not specifically distinguished [from the original]. (Jaimini 10.1.1–3)
The *iṣṭi* should be excluded from those [acts] that have become subsidiaries because of its connection with the commencement, since the commencement is connected with the principal act.

(Jaimini 10.1.4) And it should be excluded from all commencements other than the principal one because of its connection with something else, as it is not a subsidiary thereof. (Jaimini 10.1.5) But in that case, it would be like the *prayāja* offerings. (Jaimini 10.1.6)
Nor [is it so] because it is a subordinate part [of another rite], Jaimini 10.1.7; and because they form a single syntactical unit, Jaimini 10.1.8.

Furthermore, the ritual action, being for the purpose of connecting with a substance, would cease [to apply] due to the absence of that purpose, since its subservience is established by direct scriptural statement, Jaimini 10.1.9.

But in the case of the sacrificial post (*sthāṇu*), because it is merely a location, its non-removal would be understood [as the rule]. (Jaimini 10.1.10) Or rather, because it is a subordinate element (*śeṣa*), it should be understood as a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*).
(Jaimini 10.1.11) And the designation (*samākhyāna*) is likewise. (Jaimini 10.1.12)
And the wording of the mantra is likewise [indicative]; Jaimini 10.1.13. And because of that same principle, it applies to the *prayāja* offerings; Jaimini 10.1.14.
And because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*); Jaimini 10.1.15.
If it is argued that the Ājyabhāga fire is likewise [a different deity], [we reply:
on account of the specific designation, it is a different deity;
and because of its equality.
If it is argued that [the rule] applies even to the animal sacrifice, [we reply]:
No, because of the statement regarding what has not yet come into being,
and because of the observation of an indicative mark.
Or rather, it should be a subordinate element (*guṇa*), like the potsherds, because it is a modification of that which has become subordinate.

(Jaimini 10.1.22) Or rather, because it is a residual element (*śeṣa*), its refinement (*saṃskāra*) should be understood, like the utterance *svāhā*, since the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) are connected with a purpose. (Jaimini 10.1.23) And there is the mention of failure (*vyṛddha*) in the case of a conflict, because [the rite] is for that purpose. (Jaimini 10.1.24)
If it is argued that [the term] applies even to the qualities (*guṇa*), [we reply]:
No, because there is no sublation, as in the case of *karāla*. And when there is a collective performance of the cups (*graha*), that statement applies because it is for their sake.

And that statement [is made] in the absence of a *graha*; (Jaimini 10.1.28) and since the causality of the deity is well-established, he shows it by means of that. (Jaimini 10.1.29) The logical justification is not contradictory; because of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), there should be a modification of the existing substance, as in the case of the boiled milk. (Jaimini 10.1.30)

That [mantra] would have two purposes, because both are directly stated in the scripture; however, since there is a conflict, its status as a modification (*vikāra*) is asserted on account of that purpose, while its character as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is also maintained. (Jaimini 10.1.31) In the case of a conflict, there should be a modification of the name (*ākhyāvikāra*) for those [mantras].
(Jaimini 10.1.32) Or rather, it is a repetition, like the *prayāja* offerings; a portion [of the mantra] has a different deity. (Jaimini 10.1.33)

The *caru* should be a modification of the *havis* (sacrificial oblation), because of its connection with the act of sacrifice; and also because it is understood in its conventional sense. Alternatively, it is boiled rice (*odana*), because of its connection with food.
Not so, because it would have two purposes (Jaimini 10.1.37).
Or rather, it is a modification of the potsherd, because in the case of doubt, both the purpose and the logical consistency support this (Jaimini 10.1.38).
And because of the distinction between the subordinate and the principal (Jaimini 10.1.39).

Because upon hearing that [word], it is another oblation; and because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga); and because it is boiled rice (odana), since it is what is employed. Jaimini 10.1.40–42.
And because of the designation as something unprecedented (Jaimini 10.1.43);
likewise, there is the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga) [to that effect] (Jaimini 10.1.44).
It should be performed on a potsherd by its original nature, because no other [substratum] is prescribed (Jaimini 10.1.45).

Or rather, because there is a contradiction in the case of one [vessel]. (Jaimini 10.1.46) Or rather not, because of the connection with a different purpose; for in the case of the *apūpa*, the connection with cooking is for the purpose of holding [the dough], whereas in the case of the *caru*, it occurs by virtue of the purpose [of cooking the grain]; thus, the acquisition of a vessel would occur through that purpose. Since there is no specific distinction, there would be no restriction [to a particular type of vessel]. (Jaimini 10.1.47) Or rather, in the case of the *caru*, [a specific vessel is required] because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*). (Jaimini 10.1.48)
In that case, grinding should take place because its purpose is not lost; Jaimini 10.1.49.
Or rather, there is no performance [of grinding] because it is the cause for the cake; Jaimini 10.1.50.
And the kneading is for the sake of the sacrificial ball; Jaimini 10.1.51.
And the pouring together [of the grains] is for that purpose; Jaimini 10.1.52.
The heating is because of the cooking below; Jaimini 10.1.53. And the placing [of the potsherds] is for that purpose; Jaimini 10.1.54.
Because it is broad and smooth, it is like a forest cake (Jaimini 10.1.55);
and because it is for the purpose of baking on top, it is an addition (abhyūha) (Jaimini 10.1.56);
likewise, there is the act of kindling (avajvalana) (Jaimini 10.1.57).
The drawing out [of the grains] and the placing down [of the offerings] should be performed, because they are not explicitly prohibited in the archetype (prakṛti). Jaimini 10.1.58.
In the case of the *kṛṣṇala* berries, there would be an omission [of these acts], because their purpose is lost. Jaimini 10.2.1.
Or rather, they should be performed, because they are directly enjoined, just like the act of offering (*pradāna*). Jaimini 10.2.2.
The spreading [of the base] and the sprinkling [of butter] should not be performed, because they serve the purpose of making [the offering] immortal.

(Jaimini 10.2.3) Or rather, they should be performed, because they are explanatory statements (*arthavāda*) and because they are the cause of the mixture. (Jaimini 10.2.4) Or rather, they are not performed, because of the statement that the fourfold portion is obtained together; thus, when complete, it is again a fourfold portion. (Jaimini 10.2.5)

Or rather, the action is primary because of the measurement of the principal portions; it possesses that quality by virtue of the commonality [of the procedure], because those [portions] consist of a single cutting-off (avadāna). And there is an attainment [of the number] because the number is the same.
If [the portion] is already present, the statement regarding its attainment is redundant (Jaimini 10.2.9).
But there is an option because of the single cutting-off (avadāna) (Jaimini 10.2.10).

However, if there were a modification of the whole, the repetition would be purposeless; for the other oblation would [then] belong to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, since it would be improper for the other [to be modified otherwise] (Jaimini 10.2.11).

Or rather, it is not an action because it is intended for the purpose of conjunction; therefore, it possesses the capacity for attainment. (Jaimini 10.2.12) But because the portions [of the soma] serve as the objects [of consumption], it would not be an action. (Jaimini 10.2.13) Or rather, it should be so, because we observe the act of setting aside. (Jaimini 10.2.14)

The statement regarding the consumption of the clarified butter (*ājya*) should apply to the archetype (*prakṛti*), because [the sacrificer] has no share [in it]. (Jaimini 10.2.15) Or rather, the statement refers to the gold, because the clarified butter is subordinate to the act of giving, just like the gift itself. (Jaimini 10.2.16) In the case of the single offering, there is simultaneity for the Brahman’s portions, because they are prescribed as being performed together in the archetype. (Jaimini 10.2.17)
And their universality would follow from their [general] application; Jaimini 10.2.18.
Or rather, there is the removal of the persons, because they are not to be mentioned; Jaimini 10.2.19.
Due to the removal of the persons, they have their own time. Jaimini 10.2.20.
Because they have the same purpose, there should be no distinction [between them].
(Jaimini 10.2.21) The gift to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should be for the sake of merit alone, because of the force of the verb "to give" (*dadāti*).
(Jaimini 10.2.22) Or rather, it is for the purpose of hiring, because of its connection with the ritual action, as is seen in common worldly practice. (Jaimini 10.2.23)
And because of the statement regarding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); Jaimini 10.2.24.
Nor could he be directed by another, for he would have been hired, since the ritual action is for the sake of another; Jaimini 10.2.25.
And because of the statement regarding being hired; Jaimini 10.2.26.
Because of the statement regarding wages [being paid] on the very day of the performance; Jaimini 10.2.27.
And because of the praise [of the sacrifice] as being without a separate agent (naiṣkartṛka); Jaimini 10.2.28.
And the consumption of the remnants is likewise; Jaimini 10.2.29.

Or rather, the ritual action belongs to the substance, because it exists for the sake of another; and because of equality in the case of the subsidiary. Because that is seen in the case of the owner, by virtue of that commonality, the others are likewise so.
And likewise, there is the observation of another matter:

[Jaimini 10.2.33] "The choosing of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) would not take place in a *sattra* sacrifice, because it is for the purpose of hiring, and because [the sacrificers] themselves perform the work. [Jaimini 10.2.34] "And there is no purchase [of priests], because that is for their sake. [Jaimini 10.2.35]

And there would be a prohibition, as in the case of the ritual action; (Jaimini 10.2.36). Or rather, it should apply to one who has already arrived, because it is merely a property; (Jaimini 10.2.37). It is not so, because of the word "dakṣiṇā"; therefore, it must be a permanent restatement. (Jaimini 10.2.38).

The *udavasānīya* sacrifice should possess the characteristics of a *sattra*, because it is a subordinate part of it; therefore, in that context, the act of giving would be merely a ritual duty (*dharmamātra*).

But this is not so, because [the *udavasānīya*] is the archetype (*prakṛti*) and because it is enjoined as a separate act. However, on account of the specific scriptural statement, there should be a simultaneous performance of those [acts], as in the case of the two sacrifices.
In that case, they should appoint other officiating priests (ṛtvij),
because there is no prohibition against doing so individually, and because in the archetype (prakṛti) there is a connection with only one [priest];
and also because in the Kāmeṣṭi sacrifice, the word "giving" (dāna) is used.
Or rather, there is the statement because of its being a sacrificial session (sattra).

(Jaimini 10.2.45) And because of the injunction regarding one who is hated, there is the removal of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). (Jaimini 10.2.46) The sacrifice for the bones (asthiyajña) should belong to the others because there is no prohibition; whereas for the bones themselves, there is a prohibition. (Jaimini 10.2.47)

The application [of the mantra] should be as much as has been stated. (Jaimini 10.2.48) But if, on account of the scriptural statement, their recitation (*japa*) and consecration (*saṃskāra*) are rendered purposeless by the context, then the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) should be performed for that purpose.
(Jaimini 10.2.49) However, it should be performed for the sake of the sacrifice, because it serves as a subordinate element (*guṇabhūta*). (Jaimini 10.2.49*)
But optional rites do not exist [in the *udavasānīya*], because desires do not arise from knowledge, as is stated for the other [sacrifice]; Jaimini 10.2.50.
And they do not exist because there is an absence of purpose, like the *sūktavāka*; Jaimini 10.2.51.
Or rather, they may exist because they are explanatory passages (*arthavāda*); Jaimini 10.2.52.
Because there is no mention of desire, that [desire] is absent in the other case; Jaimini 10.2.53.
Or rather, there may be desires for the Hotṛ; Jaimini 10.2.54.
No, because he does not eat that [portion]; Jaimini 10.2.55.
Jaimini 10.2.56: There is no completion of the *sarvasvāra* sacrifice upon the death [of the sacrificer], because the ritual is connected with the living.
Jaimini 10.2.57: Or rather, there should be [completion], because both [the living and the dead] are directly enjoined [as participants].
Jaimini 10.2.58: Once [the sacrificer] has passed away, [the ritual should be completed], as in the case of the *asthiyajña* (bone-sacrifice).
The formula "live" is not [an injunction], because life is the object of the benediction; [Jaimini 10.2.59].
Or rather, it is a formula because of its participation [in the rite], prior to what was stated;
[Jaimini 10.2.60]. It would be a ritual act for those [items] that are merely properties (dharma); [Jaimini 10.2.61].
And when there is the omission of a subordinate quality, the primary act remains;
[however,] because the number is subordinate to it, the number should be omitted due to the omission of the handful.
It is not so, because it is a subordinate part of the *nirvāpa* (the pouring out).
The number, however, is a modification of that [original] because of its commonality with the injunction and because of its connection; furthermore, it applies beyond the handful.
(Jaimini 10.2.65) It is not so, because of the connection with the injunction and because of the application of the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*).
(Jaimini 10.2.66) But in the case of the innate [substance], there would be a modification by way of the substance, because it is not something produced [by ritual action]. (Jaimini 10.2.67)
But in the case of an occasional rite (*naimittika*), because it is something to be performed, there would be the occurrence of that [archetypal form] from the archetype (*prakṛti*).

(Jaimini 10.2.68) In the event of a conflict, there should be an omission of the archetypal qualities because of that specific statement; for by that [statement], there is a connection with the ritual action. (Jaimini 10.2.69) There should be a prohibition of the others. (Jaimini 10.2.70)
And because of the prohibition [Jaimini 10.2.71].
In the absence of a purpose, it would be a mere preparatory rite (saṃskāra) [Jaimini 10.2.72].
And when there is a reversal due to the purpose, its true nature [as that purpose] would indeed prevail because it is for the sake of that [purpose] [Jaimini 10.2.73].

In a modified sacrifice (vikṛti), because it possesses the same verbal designation as the archetype (prakṛti), there is the addition of further qualities of the principal [sacrifice] due to their proximity.
(Jaimini 10.3.1) It is like the archetype, and there is no obstruction to that [principal]. (Jaimini 10.3.2) And because of the sovereign power of the injunction. (Jaimini 10.3.3)

But the principal [rite], when conjoined with its subsidiaries, would likewise produce a new transcendental result (*apūrva*), because it is characterized by an injunction; for every injunction that possesses a prior [model] is applied without distinction. (Jaimini 10.3.4) And an injunction regarding subsidiaries cannot apply to what is not a subsidiary.

(Jaimini 10.3.5) Because of the unity of expression for the ritual action, when there is proximity, the connection of the name with the injunction indicates a modification of that [action] through a quality, since the word is directed toward the injunction and the quality is something to be taught. (Jaimini 10.3.6)
And because a name has no causal efficiency; Jaimini 10.3.7.
And the power [of the name] over the quality is equal; Jaimini 10.3.8.
If it is argued that everything is thus primary; Jaimini 10.3.9.

Because they are conjoined with that which has become such [the archetype], there would be injunctions according to the purpose; and the status of being an injunction is indeed not different in this way, because the archetypal elements are connected with the modified rites. Therefore, everything is for the sake of the primary rite. And because of the equality of its origin, there would be entitlement through the purificatory acts.
Hiraṇyagarbha belongs to the first [offering], because of the indicative mark of the mantra (Jaimini 10.3.13),
and because there is no conflict with the archetype (prakṛti) (Jaimini 10.3.14);
or rather, it belongs to the latter, because of the requirement for the mantra's meaning (Jaimini 10.3.15).
Jaimini 10.3.16: Because of the extension of the injunction, there should be a modification when that [term] is heard, since the qualities are to be taught.
Jaimini 10.3.17: And because it is observed to be non-mantric in the preceding case. Jaimini 10.3.18: But in the case of a consecration, it is a different action, because it serves as its injunction.

And because there is no contradiction with the original nature [of the substance]. (Jaimini 10.3.19) But since there is an injunction regarding that [substance] in the case of doubt, it should have the meaning of that [injunction], because of the word [used].
(Jaimini 10.3.20) And because of the capacity for refinement (*saṃskāra*) and the connection with a quality (*guṇa*). (Jaimini 10.3.21)
Because of the contradiction, it would pertain to the context of the ritual action.

(Jaimini 10.3.22) "He consecrates with six [verses]"; there is a modification of the mantras for those [actions], because of their connection with the Vedic revelation. (Jaimini 10.3.23) But because of the repetition, it pertains to the principal [action]. (Jaimini 10.3.24)
The mantra-ritual should be performed by repetition (Jaimini 10.3.25).
Or rather, because each mantra is distinct, there should be no omission of the archetypal elements; moreover, repetition of what has already been performed is improper (Jaimini 10.3.26).
Furthermore, sequence is not possible in the case of repetition, because it is contingent upon specific occasions (Jaimini 10.3.27).
And he shows their distinctness:
"Nor would there be a designation [of them] due to non-distinction" (Jaimini 10.3.29).

"In the case of a modification of the quality [performed] on account of a specific occasion for the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should be additional, because of its connection with the scriptural statement" (Jaimini 10.3.30).
Because the others remain [in their place], they are according to their respective positions. (Jaimini 10.3.31) But there is a modification because the optional rites are not in the context.
(Jaimini 10.3.32) And there is a doubt regarding the cessation, for both are heard in the scripture. (Jaimini 10.3.33)
The garment and the calf [are included] because of their commonality.

(Jaimini 10.3.34) On account of the necessary implication (*arthāpatti*), they should possess those properties, because of their connection with the designation of the cause. (Jaimini 10.3.35) In the act of giving, the cooking is characterized by its purpose. (Jaimini 10.3.36)
Because it is the cause of the preparation of the food already present in the vessel; likewise for the sprinkling [of clarified butter]. (Jaimini 10.3.37) / Similarly for the pouring over.
(Jaimini 10.3.38) / In the proximity of an injunction regarding a substance, the number [mentioned] would be subordinate to them, because it is a quality. (Jaimini 10.3.39)

But because the qualities are equal, [the rule applies] to one due to its connection with the direct Vedic statement (śruti). Or rather, it should apply to that which is in proximity, for the syntactical connection (vākya) establishes the relationship. However, since they are enjoined equally with the others without being specifically connected, there should be eligibility for all.

Because there is no connection [with the sacrifice] when the injunction is heard, the eligibility should pertain only to those born of the same caste, as this avoids contradicting the direct Vedic statement regarding the sacrifice; furthermore, the meaning of the word is like that in common worldly usage. Moreover, because of the division [of the property] from its origin, it belongs to those accompanied by cattle.
There is no restriction, because there is no distinction [Jaimini 10.3.46];
or rather, it should belong to cows, because they possess the relevant status [Jaimini 10.3.47];
because of the indicative mark [Jaimini 10.3.48].
And because of the observation of indicative marks (liṅga). Jaimini 10.3.49.
In that case, there is a distribution [of the gift], because the acts of giving are distinct. Jaimini 10.3.50.
And because of the hiring (parikraya), as is seen in the world. Jaimini 10.3.51.
And it also shows a distribution:
"It should be equal, because there is no scriptural statement to the contrary" (Jaimini 10.3.52);
"Or rather, because of the inequality of the ritual acts" (Jaimini 10.3.53–54).

They would be unequal in the act of purchase, as they are designated as distinct in the scriptural injunction; it is not appropriate for [the term] to apply to the ritual action through purchase, because a specific distinction is observed in the case of the *abhyudaya* sacrifice. Jaimini 10.3.55.

In the phrase "his [sacrifice] has a cow," since cows are enjoined as distinct in the archetype (*prakṛti*), it should be a modification of that based on the commonality, just as the *iṣṭi* is [modified] by means of a word denoting a quality. Jaimini 10.3.56. Or rather, there is unity for the entire [sacrifice] due to its connection with the rite; because the purpose of the sacrificial fees is one, the qualities [of the fee] serve a single function, and thus in the modified rite (*vikṛti*) it should be understood according to the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). Therefore, this is indeed due to the connection with the ritual actions. Jaimini 10.3.57.
Because there is no basis for the injunctions, there should be a restriction by means of the inferential mark (liṅga). [The rule] "one" or "five" is like that of the cow (dhenu).
And [the same applies to] the three-year-old calf (trivatsa).

And likewise there is the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga): "But some [hold] that because it has become a scriptural statement, [the number applies] to the cows by means of the number and the specific gender.
"If it be argued that the two *prākāśas* are likewise [to be understood]," [it is replied: Jaimini 10.3.63.

However, because it refers to a constituent part and because its original form is distinct, there should be a modification of the quality "this-ness" (idantā). (Jaimini 10.3.64) And like the word *dhenu*, the horse-sacrifice fee belongs to the Brahman priest; thus there is a removal of the person, just as in the case of the gold.
(Jaimini 10.3.65) But some [hold] that, due to the connection with the agent, it is like the garland, by virtue of its specific gender. (Jaimini 10.3.66)
Or rather, because it pertains to that [context], there should be a modification as in the case of gold;
and thus there is the *somacamasa* (Soma-cup).
Or rather, there is a complete modification because of the prohibition of animals for the sake of the sacrifice.
If it is argued that [the gift] to the Brahman priest is not distinct [from the sacrificial fee], [we reply:

because the relinquishing [of the fee] is for the sake of the sacrifice, there would be a performance of what is prohibited; furthermore, the purpose of the sacrificial fees would not be merely secondary. If, however, that [gift] belongs to the Brahman priest, it would be a modification (*vikāra*) of that [general fee].
Or rather, everything [is lost] due to the removal of the person, because those [priests] are the primary agents of the sacrifice.

(Jaimini 10.3.73) In the case of the *yajuryukta* [chariot], the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should be a modification for the Adhvaryu. (Jaimini 10.3.74) Or rather, because it is established by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), his share is restricted from among all [the fees]. (Jaimini 10.3.75)

Jaimini 10.4.1: Due to the non-connection with the characteristic marks of the archetype, there should be an additional performance of the ritual refinements (*saṃskāra*) in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
Jaimini 10.4.2: When there is a connection with the characteristic marks of the injunction (*codanā*), that modification should be understood [as applying] because of the proximity of the archetype.
Jaimini 10.4.3: But in all cases, the mention of the cups (*graha*) should be additional, just as in the archetype.

Because it forms a single syntactical unit with more [than one] [sacrificial animals], because of the observation of an indicative mark, and because of the traditional teaching regarding the Prājāpatya [animals]. (Jaimini 10.4.4–6)

On account of the observation of indicative marks, [the rule] applies to the *āmana* vessels. (Jaimini 10.4.7) In the case of the *upaga* vessels, it should be as with the *śara* grass, because of the connection with the indicative mark of the archetype.
(Jaimini 10.4.8) But because it would otherwise be purposeless, there should be an addition. (Jaimini 10.4.9)

And because of the connection with another [element] in the case of the *saṃskāra* (preparatory rite), [it is] like the *prayāja* [offerings]. If this is argued, [we reply]: no, because the purpose is different.
But regarding the covering, because they serve a single purpose, there should be a modification of the original;
or rather, it should be additional because it serves a different purpose;
and the text also indicates their combination.

Because another meaning is heard [in the case] of the *sāman*, no modification would be perceived. (Jaimini 10.4.16) But when no other meaning is heard, there should be a modification of the original (*prākṛta*) because it is a subordinate element (*śeṣatvāt*).
(Jaimini 10.4.17) Because it applies to all without distinction. (Jaimini 10.4.18)
Either [the modification] would apply to one [verse] due to the force of the scriptural statement, because there is no modification of the original form;

or, when there is an increase in the *stoma*, there should be an addition [of verses], whereas when there is no increase, there should be a modification of the substance, because the other alternative is not heard in scripture.
Both [addition and modification] should apply to the *pavamāna* [laud], because an insertion (*āvāpa*) and an extraction (*udvāpa*) are observed therein.
But the words [of the mantra] are [authoritative], because they convey what is not already known (apūrvatvāt).

(Jaimini 10.4.22) If the injunctive word were the mantra, there would be the existence [of the injunction] through it; by that, there would be the impulsion (codanā). (Jaimini 10.4.23) Or rather, because the impulsion is one for the remaining [parts], therefore it is heard everywhere. (Jaimini 10.4.24)
Likewise, in the subsequent extension (*uttarā tati*), because it has that as its archetype (*tatprakṛtitvāt*),
when there is a scriptural mention of a quality (*guṇaśruti*) regarding the archetypal [rite], there should be a designation by means of that which possesses the quality (*saguṇena*).
Or rather, there should be no modification (*avikāraḥ*), because the meaning and the word do not depart [from their original state], just as in the case of a substance (*dravyavat*).

Likewise, there would be a designation by means of what is enjoined due to the non-inherence in the commencement; for the meaning is inherently connected to the direct audition (*śruti*), and if it were not so stated, the teaching regarding the subordinate quality (*guṇa-śāstra*) would be purposeless.

(Jaimini 10.4.28) In the case of substances, because they pertain to the commencement, there is a modification in the meaning according to their capacity. (Jaimini 10.4.29) The [cup] containing *budhna* is like the *pavamāna*, because of the specific indication. (Jaimini 10.4.30)
Jaimini 10.4.31: Due to the specific instruction regarding the mantras, there should be no modification of the deity.

Jaimini 10.4.32: Because of the difference between the injunction and the explanatory passage (*nigama*), and because the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) has that [archetypal sacrifice, *prakṛti*] as its model, there should be a distinction in the modified sacrifice as well.
Jaimini 10.4.33: Or rather, it is as stated; because of the contradiction, there is no such injunction.

If there is a change in the deity of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, the word [denoting that deity] would cease [to be used] because it refers to that specific [deity]. (Jaimini 10.4.34) Or rather, there is a connection [of the term] due to the necessity of the sense, since the designation arises from the ritual act. (Jaimini 10.4.35) When there is an omission of a quality of that which possesses qualities, in the *nigama* formulas, only what has been prescribed [should be used]. (Jaimini 10.4.36)

Because everything serves a single purpose, [the *sviṣṭakṛt*] should be included in the *anuyāja* as part of the insertion (*āvāpika*), since the subsidiary elements have a purpose through their connection with the primary meaning. (Jaimini 10.4.37) And because it says "he recites after," the act should be like a *śastra*, due to a separate injunction. (Jaimini 10.4.38–39)

Or rather, it is a modification (*saṃskāra*) because the word that has been enjoined is intended for the purpose of speaking; [this would be so] because it serves the purpose of indicating a quality (*guṇa*). But in the case of the *manotā*, there should be no modification because of the specific scriptural statement.
For the sake of the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra], there should be another [sāman] than the *rathantara*, because the verses have that as their source and because they are distinct;
or rather, it should be in its own source, because it is designated by the name "all" (*sarva*).
If it is argued that it is like the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), [we reply: no. *Jaimini Sūtra* 10.4.43–45.

Not due to the connection with the ritual action; because the latter two are effects, they follow the original model (Jaimini 10.4.46). Or rather, they have the same deity, because there is no division of the *tṛca* triplet (Jaimini 10.4.47–48).

If the deities of the *grahas* are different, there would be no modification in the *stotra* and *śastra*, because they constitute the ritual action itself. (Jaimini 10.4.49) In the case of *pṛṣadājya*, because both [the deity and the substance] are consumed, there should be a mention of the curd (*dadhi*) in the *nigamas*, since it is the drinkable portion that is to be indicated.
(Jaimini 10.4.50) Or rather, it is not so, because it is for the sake of another, like the term "sacrificer" (*yajñapati*). (Jaimini 10.4.51)

Or rather, [the term applies] because the invocation has that as its purpose; (Jaimini 10.4.52) or rather not, because it is a word for a consecration; (Jaimini 10.4.53) or rather it should apply, because it denotes a substance. (Jaimini 10.4.54)

But because the curd is subordinate, the *ājyapāḥ* (butter-drinkers) should be the recipients, since its subordination is established by the Vedic text through the primacy of the clarified butter (*ājya*).

Or rather, the curd should be the primary element, because of its connection with both the first and the last [of the deities]. Or again, because the clarified butter is primary, the term for the consecration (*saṃskāra*) should be used figuratively in the designation for the sake of the subordinate element.
Or rather, because it is a modification of the expression, there might be an indication by that [term]; Jaimini 10.4.58.
Or rather, it would not be so, because it is an instruction regarding a subordinate quality (guṇa-śāstra); Jaimini 10.4.59.
When parts of things arranged in a sequence are grasped, there should be elision of the final [element], as in the case of grammatical augmentations; Jaimini 10.5.1.
And because of the observation of indicative marks (liṅga). Jaimini 10.5.2.
Or rather, there is an option (vikalpa) because of equality. Jaimini 10.5.3.
There should be an addition at the end according to the sequence. Jaimini 10.5.4.
The indicative mark (*liṅga*) is not specific, for that statement refers to the number.
(Jaimini 10.5.5) Or rather, the application should begin from the start, because the commencement is at the beginning; however, due to the explicit statement, there should be a rule for the end.

(Jaimini 10.5.6) In the *ekatrika* sacrifice, [the rule applies] to the *tṛca*s and so forth in the midday pressing, because the meters are established by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). (Jaimini 10.5.7)
Or rather, [the rule applies] from the beginning, because that is the logical principle and the other case is merely inferential (Jaimini 10.5.8).
And [the arrangement] should be according to the placement, like the archetype, because there is only a modification of the number (Jaimini 10.5.9).
The triplet should be placed on the first two verses of the *tṛca* (Jaimini 10.5.10).
Or rather, because the nature of the *stoma* consists in its repetition within a single [verse]. Jaimini 10.5.11.

But in the case of injunctions, because they involve something not previously established (*apūrva*), there would be a restriction of the ritual properties (*dharma*) by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*). Jaimini 10.5.12.
However, the attainment [of the result] follows from the connection with the word "night" (*rātri*). Jaimini 10.5.13.

But in the case of unprecedented numbers, there should be an option among all [the verses], because all are purposeful. (Jaimini 10.5.14) When the *stoma* is increased, the fulfillment of the number is achieved by the repetition of the original verses, because the number is a term denoting a quality and no other [method] is heard in the text.
(Jaimini 10.5.15) Or rather, it is by way of addition (*āgama*), because repetition is not what is heard in the scripture. (Jaimini 10.5.16)

And because number is established as distinct [from the substance]; because it is expressed by a word denoting distance; and because there is no modification of what has been stated. (Jaimini 10.5.17–19)
If it is argued that [the rule does not apply] because there is no scriptural statement [to that effect], [we reply:
there would be a scriptural injunction regarding the measure of those things impelled by the purpose. Furthermore, the mention of "insertion" (āvāpa) is not possible in the case of mere repetition.
And because of the inherent capacity for the production of the *sāmans*;
[if it is argued] "this applies even to the *dhurya* [stotras]," [we reply] no,
because they possess the nature of repetition.
In the *vahiṣpavamāna*, there is no addition of *ṛc* verses because of the unity of the *sāman*.
However, the completion of the number is achieved through repetition, because the *sāmidhenī* verses have repetition as their archetype.
If it is argued that this is not so because there is no specific distinction [in the case of the *vahiṣpavamāna*], [the response follows].
It might be that one should practice [the rite] like the archetype because it possesses that nature, until the completion of the count;
or rather, only as much as has been stated, because its measure has been fixed; and because more [repetitions] are observed. Jaim_10.5.29–31.
If it is argued that [the rule] applies even to ritual actions (*karma*), [we reply]:
No, because it is not enjoined [there]. (Jaimini 10.5.32) The *ṣoḍaśin* cup is a modification (*vaikṛta*) because its complete prescription occurs therein. (Jaimini 10.5.34)
And because the absence [of the rite] is observed in the archetype; Jaimini 10.5.35.
And because it is not mentioned as part of the sacrifice; Jaimini 10.5.36.
Or rather, it belongs to the archetype because it is prescribed therein; Jaimini 10.5.37.
And because of the observation of the original form [Jaimini 10.5.38];
the traditional text is for the purpose of exclusion [Jaimini 10.5.39];
the observation of non-existence has been stated [Jaimini 10.5.40].
On account of its qualities, it is not part of the sacrifice; Jaimini [says] its drawing is from the Āgrayaṇa vessel (Jaim_10.5.42),
and also from the Ukthya by virtue of a scriptural statement (Jaim_10.5.43).
It should occur at the third pressing because of the explicit statement;
because the word *parāc* refers to that [third pressing] when there is no repetition;
and because it expresses the non-interruption of the *ukthya*.
Or rather, there is a separation from the *āgrayaṇa* because the word "parāk" denotes a location, as in the case of the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*).

(Jaimini 10.5.47) There is a separation because of the commonality of the *stoma*. (Jaimini 10.5.48) Due to its connection with the *ukthya* and *agniṣṭoma*, it should be without *stotra* and *śastra*, for if it were otherwise, there would be a difference in the sacrificial terminus (*saṃsthā*). (Jaimini 10.5.49)
Or rather, it is a weapon already consecrated, because it is an integral part of that [rite];
and because of the observation of an indicative mark;
and because of the scriptural statement, there is a difference in the form of the sacrifice.

It is taken at the Atirātra sacrifices because of its absence [elsewhere]; or rather, it is a subsidiary element because it is prescribed as an independent injunction (anārabhya-vidhāna). It should be understood that for the Ahīna sacrifice, it is taken on every fourth day through repetition, just like eating.
Alternatively, because it possesses a number, it is taken as applying to various *ahīna* sacrifices, just like the *pakṣa* [sacrifice], since the purpose of the number exists in that single instance.

(Jaimini 10.5.56) At the meal, there should be that same number. (Jaimini 10.5.57) Since there is no *sāman* in the *jagatsāman*, that which is named after it should be a *sāman* derived from the *ṛc*. (Jaimini 10.5.58)
In the case of a *ubhaya-sāman*, there should be an optional alternative for the contingent rite because of its equality;
or it should be restricted by the primary [sāman];
or, due to the obstruction of the occasion, the ritual act belonging to the sacrifice should take place. (Jaimini 10.5.59–61)
Because of the mention of the Aindravāyava cup first, there should be a displacement [of the order] from the beginning (Jaimini 10.5.62).

Or rather, because there is no difference in their ritual properties, the priority of those possessing those properties is stated according to their own position due to the context (prakaraṇa) (Jaimini 10.5.63).
And because of the connection with the stream [of soma] (Jaimini 10.5.64).

But in the case of a connection with a specific desire (*kāmasaṃyoga*), there would be a displacement [of the ritual] from the beginning on account of the scriptural statement (Jaimini 10.5.65). Or rather, because of the connection with the word "first" (*agra*) regarding those locations, that injunction of desire (*kāmaśāstra*) should be connected with them, since it is permanently connected [with them] (Jaimini 10.5.66).
And in the subsequent [passages], the word "first" (*agra*) should apply to those that begin with them, just as before (Jaimini 10.5.67).
Or rather, there is a displacement of the first [cup] for the sake of the permanent [rule], because it is not connected with that;
and he shows this displacement, because the place for the first cup, dedicated to Indra and Vāyu, has already been established beforehand. (Jaimini 10.5.68–70)
And because they possess equal characteristics; likewise, there is the observation of an indicative mark;
and the placing [of the offering] also [applies], because it is a subordinate element.
And because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga);
and the offering [is performed] like the placing [of the oblation]. Or rather, it is not so, because the offering is the primary act, whereas the placing is subordinate, and thus it is not like that.
In the *tryanīkā* sacrifice, as stated in the *Nyāya*, the traditional injunction (*āmnāna*) would be for the purpose of [specifying] subordinate qualities (*guṇārtha*).
(Jaimini 10.5.77) Alternatively, in the case of multi-day sacrifices (*ahargaṇa*), there should be a uniform rule (*samānavidhāna*), just as in the case of the *agni*.
(Jaimini 10.5.78) The expanded (*vyūḍha*) and contracted (*samūḍha*) forms of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) should have a uniform rule, just like the *pṛṣṭha* chants. (Jaimini 10.5.79)
Either the expanded form (vyūḍha) should be a modification of the condensed form (samūḍha), because of the observation of indicative marks;
because of the connection with specific desires;
