and its application occurs in both ways because of the unity of the ritual action.

The threefold series (*tryanīkā*) should undergo rotation like the *ekādaśinī* sacrifice; or rather, there should be an expansion in its own place, because the number [of days] is not directly perceived [as fixed]. Furthermore, since the *āgrayaṇa* cup is seen at the rotation of the *pṛṣṭhya* period, the *aindravāyava* cup should appear again at the thirty-third day upon the completion of the cycle.
In the case of the *aikādaśina* animals, there is a transposition [of the mantras] because of the explicit statement;
this is also because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*).

In the *vyūḍha* sacrifice, due to the transposition of the meters, the mantras for the *bhakṣa*, *pavamāna*, *paridhi*, and *kapāla* should follow their original order of occurrence, as in the case of *ūha*.
In a sacrifice, the *ekarca* verses should occupy the position [of the *sāman*], as in private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*);
or rather, they should be on the *tṛca* triplet, because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*).
Looking at the sun (*svardṛśam*) is merely a time-indication, because it serves the purpose of another.
Jaimini 10.6.4: Because the *pṛṣṭhya* [stotra] is prescribed simultaneously, it possesses two *sāmans*, just like the *ekāha*.
Jaimini 10.6.5: Or rather, when [the *pṛṣṭhya*] is divided, because there is a prescription for the whole, its division would be contradictory.
Jaimini 10.6.6: But there is a combination in the case of the *ekādaśina* animals, because they have that as their archetype.
And because of the prohibition of the *vihāra* [in the case of the *agniṣṭoma*]; Jaimini 10.6.7.
Or rather, there should be a division based on the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), as in common worldly practice; Jaimini 10.6.8.
And because the *vihāra* serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*); Jaimini 10.6.9.
And because of the proximity to that object;
[if it is argued] "the three are likewise," [we reply] no, because of their equality, like the *prayāja* offerings.

Because the term *pṛṣṭha* occurs in the phrase "on every *pṛṣṭha*," they would occupy a single location, since the *pṛṣṭha* has already been assigned a specific place. (Jaimini 10.6.13) But there would be a remoteness from the injunction. (Jaimini 10.6.14) Having the *Vairūpa* as its *sāman*, because of its connection with the sacrifice, it should have a single *sāman*, like the *Trivṛt*. (Jaimini 10.6.15)

Or rather, it is for the sake of the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra], because of its connection with the characteristic mark of the archetype (*prakṛti*). (Jaimini 10.6.16) If it is argued that it is "like the *trivṛt*," (Jaimini 10.6.17) [We reply:
No, because in the archetype there is no connection with the whole. (Jaimini 10.6.18)
If it is argued that this is not so because it is an injunction (vidhi), [we reply:
it would be so in a case of doubt, because that is the logical principle, since there is no division of the ritual action;
and because there is no modification of the archetype (prakṛti).

In the case of the *trivṛt*, there would be a modification of all numerical counts by virtue of its being a specific number; or rather, it belongs to the *stoma* because it possesses that characteristic mark. In the case of a sacrifice with both *sāmans*, there should be a division, as in the *viśvajit*.
Because it concerns the matter already asked about; and because of the observation of an indicative mark (Jaimini 10.6.25). And because of the observation of a sign (liṅga) (Jaimini 10.6.26):

the eating of the *rasa* [milk] at the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra] should take place when the *trayastriṃśa* day has been completed and concluded, because of its immediate sequence, as in the archetype (prakṛti) (Jaimini 10.6.27).
Or rather, it should be at the end, because its time has already been fixed;

and in the case of repetition, there is a repetition of that [act] because of the repeated performance of the ritual action. Or rather, it should be at the end, because its time has already been fixed.
But there would be a repetition [of the rite] when there is an intervention, because of the difference in time.
(Jaimini 10.6.31) The initiated ones do not eat honey, because they are under a vow of celibacy.
(Jaimini 10.6.32) They may eat it, because it is for the sake of the sacrifice. (Jaimini 10.6.33)
The *mānasa* [offering] should be an intermediate day, because there is a designation of distinction;
because it is praised along with that [preceding day];
and because there is an injunction subsequent to the end of the day.
In this case, the number is like that of the thousand [in the *sāhasra* sacrifice], Jaimini 10.6.37;
or rather, the day is a subordinate element because there is no separate injunction for it, Jaimini 10.6.38;
and also because of the statement regarding the release at the tenth [day], Jaimini 10.6.39.

"And [the phrase] 'on the tenth day' is so because of the scriptural statement of its quality; because of the consistency of the number; and because of the existence of one [animal] when there is a surplus of animals. (Jaimini 10.6.40–42)
The designation as praise is prohibited by the limb [of the rite], like a vow; Jaim_10.6.43.
Because of the scriptural statement, it does not end with that; Jaim_10.6.44.
One person performs the sacrificial session (sattra) as in the archetype; Jaim_10.6.45.
But [the sacrifice] would belong to many because of the statement. If it is argued that this is a mere reference (apadeśa),
we say no, because there is a singular designation.
And it demonstrates the co-residence [of the priests]. Jaimini 10.6.49:
Furthermore, the specific mention of "many" in reference to a single [entity] would be purposeless. Jaimini 10.6.50:
There should be other officiating priests (ṛtvij), as in the archetype (prakṛti). Jaimini 10.6.51.

Or rather, they should be the sacrificers, because of their connection with the designation [of the priests]; thus, the status of being a sacrificer should belong to them. (Jaimini 10.6.52) If it is argued that this is a refinement of the agent and should apply like the act of kindling the fire (*ādhāna*) because of a specific scriptural statement, (Jaimini 10.6.53) [We reply: It should be so in a case of doubt, because that is the logical principle, as in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*). (Jaimini 10.6.54)

If it be argued that those designated as "masters" (svāmin) should be like the *gṛhapati* [of the *sattras*], [we reply: no, because the term refers to what is well-known [in common usage], and because one who is not connected [to the ritual] cannot possess its specific characteristic. Furthermore, the designation of "consecrated" (*dīkṣita*) and "unconsecrated" (*adīkṣita*) would be untenable, since these two states are permanently inherent to the respective objects.
And because there is no giving of dakṣiṇā [Jaimini 10.6.58].

The twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha) has the nature of a sattra because of the injunction regarding sitting and subsistence, and because of the plurality of sacrificers, due to its connection with the term "sattra" [Jaimini 10.6.59]. It has the nature of an ahīna because of the injunction involving the verb "to sacrifice" (yajati), and because the number of the masters is not fixed [Jaimini 10.6.60].

Jaimini 10.6.61: Regarding the *ahīna* sacrifice, the scriptural injunction concerning the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) would constitute a distinct ritual act for each day, because it is a subordinate element (*guṇa*).
Jaimini 10.6.62: Or rather, because the entire [sacrifice] constitutes a single action, [the injunction applies to the whole].
Jaimini 10.6.63: Or, like the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), the scriptural injunction regarding the [fee] would be a subordinate element of the [daily] offerings.

But the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* belong to all [the sacrifices] because they constitute a single ritual action, just as in the archetype; therefore, there should be no modification of them.

(Jaimini 10.6.64) However, in the case of the *Dvādaśāha*, because of a specific scriptural injunction, there is a distinction of sacrificial fees for each day; since those [later sacrifices] have that [archetype] as their model, there should be a modification of their number. (Jaimini 10.6.65) Or rather, because the purchase [of services] is indivisible, there should be a modification of the whole. (Jaimini 10.6.66)

But there is a distinction due to the connection with specific qualities. (Jaimini 10.6.67) Every day, the entire consecration [is performed] as in the archetype, because all [consecrations] are subsidiary to all [the rites].
(Jaimini 10.6.68) If it is argued that this is not so because they serve a single purpose, (Jaimini 10.6.69) [we reply: no.

It might be so at the time of production because of the difference in time. (Jaimini 10.6.70) But rather, it is through the distribution [of the rite] because of the statement regarding the consecrations, as in the case of the Dvādaśāha sacrifice.

(Jaimini 10.6.71) When there is a designation of a substance by means of a characteristic mark (*liṅga*), there should be an application [of the rite] everywhere, because the characteristic mark applies to all cases, as in the case of the Āgneya [offering]. (Jaimini 10.6.72)

Or, because it serves as a remainder for the purpose [of the ritual], there may be a small quantity; and in that case, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) would have its efficacy. (Jaimini 10.6.73) In the *Āgneya* [offering], there is a complete injunction.

(Jaimini 10.6.74) Because the *ṛjīṣa* (the soma-residue) is the primary object, there should be the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the whole [residue] in a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*). (Jaimini 10.6.75)

Regarding the measuring and the bringing down [of the Soma], the cloth is the archetype (prakṛti) for the Soma sacrifice because of a specific scriptural statement. In that case, within a multi-day sacrificial session (ahargaṇa), the cloth would naturally be the archetype. One should produce the measurement in the archetype, because the bringing down [of the Soma] is observed to be performed by means of it.
Or, because there is no connection with the Vedic text regarding the taking [of the portions], it applies to the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) by virtue of the sense;
[thus] the animal is a single oblation (ekahaviṣṭva) because it is enjoined as a whole. Or rather, it is for each limb, like the drawing of cups (graha), because the limbs are conceived separately.

Because of the difference in the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), there is a repetition for the sake of the ritual; therefore, the cutting off (*avadāna*) should be performed from each of them. (Jaimini 10.7.3) Or rather, like the *ājyabhāga* offerings, because of the specific designation, there should be a restriction (*parisaṃkhyā*).
(Jaimini 10.7.4) Or else, intending to express that they consist of two cuttings, he would designate them specifically, because the animal sacrifice consists of five cuttings. (Jaimini 10.7.5)

Furthermore, the prohibition regarding the shoulder, head, back, and thigh would be purposeless if it were merely an exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) of those other than them, because they are intended for offering; thus, there would be a prohibition against offering them at all. Jaimini 10.7.6.
Or rather, it should be an exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*), because of the word "not to be cut off" (*anavadānīya*). Jaimini 10.7.7.
And because it is seen [to apply] even in the case of one who is not a Brāhmaṇa. Jaimini 10.7.8.
And because of the instruction regarding both the cooked and the uncooked, they are not remnants of the sacrifice, like the general rule [of disposal].

(Jaimini 10.7.9) The *sviṣṭakṛt* offering should be performed from the remnants of the sacrifice, as in the archetype. (Jaimini 10.7.10) Or rather, there should be a modification using three limbs, as in the case of the *śara* grass. (Jaimini 10.7.11)
The *adhyūdhnī* [portion] of the Hotṛ should be a modification of the *iḍā*-consumption, like the three parts (*tryaṅga*).
Or rather, since it is included in the remainder, there should be a restriction as in the case of the chariot. But this cannot be so, because it is not based on scriptural injunction.

Or rather, it may be a mere gift, because it is not connected with the word "eating" (bhakṣa). But since the giver is absent, it should be a modification of the eating of the *iḍā*, because it is indistinguishable with respect to the remnant.
And the *vaniṣṭhu* belongs to the *agnīdh* priest, like the *adhyūdhnī*.
Because he is not an ordinary priest (*aprākṛta*), the Maitrāvaruṇa should not consume [the portion]; Jaimini 10.7.18.
Or rather, there should be consumption because he is a modification (*vikāra*) of both the Hotṛ and the Adhvaryu, due to his connection with their respective duties; Jaimini 10.7.19.
He should receive two shares because he performs two functions; Jaimini 10.7.20.
Because it is a single [act], there should be a single portion, since no specific portion is heard in the scripture;
and because the Pratiprasthātṛ performs the cooking of the omentum (Jaimini 10.7.21).
Or rather, he does not eat [of it] because of the difference in the ritual action, since that [omentum] is to be offered in its entirety (Jaimini 10.7.23).
Because the original injunction is adopted in the modified rite, the restatement [of it] would be purposeless.
Or rather, there would be a dual verbal expression, as in the case of the Āgneya. Or not so, because of the distinctness of the words.

It should be more, because it possesses a purpose; for in the absence of a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*) or a specific quality, there is no modification due to the direct scriptural injunction, since those [injunctions] must serve that purpose on account of their being *apūrva* (unprecedented).
If it is argued that there should be a prohibition, we say no, because it is not so stated in the scripture. (Jaimini 10.7.27–29)
If it is argued that [the rule does not apply] because of non-mention, [we reply]:
no, because of equality;
for if it were so, there would be mention of it in that case as well.
But one should show its novelty (apūrvatā), because the act of taking [the portion] must have purpose;
therefore, too, it should be as much as is stated. There would be a prohibition of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the consumption [of the remnant], because the reason is the same.
Or rather, there would be a prohibition because of the observation regarding the *iḍā* [offering].
(Jaimini 10.7.36) Or rather, it is a prohibition of that which was previously enjoined, because of the observation [of such a case].

(Jaimini 10.7.37) If there were an option between ending with the *śaṃyu* formula and the *iḍā*, then the prohibition of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings in the subsequent rites would be meaningless. (Jaimini 10.7.38)

Or rather, it may be a constant restatement (nityānuvāda) of the ritual act, because there is no scriptural injunction [to the contrary] (Jaimini 10.7.39). And because the subsequent [text] serves the purpose of a prohibition, the prohibition would apply to what follows (Jaimini 10.7.40).
Or, because of the attainment [of the previous state], there would be a transgression [of the rule] due to the statement regarding the former (Jaimini 10.7.41).
Because the prohibition is characterized by urgency, it cannot apply to another location. (Jaimini 10.7.42) In the *upasads*, there should be no performance beyond what is expressly stated.
(Jaimini 10.7.43) Or rather, by means of the *stotra*, because it is subordinate (*guṇatva*), there should be a prohibition of the remaining [rites]. (Jaimini 10.7.44)

Or rather, it is not a prohibition, because there is no counter-exception to what has been prohibited. (Jaimini 10.7.45) Or rather, there is no performance of the remaining [rite], because the principal deities are not to be worshipped. (Jaimini 10.7.46) Since there is a prohibition of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) at the *avabhṛtha* bath, there would be a performance of the remaining ritual acts. (Jaimini 10.7.47)
Or rather, because the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are subordinate elements, there would be a prohibition of the remainder [of the sacrifice].

(Jaimini 10.7.48) But since the *prayāja* offerings involve a partial prohibition, they function as a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*); therefore, it must be a permanent restatement (*nityānuvāda*). (Jaimini 10.7.49) The mention of the two *ājyabhāga* offerings may be either a permanent restatement or, like the *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice, [an injunction]. (Jaimini 10.7.50)

When there is a single scriptural mention of conflicting items, there should be a restrictive rule regarding their inclusion, because such inclusion is purposeful; furthermore, it is distinguished by direct scriptural statement, as in the case of the *śara* grass. Jaimini 10.7.51.
If it is argued that this is not so because of the application of both [types of materials], Jaimini 10.7.52.
If it is further argued that this applies to the *śara* grass as well, Jaimini 10.7.53.

If it is argued that [the rule does not apply] because there is no perception of contradiction in the case of arrows, then it would likewise apply to the other case. If it is argued that this results in the scriptural statement being purposeless, [we reply: Jaimini 10.7.56.
Because the act of taking up has a purpose, the taking up should occur before [the ritual] has commenced; Jaimini 10.7.57.
And because all the subordinate elements have a purpose, the taking up should occur before [the ritual] has commenced; Jaimini 10.7.58.
If it is argued that [the subordinate element] would be redundant [once the main action has begun]; Jaimini 10.7.59.
Not so, because of the absence of purpose (Jaimini 10.7.60).
Likewise, when there is a modification of a single purpose, the archetypal rule does not apply; for if it were to apply, there would be an option (vikalpa) (Jaimini 10.7.61).
If it is argued that it applies as far as the scriptural injunction extends (Jaimini 10.7.62), [the reply follows].

It does not apply to the archetype because it is not explicitly stated in the word [of the injunction]. (Jaimini 10.7.63) But in the ectype, there would be no restriction, because the taking [of the substance] is for the sake of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), like the *pṛṣadājya* (spotted butter), and because both [substances] are prescribed; thus, the scriptural rule regarding the quality would apply whichever [is used].
(Jaimini 10.7.64) Or rather, it should be restricted because they serve the same purpose, since it is distinguished by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). (Jaimini 10.7.65)
And because of their mutual contradiction, as in common worldly experience (Jaimini 10.7.66);
and because the sacrifice possesses those qualities (Jaimini 10.7.67);
and when contradictory [injunctions] are heard, there would be an option, since they are not [simultaneously] expressed by the word (Jaimini 10.7.68).
Jaimini 10.7.69: Because there is a combination [of substances] in the *pṛṣadājya*, the taking up [of the substance] is for the sake of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*).
Jaimini 10.7.70: However, even if one is "one who takes four portions" (*caturavattin*), this is not tenable as a restrictive rule (*niyama*).
Jaimini 10.7.71: Or rather, it applies to another sacrifice, because that is the logical principle due to the difference in ritual acts (*karmabheda*).
If it is argued that it is "according to what is heard" [in the specific context], [we reply]:

No, because the injunction is one and the same. A prohibition would apply both to a specific rule (*pradeśa*) and to an unattached general rule (*anārabhyavidhāna*); since both are established and yet prohibited, there would necessarily be an option (*vikalpa*).
If it is argued that it is like the attainment of the purpose (*arthaprāptivat*), [we reply]: No, because the reason is the same; both are characterized by the word (*śabdalakṣaṇa*).

Rather, it should be a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), because an option (*vikalpa*) among injunctions (*vidhi*) is improper; it would be a partial specification (*ekadeśa*) of the injunctions.
And in the case of something unprecedented (*apūrva*), it would be an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). (Jaimini 10.8.5) But having enjoined [something], there would be a prohibition.

(Jaimini 10.8.6) If one does not postulate another [injunction], it would be an explanatory praise regarding what has already been established, because [otherwise] it would be purposeless and because of the capacity of the subsequent [text]. (Jaimini 10.8.7)
And because it is simultaneous with the former; Jaimini 10.8.8.
And the censure is likewise; Jaimini 10.8.9.
If it is argued that it is not an action because of a prohibition; Jaimini 10.8.10.
Not so, because it is preceded by the word [of the Veda].

(Jaimini 10.8.11) The prohibition of giving, offering oblations, and cooking for one who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*) would, due to the lack of specification, apply as a prohibition of all giving, offering oblations, and cooking.
(Jaimini 10.8.12) Or rather, this rule should apply to those acts not connected with a sacrifice, because the [acts] connected with the sacrifice are directly enjoined by scripture. (Jaimini 10.8.13)
Or rather, there would also be an inferential [prohibition] because there is no distinction;

however, because it is a supplementary part of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), there should be an exclusion of the other, for if it were a prohibition, there would be an option (*vikalpa*). Since a general scriptural injunction is doubtful due to the impropriety of an option, it should be set aside by a specific rule that is further removed [in time].

But when a scriptural injunction is heard in a specific context outside of a particular ritual section (*aprakaraṇa*), it serves to exclude the archetypal (*prākṛta*) elements, provided it remains unmodified, as in the case of the *ājyabhāga* offerings. (Jaimini 10.8.17) However, if there is a modification (*vikāra*), that [injunction] would be for the sake of that modification. (Jaimini 10.8.18) Or rather, because it is grasped by the sacrifice, it should be a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) to the injunction not established by a specific context (*anārabhyavidhāna*). (Jaimini 10.8.19)

In the case of mantras, there can be no supplementary explanatory statement (*avākyaśeṣatva*) because they teach specific qualities (*guṇopadeśa*). (Jaimini 10.8.20) And because such [supplementary statements] are not seen in those [mantras] that are not recited [in the Brāhmaṇas]. (Jaimini 10.8.21) And because of prohibitions. (Jaimini 10.8.22)

Because the *agnyatigrāhya* cup is specifically taught in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), it would not apply [to the archetype]. (Jaimini 10.8.23) And its monthly extraction is likewise [restricted].
(Jaimini 10.8.24) Or rather, there is an extraction [of it] because of the equality [of the rule]. (Jaimini 10.8.25)
And because of the observation of an indicative mark [Jaimini 10.8.26],
the taking up [of the draught] would be subject to the same rule [Jaimini 10.8.27].
The mention of "month" is for the purpose of prohibiting repetition [Jaimini 10.8.28].

Because it is for the sake of the production [of the offering], the fourfold cutting belongs to the principal [offering] due to its connection with the oblation; there is additional clarified butter because of the inequality, as in common worldly practice, since the production [of the butter] is subordinate. (Jaimini 10.8.29) And because of the scriptural injunction regarding its consecration. (Jaimini 10.8.30) Or rather, together with those two, the *sviṣṭakṛt* is performed once, because the text states that the requirement is met by the double sprinkling. (Jaimini 10.8.31)

And because all [the deities] are mentioned as being equal, and because they are enumerated according to their devotion, [the rule] would be restricted like the case of the *sāptadaśya* (the number seventeen). (Jaimini 10.8.32) Or rather, since the oblation (*havis*) is a subordinate factor (*guṇa*), there would be an intention to express it as such. (Jaimini 10.8.34)
The instruction regarding the two *puroḍāśa* cakes applies to those who are already qualified [for the sacrifice], because that is what is heard in the text, as in the case of the *vaiśyastoma*.

(Jaimini 10.8.35) However, there is no non-permanent qualification [in the injunction]; rather, there is a connection with what is permanent. Therefore, it is not a supplementary part of the sentence (*avākyaśeṣa*). (Jaimini 10.8.36) And even if it were so, [the agent] would not be [qualified] by a single part, because the agent is the primary factor. (Jaimini 10.8.37)
But because it is complete, it should be so in the case of the *stoma*;
if it is argued that it should belong to the agent [Jaimini 10.8.38],
we say no, because it serves as a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) and, since it is already established, it has no purpose as an instruction [Jaimini 10.8.39–40].
But since that principle applies to the context of the ritual action, the scriptural injunction regarding time for the subordinate elements should be determined by their indicative mark (*liṅga*).

(Jaimini 10.8.41) If, however, the *sānnāyya* belongs to one who has performed the *soma* sacrifice, there is no connection between it and those two [offerings], because their times are distinct. (Jaimini 10.8.42) Or rather, since it is already prescribed, when there is doubt regarding a repetition of the text for the sake of a subordinate quality, the scriptural statement should be for the purpose of the two deities; just as the *āgneya* is not intended [for the two deities] because of the observation of the single deity. (Jaimini 10.8.43)
But Bādarāyaṇa [holds] that there is a rule; or rather, because of the cognition of what is prohibited;
and likewise, there is the observation of another purpose.

Regarding the injunction "one performs the *upāṃśuyāja* in between," since there is no mention of a specific oblation (*havis*) by its characteristic mark, one might assume that it may be performed according to one's desire.
[However,] it must be from the *dhruva* vessel, because of the connection with the whole;
and likewise, this would apply to the deity.

Because of the context of the *tāndrī* [hymns], [the subject] would be Prajāpati on account of his *dharma*; however, there is no explicit designation of a deity there, whereas here the word is soft [in its application]; therefore, it is by virtue of the specific qualification here.
Or rather, Viṣṇu [should be the deity] because of the recitation in the *hautra* manual, and there should be an oblation to him at the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), since he is seen there in the *hautra*.

(Jaimini 10.8.53) Or rather, it should be at the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), because of the connection with the word for the principal [rite]; the mantra, being subordinate, should follow the principal.
(Jaimini 10.8.54) Furthermore, the sequence of the *sānnāyya* with the cake (*puroḍāśa*) indicates that this modification belongs to the new moon sacrifice. (Jaimini 10.8.55)
However, because of the injunction regarding Agni and Soma, both [offerings] are prescribed on the full-moon day; Jaimini 10.8.56.
Or, because of the non-prescription of what has been prohibited, Viṣṇu would occupy the same location; Jaimini 10.8.57.
And likewise, there is an observation of another purpose; Jaimini 10.8.58.

And it is not the case that when "anaṅga" is heard once, it is prescribed for both [the original and the modified form], because there is no connection [between them]. (Jaimini 10.8.59) Furthermore, since subordinate elements exist for the sake of another, he shows the indicative marks of injunction regarding their application. (Jaimini 10.8.60) And because there is no scriptural statement regarding modification. (Jaimini 10.8.61)
In the case of the two *puroḍāśa* cakes, it should apply because it serves an intermediate purpose (Jaimini 10.8.62),
and also because it serves the purpose of preventing *ājāmi* (Jaimini 10.8.63).
If it is argued that it is for that purpose [of the intermediate], we say no, because that is not the primary purpose (Jaimini 10.8.64).
And because of the connection with that which is not prescribed [as a rule]. Jaimini 10.8.65.

But its application should be at the time of origin, because the purpose exists without obstructing the subordinate quality, because it is a prescription, and because the intermediate purpose is contingent; in the absence of that, it would not exist even if it were not explicitly heard. Jaimini 10.8.66. But because both are prescribed. Jaimini 10.8.67.

And because qualities are for the sake of another, it should be as in the case of the *upaveṣa* [wooden splinter]; [this applies] when there is [the word] *yadā*. (Jaimini 10.8.68) Furthermore, there is no exclusion of time, for the two *puroḍāśa* cakes are indeed the indicators (*lakṣaṇa*). (Jaimini 10.8.69) The absence of *ajāmitva* (non-repetitiveness/non-monotony) is for the purpose of praise (*praśaṃsā*). (Jaimini 10.8.70)

Because they are connected with distinct purposes, there would therefore be a single performance [of the action] due to their being joined by a single term. Or rather, like the subsidiary elements (*śeṣavat*), the purpose would be divided for each person and each action. But this cannot be so, because it is not thus prescribed.
For since the remainder is for the sake of another, its performance would apply to each primary separately (Jaimini 11.1.4).

But because the subsidiary parts have distinct verbal designations, they should have separate results, as in the case of sacrifices (Jaimini 11.1.5). However, while there is a difference in purpose there, here there is a single action because of the unity of purpose (Jaimini 11.1.6).
If it is argued that [the acts] are distinct because of the difference in words, [we reply: No;
because the purpose is the ritual act, the designation by those words would apply during the performance, since they serve that purpose.
Because the injunction regarding the agent has multiple purposes among the subordinate and principal elements.
Because the commencement [of a rite] is preceded by the word [of the injunction].
(Jaimini 11.1.10) It may be completed even by one [verse], because the purpose has been fulfilled; as in other sacrifices, when [verses] have been obtained, it should be like the subsequent ones.
(Jaimini 11.1.11) If it is argued that it is not so because of the absence of a fruit, (Jaimini 11.1.12)

There would not be a defect in the word due to its purpose by virtue of its connection with the ritual action. (Jaimini 11.1.13) If it is argued that this is because of the identity of the word, (Jaimini 11.1.14) [we reply: no, because the meanings are distinct; since they are equal, there is no status as a subordinate quality. (Jaimini 11.1.15)

But because the injunction has a single form, because it prescribes [the acts] simultaneously, because there is a connection with what is heard as being eternal, and because they are obtained together by their very nature, the word itself—just like the *nivīta*—should apply to all performances according to how they are obtained;
likewise, because of the instruction regarding the ritual action. (Jaimini 11.1.16–17)
Jaimini 11.1.18: There is a restatement regarding other sacrifices;

because the subsequent [sacrifices] are not explicitly heard [as having specific details], and because the specific features have already served their purpose, one may be understood as acting according to one's desire when there is a doubt.

Jaimini 11.1.19: Since the fruit is to be realized at the commencement of the ritual action, the fruits should accrue with each commencement, just like [the harvest from] agriculture. Jaimini 11.1.20: [This is so] because the fruit is to be brought about through the undertaking of the rite.

And the entitlement of all [to perform the rite] is established because it is something to be accomplished; there is no distinction [among them]. (Jaimini 11.1.21) But it should occur only once, because the purpose has been fulfilled, as in the case of the subsidiaries.
(Jaimini 11.1.22) And such is the meaning of the word in common worldly usage. (Jaimini 11.1.23)

Alternatively, in the case of the application [of mantras], one may be understood to act according to one's desire, because there is no scriptural injunction; for in the case of ritual prescriptions, the words would be [mere] descriptive statements.

(Jaimini 11.1.24) Because of the identity of the word, it is so with respect to the subsidiary parts. (Jaimini 11.1.25) In common worldly usage, the purpose of an action is the defining characteristic. (Jaimini 11.1.26)
Since ritual actions are subordinate to a purpose, liberation (apavarga) would occur through their direct accomplishment; [Jaimini 11.1.27].

But since this is not observed in the case of mere dharma, liberation would occur through the meaning of the word [itself]; [Jaimini 11.1.28]. And as in the case of a sacrifice, there would be an abundance of fruit through repetition, as inferred by analogy; [Jaimini 11.1.29].
Or [the action] may be performed once, because the cause is one; Jaimini 11.1.30. And the measurement would be without restriction; Jaimini 11.1.31.
Because the commencement and completion of the fruit occur [simultaneously], there would be a difference in the fruits among the sacrifices; Jaimini 11.1.32.

But it cannot be a meaningful repetition because of its unity; otherwise, the repetition would be purposeless, just as eating [the same meal] once is not repeated for no further purpose. Since the object is immeasurable in a single instance, and since the primary element is for the sake of action, there would be no fixed rule. (Jaimini 11.1.33) There should be a definite measure due to the distinctness of the injunction. (Jaimini 11.1.34) Or rather, there is no repetition because the statement of performance is a single unit; since the entire thing is taught simultaneously by the scripture, and because the ritual act would be fruitless [if repeated], it exists for the sake of the action itself. (Jaimini 11.1.35)
Jaimini 11.1.36: Or rather, there should be repetition in the acts of cutting, cleansing, and slicing, because of the scriptural statement regarding the singular performance [of each].
Jaimini 11.1.37: But there is no repetition, because it is explicitly stated [that the action is performed once].
Jaimini 11.1.38: Since the plural number would imply that all [the parts] are to be taken, there would be an option [between performing them all or one].
If it is argued that the application has been observed;
if it is argued that it is by way of figurative usage;
likewise in the other case.

Or rather, the first [verse] should be restricted; for there would be a transgression [of the rule] due to a specific cause. (Jaimini 11.1.42) Because there is no difference in the meaning of the Vedic text. (Jaimini 11.1.43) And likewise, there is a scriptural indication of another purpose. (Jaimini 11.1.44)
And because of their proximity to that [original form], it is by nature as before; Jaimini 11.1.45.
In the subsequent [rites], it applies to as many [deities] as there are, because of their being previously unknown (apūrva); Jaimini 11.1.46.
Or rather, it would be a restatement (anuvāda) of as many [deities] as there are, due to the injunction of others. Jaimini 11.1.47.
Because of the prescription of completeness;
because of the multiplicity of purposes; and because in the Agnihotra there is a restriction regarding the porridge as being without remainder, there is a prohibition for children.
Even though it applies to all [the offerings], the deity is connected [with each] because of its connection with the deities; Jaimini 11.1.51.

Since the subordinate elements (aṅga) exist for the sake of the principal action (pradhānakarma), there would be a distinction of actions in the performance due to the distinction of those [deities]; Jaimini 11.1.52. And there would be a disruption of the sequence due to simultaneity; Jaimini 11.1.53.
But for those that are equal, there should be simultaneity because of the instruction of a single term and because no distinction is perceived (Jaimini 11.1.54).
There should be no interval because they serve a single purpose (Jaimini 11.1.55).
And likewise, Kāmukāyana observes an indicative mark to this effect (Jaimini 11.1.56).
Because that is the logical principle, there would be a sequence due to incapacity, since the refinement (saṃskāra) is for that purpose.
(Jaimini 11.1.57) Even though it is not conjoined [with all things], it is because it is for that purpose.
(Jaimini 11.1.58) Or rather, because of its pervasiveness, like a lamp. (Jaimini 11.1.59)
But in fact, according to the purpose in the world, there should be [repetition] for each principal act (*pradhāna*). Jaimini 11.1.60.
Kāmukāyana says that the sacrifice should be performed only once, because of the contradiction regarding the measure. Jaimini 11.1.61.
But since the injunction serves another purpose, there would be a departure from the scriptural statement of a single performance. Jaimini 11.1.62.
Bādarāyaṇa [holds that] there is a performance [of the entire procedure] according to rule in the division of the context;
moreover, proximity by means of a single [element] is not a non-distinguishing reason.
If it is argued that it is not so because of the injunction in certain cases, [the reply is: no. Jaimini 11.1.63–65.
Not so, because it is enjoined [as such]. Jaimini 11.1.66.
It has been explained that there is simultaneity for equal [acts] when no distinction is perceived. Jaimini 11.1.67.

But there would be a distinction due to a difference in time, because of the intervention of the injunction; for there is an injunction for those [acts] that are distinguished, since they have the time of the principal act as their time. Jaimini 11.1.68.
And likewise, there is the observation of another purpose. (Jaimini 11.1.69) If it is argued that this is an injunction, we say no, because it is a statement in the present tense.
(Jaimini 11.1.70) There is unity of place, time, and agent for the primary [rites], because they are taught by a single word. (Jaimini 11.2.1)

If the connection of actions were understood as being non-injunctive (*avidhi*), then because of their association with the purpose characterized by that [injunction], and because of the injunctive nature of the others, there would be a state of subordination for each primary action (*pratipradhānabhāva*). (Jaimini 11.2.2) And in the case of the subsidiaries (*aṅga*), there would be an absence of that [subordination], because of the specific reference to the primary.

(Jaimini 11.2.3) But if the connection of the action were with the injunction, then due to the unity of the expression, there would be a connection with the denotation of the purpose of the primary. (Jaimini 11.2.4)
Likewise, there is the observation of their purpose (Jaimini 11.2.5);
and there is the scriptural authority for them, because, like the primary [sacrifice], they are heard as being for the sake of another (Jaimini 11.2.6),
and because the [independent] action is not heard in the text (Jaimini 11.2.7).

But because they are prescribed as constituent parts, the subsidiaries should be taught along with the principal act; therefore, there would be a single location [for them]. (Jaimini 11.2.8) If it is argued that the substance and deity are likewise [to be taught together], (Jaimini 11.2.9) [We reply:
No, because they are supplementary to the injunction of the primary command; the specific detail is for the purpose of restriction. (Jaimini 11.2.10)

Jaimini 11.2.11: Because there is a combination of those [rites] performed together, there is a common procedure (*tantra*) for the subsidiaries; however, due to their difference, there would be a difference in the performance of the actions, because they are designated by distinct primary terms, and likewise there is a scriptural indication to that effect. Jaimini 11.2.12:
In the *iṣṭi*, *rājasūya*, and *cāturmāsya* sacrifices, because they constitute a single ritual action, there should be a common procedure (*tantrabhāva*) for the subsidiaries.
Jaimini 11.2.13: If it is argued that this is not so because of the difference in time.
[The view is] not so, because they occupy a single location, like the animal sacrifice (paśu).

Or rather, because the actions are distinct, there should be an instruction for them as a whole, including their subsidiaries, since they are prescribed by a single ritual framework (tantra). And likewise, there is a scriptural indication to that effect.

Likewise, it would apply to its constituent parts. (Jaimini 11.2.17) But in the case of the animal sacrifice, because the injunction is a single unit, there would be a temporal separation of the *tantra* (common ritual procedure). (Jaimini 11.2.18) It would be so also in the *adhvarakalpa* sacrifice, because of the unity of time for the specific details. (Jaimini 11.2.19)

And the word "iṣṭi" is heard in the singular. (Jaimini 11.2.20) Or rather, because the actions are distinct and because they are enjoined as a single ritual framework (tantra), there should be an instruction for them along with their subsidiaries.
(Jaimini 11.2.21) Or else, it is a statement of the time for the first [action]. (Jaimini 11.2.22)

Because the fruit is one, the term "iṣṭi" applies as elsewhere. (Jaimini 11.2.23) The *vasā-homa* (fat-offering) should be a single ritual procedure (*tantra*) for those sacrifices having a single deity, because the time of offering is the same. (Jaimini 11.2.24) But due to the difference in time, there is repetition when there is a difference in deities. (Jaimini 11.2.25)
Likewise, there is the oblation to the sacrificial post (*yūpāhuti*) at the beginning;
[this is] either a prohibition of the other [oblations],
because the specific locations are not prescribed by scripture.
In the *avabhṛtha* [concluding bath], there should be a modification of the fire, for the connection with fire is not the cause of that [modification].

(Jaimini 11.2.29) Or rather, it includes the subsidiaries, because the injunction regarding the performance is a single unit. (Jaimini 11.2.30) And because of the observation of an indicative mark. (Jaimini 11.2.31)
And because of the distinction in the word, there is no removal of the deity.

(Jaimini 11.2.32) In the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, everything is performed at the southern fire because of the difference in location. (Jaimini 11.2.33) If it is argued that this is not an injunction, (Jaimini 11.2.34)
It may be like the full-moon sacrifice;
if it is argued that there is no performance [of the subsidiary],
[we reply] that here too the performance of the offering to Marut is enjoined.
If it is argued that [the term] refers to the act of reaching [the altar], [we reply]:
no, because it forms a single syntactical unit with what follows;
and because [the act of reaching] cannot be expressed [by the word]. (Jaimini 11.2.38–40)
The scriptural statement is likewise [authoritative].
(Jaimini 11.2.41) If it is argued that there is a difference of agents in that case as well, (Jaimini 11.2.42) [we reply:
no, because of their inherent connection. (Jaimini 11.2.43)
And because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga).
[Objection: "Because of the connection with the altar (vedi)," [it is argued]. [Reply:
No, because it is merely a location.
Because they form a single syntactical unit (Jaimini 11.2.47).

Because there is only one fire, the *tantra* (common procedure) should apply to the subsequent rites (Jaimini 11.2.48). Or rather, they are distinct because of the difference in performers (Jaimini 11.2.49).

At the abandonment of those animals for whom the fire has been carried around, there is an abandonment of the ritual action of the Prājāpatyas because of the similarity of the scriptural statement, as in the case of the forest-dwellers; therefore, there should be a distinct injunction regarding the Brahmasāman. Or rather, it is a prohibition of the purificatory rite (saṃskāra), because of the unity of the sentence and the commonality of the sacrifice.
Because of the unity of the sentence and the commonality of the sacrifice. Jaimini 11.2.50–52.
If it is argued that the Pañcaśāradīya sacrifices are likewise [to be performed without sprinkling], because of the observation of the non-sprinkling of the omenta (Jaimini 11.2.53), we say:
no, because of the syntactical unity with the injunction (Jaimini 11.2.54–55).
And because of the state of being "worn out" (yātayāma);
and because of the observation of that [state] in the case of consecrations (saṃskāra). Jaimini 11.2.56–57.

Because of the anticipation of the purchase in the Daśapeya sacrifice, there is an anticipation [of the ritual]; therefore, the *tantra* (common procedure) for those [acts] preceding it should be the same. Jaimini 11.2.58.
The same applies to the use of the plural number.
(Jaimini 11.2.59) Or rather, there is an extraction [of the mantra] because it is for the sake of the purpose;
(Jaimini 11.2.60) and because the *avabhṛtha* is seen in the preceding [text]. (Jaimini 11.2.61)

It is common [to the other offerings] because of the equality of time. (Jaimini 11.2.62) Regarding the *niṣkāsa* (scum), since it is a single portion of that [offering], there would be a separation from the offering, as in the case of the animal sacrifice. (Jaimini 11.2.63) Or rather, it is an exclusion, because of its connection with what is well-known. (Jaimini 11.2.64)
If it is argued that it is a disposal (*pratipatti*), we say no, because of its connection with a ritual action (*karma*). Likewise in the case of the *udayanīya* sacrifice.
It is indeed a disposal, because of its lack of connection with a ritual action.
Or rather, it is a ritual act for the sake of the purpose, because it is subsidiary, like the act of pouring; for it is enjoined for that purpose.
(Jaimini 11.2.68) Because the subsidiaries follow the time of the principal, their time may be different due to a specific scriptural statement.
(Jaimini 11.3.1) Since the substance is produced at the time of the ritual act, its performance should be for the sake of all [the rites], because it has its own specific time. (Jaimini 11.3.2)
And the sacrificial post [is established] because it is not performed at the time of the ritual action; Jaimini 11.3.3.
And it indicates a single post; Jaimini 11.3.4.
But the consecrations would repeat, because their purpose is realized at the time [of the sacrifice]; Jaimini 11.3.5.

But because that [time] is for the purpose of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and because its ritual properties (*dharma*) are prescribed [for that specific time], and because of the scriptural statement regarding all purposes, it belongs to a different time.
(Jaimini 11.3.6) And it shows that the measuring is done once.
(Jaimini 11.3.7) The *svaru* should conclude with the completion of the main ritual (*tantra*), because it does not have its own specific time. (Jaimini 11.3.8)
Or rather, there is a co-arising [of the result] because it is common;
(Jaimini 11.3.9) and because a ritual disposal (*pratipatti*) is seen at the conclusion of the Soma sacrifice.
(Jaimini 11.3.10) Nor is it so because of the originative statement, as in the case of the *prastara* grass-bundle due to its specific location. (Jaimini 11.3.11)

In the case of a multi-day sacrificial session (*ahargaṇa*), because of a conflict with the established rule, the casting away of the horn (*viṣāṇā-prāsana*) would be optional—either at the end or on the first day. (Jaimini 11.3.12) However, there should be a restriction regarding the horns, as the hand is not explicitly mentioned [as the agent of disposal]; this is because [the disposal] occurs in the midst of the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) and because it has already been commenced during what remains [of the rite].
(Jaimini 11.3.13) And because it has already been commenced during what remains [of the rite]. (Jaimini 11.3.14)
The utterance of the speech [of the Hotṛ] should likewise occur during the division of the seed-syllables by the Haviṣkṛt;

if it is argued that this should also be according to the invocation (yathāhvānam), then there would be a common ritual procedure (samānatantra) for both the animal sacrifice and the cake offering. Jaimini 11.3.15–17.

The *yoga* (connection) has the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the principal (*pradhāna*) as its purpose; there would be release (*vimoka*) upon the completion of all [of them]. Or rather, [there is release] upon the completion of the principal, because it is for the sake of that. And likewise in the case of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), there is a prohibition of what is for the sake of the principal, because its purpose has been fulfilled.

And in the case of a multi-day sacrificial session (*ahargaṇa*), it should be performed every day, because it is for that purpose. (Jaimini 11.3.21) But the *subrahmaṇyā* invocation is a single performance (*tantra*), like the initiation (*dīkṣā*), because it occurs at a different time [from the main sacrifice]. (Jaimini 11.3.22) However, because of its specific connection with the *prayāja* offerings, it should be repeated at the beginning of each day's time. (Jaimini 11.3.23)

If it is argued that [the mantra] is not a constituent part of the performance (*aprayogāṅga*), [we reply]: No, because there is an instruction for its performance, just as in the case of the difference between the performers (*kartrbheda*).

If it is argued that it belongs to that [particular rite] by virtue of its position, like the word "Agni," [we reply]: That [position] ceases [to apply], because [the mantra] exists for the sake of that [general purpose].
If it is argued that it is like fire, [we reply:
no, because the application is common [to all],
and because of the observation of indicative marks.

If it is argued that "it is indeed so," [we reply] no, because it is not the teaching of the learned and because the other method is more logical. If it is argued that "because the injunction is one," [we reply] no.

Nor [is there a requirement for the whole] because of the repeated performance, as in the case of the principal [sacrifice] (Jaimini 11.3.33). In the worldly [case], however, one may act according to desire, because the purpose of the purificatory rites is not lost (Jaimini 11.3.34). The sacrificial implements should be retained, because their disposal is prescribed, like the *ṛjīṣa* (Jaimini 11.3.35).

Or rather, it is heard that this is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificer for his sake; in that case, one may act according to one's desire, because it is for his sake (Jaimini 11.3.36). Or rather, there is the primary holding [of the vow], because death is uncertain (Jaimini 11.3.37). Or he who dies on the day of sacrifice would be entitled [to the fruit], like the *upaveṣa* (Jaimini 11.3.38).
It is not so, because it possesses the characteristics of an injunction (Jaimini 11.3.39).

Or rather, it is an original production because it serves as a motivator, like the milk-mixture (āśira) (Jaimini 11.3.40). If it is argued that there is an inconsistency of the words (Jaimini 11.3.41), [we reply: no.

Likewise, even in the case of the *āśira* [mixture], there is a separation [of the details] from the primary injunction (*śāstra*). In that context, there is a desire to prepare a single substance; whereas in the archetype (*prakṛti*), it was for the sake of the original purpose, here the instruction concerns what has already come into being, like something new (*apūrva*).
Because they serve the purpose of the archetype, the rites should be performed on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*).

In the *agnyādheya* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires), one should maintain those fires because there is no prohibition and because death is not a fixed cause [for their cessation]. Or rather, they are to be treated as a final disposal (*pratipatti*), as is the case with other [materials].
For it is said: "After the *soma* sacrifices, they perform the *prājāpatya* offerings."
If it is argued that there is a transposition of the constituent parts even without an explicit statement [Jaimini 11.3.48], [we reply:
there is a displacement due to a connection; in the other case, it is merely a matter of time [Jaimini 11.3.49].
If it is argued that this is because the time of the archetype is not applicable to those things which possess the *śastra* recitations [Jaimini 11.3.50],...
Not so, because of the prohibition in the scriptural text (Jaimini 11.3.51).
If it is argued that it applies to the place of modification (vikāra) (Jaimini 11.3.52),
we say no, because of the distinctness of the injunction (codanā) (Jaimini 11.3.53).

In the case of the displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the *sūktavāka*, there is no displacement of the deities of the Soma sacrifice, because they are not auxiliary elements (*anaṅga*) of the animal sacrifice; thus, as in the case of extraction (*niṣkarṣa*), there is no syntactic connection (*ananvaya*). Jaimini 11.3.54. Or rather, there is displacement due to the connection of the sentence (*vākya-saṃyoga*); however, because of the commonality of the ritual procedure (*samāna-tantra*) and the loss of purpose (*artha-lopa*), there is no syntactic connection. Jaimini 11.3.55.

Because the injunction is one and the same (*codana-ekatva*), in the *rājasūya* sacrifice, the auxiliary rites (*aṅgāni*) constitute a common procedure (*tantra*) since those whose place and time are not specifically mentioned are brought together. Jaimini 11.4.1.

Or rather, because it is connected to the agent in each individual case, like the *iṣṭi* sacrifice, it is a subordinate element; for since the collection [of acts] accomplishes that [result], and because of its unity, there would be the designation by a single word due to that oneness.
And thus there is the observation of another purpose. If it is argued that there would be no fixed rule, [we reply: Jaimini 11.4.4.
Because it has not been taught [as such];
because of the unity of purpose; and the repetition of the scriptural statement is for the sake of non-distinction.

And in the Aveṣṭi sacrifice, there should be a single performance (aikatantrya), because of the observation of indicative marks (liṅga) and because of the scriptural statement (vacana) connected with desire (kāma). [Objection:
If it is argued that this applies to the sacrifice for the sake of the ritual (kratvarthā), [we reply: no, because of the connection with specific social classes (varṇa). Jaimini 11.4.8–9.
In the Pavamāna oblations, there is a single performance because of the unity of the injunction regarding the performance (prayoga-vacana). Jaimini 11.4.10.
And because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga). Jaimini 11.4.11.
But because of the statement expressing a present action, there would be a distinction of ritual procedures (tantra-bheda). Jaimini 11.4.12.
If they were performed together, it would be a constant restatement (nityānuvāda). Jaimini 11.4.13.

But on the twelfth day, because it is the archetype, each individual day should be concluded separately due to the distinctness of the rites. (Jaimini 11.4.14) Or rather, because the days are established by direct scriptural statement, the rite with its subsidiaries should be performed there [on that day], just as at the midday pressing.
(Jaimini 11.4.15) Or else, because of the connection between the fruit and the agent, there should be a simultaneous performance, like the Āgneya and Agnīṣomīya sacrifices. (Jaimini 11.4.16)
Or rather, because they are heard as having specific times for their constituent parts, there should be a modification of those [rites] remaining in their own places (Jaimini 11.4.17).
Furthermore, the number of *dīkṣā*s and *upasad*s is distinct for each, due to their direct connection with the scriptural injunctions (Jaimini 11.4.18).

The preceding rites up to the *vasatīvarī* waters constitute a single *tantra* because they belong to a different time; the subsequent rites beginning with the *avabhṛtha* bath constitute another *tantra* because they serve the purpose of releasing the *dīkṣā* (Jaimini 11.4.19).
And likewise, there is the observation of another purpose:
*Jaim_11.4.20* — "But when there is a distinct injunction, there is a single performance (*aikatantrya*) of those [acts] that are combined, because of their connection with the time.

*Jaim_11.4.21* — "But there is a distinction; due to that distinction, there would be a difference in the performance of the acts, because they are designated by the term 'principal' (*pradhāna*). *Jaim_11.4.22*.
And likewise, there is the observation of another purpose (Jaimini 11.4.23).
The mention of the Soma-pressing on the day after [the animal sacrifice] is similar (Jaimini 11.4.24).
And there is the surplus of animals (Jaimini 11.4.25).

In the case of an extension of the *sutyā* (Soma-pressing day), there should be an indication of all [the deities] in the *subrahmaṇyā* formula, because it follows the model of the archetype, just like the invocation (*āvāhana*).
Or rather, there should be a single indication because it denotes Indra; for the time is indicated merely for the sake of marking it.
And because there is no division [of the formula]. (Jaimini 11.4.26–28)

In the case of a group of animals, there should be a single performance (*tantra*) because the cauldron (*kumbhī*), the spit (*śūla*), and the omentum-cooking spits (*vapāśrapaṇī*) are sufficient for all; Jaimini 11.4.29.

But there would be a distinction (*bheda*) due to doubt when there is a different deity; Jaimini 11.4.30. Or rather, the action [of the implements] would be according to their specific purpose or indicative mark (*liṅga*); Jaimini 11.4.31.
Jaimini 11.4.32: There would be a distinction [of the portions] because they are to be offered, since they are given as their own *yājyā* verses.
Jaimini 11.4.33: Or rather, it should be a single performance (*tantra*) because it is a disposal (*pratipatti*), and because ownership has not been established by scriptural statement.
Jaimini 11.4.34: If it is argued that it should be done once.
Not due to a difference in time; [Jaimini 11.4.35].

There would be a distinction among the cooking-pot, the spit, and the omentum-vessel due to the difference in the manner of cooking [Jaimini 11.4.36]. Among different species, there is a distinction because of the disparity in cooking [Jaimini 11.4.37].
And because an increase is observed; Jaimini 11.4.38.
And the potsherds, like the cooking-pot, belong to those of equal number; Jaimini 11.4.39.
Or rather, there is one for each principal [offering], as in the archetype; Jaimini 11.4.40.
Or rather, it should apply to all [the substances] at once. (Jaimini 11.4.41) Regarding a single substance, it has been explained that the purificatory acts constitute a single action.

(Jaimini 11.4.42) However, in the case of a different substance, because its purpose has already been fulfilled, there is a repetition [of the act]; and since the mantra is subordinate to that [substance], there should be a repetition of the mantra as well, because it is prescribed for the sake of that [substance]. (Jaimini 11.4.43)
And in the acts of scattering, cutting, strewing, and taking the clarified butter, there is a single performance because the purpose is one, as if it were a single substance.

(Jaimini 11.4.44) Or rather, it should be like a different substance, because it is a refinement of that [substance]. (Jaimini 11.4.45) In the sprinkling of the altar, there is a repetition of the mantra because the ritual act is performed again. (Jaimini 11.4.46)
Or rather, it would be an injunction regarding the quality of a single substance; therefore, there should be a single performance. (Jaimini 11.4.47) [Objection:
In the case of scratching, because the action differs for each limb, there should be a repetition. (Jaimini 11.4.48) [Response:
On the contrary, since the injunction refers to a single time, there should be a single act. (Jaimini 11.4.49)
The same applies to crossing a river in a dream, being rained upon, and the recitation of mantras over impurity.
(Jaimini 11.4.50) But in the case of a journey, [the mantra is used] until the purpose is accomplished.
(Jaimini 11.4.51) The mantra for the *uparava* holes should be performed as a single ritual act (*tantra*), because of the plural number, as is seen in common worldly usage. (Jaimini 11.4.52)
Jaimini 11.4.53: Because they do not occur simultaneously, there is a single mention [of the formula] for those actions that do not occur simultaneously, since the time [of their performance] is one.
Jaimini 11.4.54: There should be a repetition of the *haviṣkṛt*, the *adhrigu*, the *puronuvākyā*, and the *manota* formulas, because of the difference in time.
Jaimini 11.4.55: And because of the reversal of the *adhrigu* formula.

Because of the statement "he will do. (Jaimini 11.4.56) When there is a combination of *tantras*, those that are identical [in nature] share a single *tantra* due to the injunction; however, among unequal things, there should be a distinction because of the commencement of the injunction and its purpose, as well as the specification of the time in the sacred text.
(Jaimini 12.1.1) Furthermore, there would be a division of the *tantra* due to differences in accessory details (*guṇa*) and time. (Jaimini 12.1.2)

Or rather, there may be accomplishment through the principal tantra because of the prescription within the tantra, since the meaning of the tantra is not different [from that of the subsidiary]. (Jaimini 12.1.3) And there can be no distinction on account of modification, because the meaning remains unmodified. (Jaimini 12.1.4) Or rather, it belongs to some [tantras] alone, because [in others] it is impossible. (Jaimini 12.1.5)
It would be mere boastfulness (āhopuruṣikā).
And there is a scriptural observation regarding the single fire (ekāgni).
According to Jaimini, because [the agent] would fall into a state of dependence, there must be a prohibition of independence.

Because they serve different purposes, the rite of preparing the altar (*vedikarma*) should take place at the Soma sacrifice, as it has the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices as its archetype. Or rather, there should be no such rite, because [the altar] has already been prepared [for the archetype]. Furthermore, the same principle of extension (*prasaṅga*) would apply to the sacrificial vessels, since they are intended for the purpose of offering oblations (*homārtha*).
Or rather, [the fires] are appropriate because they have been employed; otherwise, there would be an undesirable consequence regarding that which has not been employed.

(Jaimini 12.1.12) Furthermore, the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) would not take place at the *śāmitra* fire, because the other [fire] has already been employed. (Jaimini 12.1.13) Or else, the cooking of the *agnihotra* oblation would not take place at the *śālāmukhīya* fire, because the *prājahita* fire is already present. (Jaimini 12.1.14)
The two [cart-poles] should be prepared for the purpose of pouring the oblation in the Havirdhāna shed, because they have already been employed [for that purpose].

(Jaimini 12.1.15) Or rather, there is no accomplishment [of the purpose], because the location is different; since the primary act would be deficient, if there were no deficiency, it would result in a case of "extended application" (prasaṅga).
(Jaimini 12.1.16) And because of the observation of [the use of] carts. (Jaimini 12.1.17)
And its connection [to the rite] is due to the difference in time;
(Jaimini 12.1.18) and the mantras are [connected] because they are directly applied (sannipātin).
(Jaimini 12.1.19) Because it serves the purpose of maintaining [the sacred fires], the adding of fuel to the fires (agnyanvādhāna) does not exist in the Soma sacrifice. (Jaimini 12.1.20)
Likewise, because the vow has departed;
and because of contradiction.
If it be argued that [the sacrificer] speaks the truth, [we reply: no. Jaimini 12.1.21–23.
Not so, because of the principle of "separateness despite connection" (saṃyogapṛthaktva).
And [the offering] is for the sake of the cup (*graha*), because it was previously intended for that purpose.
If it is argued that it is like the "remnant" (*śeṣavat*), we say no; for it would be a *vaiśvadeva* offering, due to the specific designation.
It is not so, because it serves as a means of livelihood (Jaimini 12.1.27).
And the girding is [included] because it has already occurred (Jaimini 12.1.28).
Because of the injunction of something else, there should be no eating of forest-food; for both [the girding and the eating] serve the purpose of livelihood (Jaimini 12.1.29).

If it is argued that the consumption of the remnants is likewise [for the sake of the priests], we say no, because it serves another purpose; and because they have already been remunerated, their hiring is accomplished. If it is argued that the consumption of the remnants is likewise [for the sake of the priests], [we say no]. Jaimini 12.1.30–32.

Not because of the connection with the ritual action. (Jaimini 12.1.33) Because the choosing has already occurred; since the choosing occurs for each ritual cycle (*tantra*), the choosing of the *hotṛ* priest should be performed for each ritual cycle. (Jaimini 12.1.34) If it is argued that the same applies to the *brahman* priest as well, (Jaimini 12.1.35) [the response follows].
Not before the restriction, for it is for that purpose;
[if it is argued] "because of what is specified," [we reply] no, because it is explicitly stated in the scripture.
If it is argued that "let it be so," [we reply]:
No, because of the connection with the ritual action (Jaim_12.1.39).
Since there is a distinction in the application of completed rituals when the origin of the sacrifice is taught, the rite should be performed for each individual *tantra* (Jaim_12.1.40–41).
The mantra is set aside because of the separation of locations;
[if it is argued] that the same applies to the binding and the taking away,
[we reply] no, because they serve a different purpose.
The dwelling (vihāra) should accomplish the purpose of worldly people because of its sovereign power;
likewise, there is a prohibition against cooking meat. Or rather, it should pertain to Vedic matters because of the specific instruction.
And because meditation is observed [in the case of the fire-altar], Jaimini 12.2.4;
and because the absence [of meditation] is observed [in the case of the ordinary fire], Jaimini 12.2.5;
the cooking of meat would be both enjoined and prohibited, due to its connection with the oblation, Jaimini 12.2.6.
Or rather, it is a supplementary statement regarding the rite prescribed without reference to a specific context in the southern [fire].
(Jaimini 12.2.7) In the *savanīya* sacrifice, there should be no animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), because its purpose is to fill the gaps; for other [cakes] serve that same purpose.
(Jaimini 12.2.8) Or rather, there must be an action [of offering], because it is intended for the deity. (Jaimini 12.2.9)

On account of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga). Jaimini 12.2.10: The *haviṣkṛt* (the call to the preparer of the oblation) should not occur at the *savanīya* offerings; for if it were intended for all purposes in the archetype (*prakṛti*), then once she has been summoned for the sake of the animal sacrifice, she would perform [the function] because of her presence. Jaimini 12.2.11:
But because the injunction occurs when the animal has been prepared. Jaimini 12.2.12.
Or rather, there should be a release [of the vow] upon the completion of the sacrifice for the sake of the yoga; Jaimini 12.2.13.
At a nocturnal sacrifice, there should be no application of the archetypal rule, because it is directly enjoined; Jaimini 12.2.14.
And because of the difference in time and the difference in the sentences, there would be a difference in the ritual procedure (*tantra*); Jaimini 12.2.15.
Jaimini 12.2.16: Because of the contradiction, it should be that very same vow [pertaining to the Vedic sacrifice].
Jaimini 12.2.17: Or rather, because it is prescribed in the middle of the *tantra*, it belongs to that *tantra* like the *savanīya* offering.
Jaimini 12.2.18: Due to deficiency, the fuel and the sacrificial grass would not accomplish the purpose, nor would the adding of fuel to the fires, if these were intended for the deities.

And if the *agnyanvādhāna* is for the sake of the deities, the *ārambhaṇīyā* [offering] should not occur in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), because it falls within the time of the archetype (*prakṛti*) and has already been performed for that purpose; this is because the commencement is connected with a single performance. (Jaimini 12.2.19–21)

Or rather, it may be so because time is all-encompassing; (Jaimini 12.2.22) and because of the distinction between commencement and division; (Jaimini 12.2.23) when there is a conjunction of conflicting properties, the property of the majority shall prevail. (Jaimini 12.2.24)

Or rather, the primary [act] [is more important], because of the prior injunction, as in common worldly practice; likewise, there is the observation of another purpose; and when there is a conflict between a subordinate element and its quality, [the quality prevails] because it exists for the sake of that [subordinate].
Because the enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) serves two purposes, it would possess the characteristics of both.
(Jaimini 12.2.28) But it should be made of wood when there is a conflict, because of its primary proximity [to the post].
(Jaimini 12.2.29) Or rather, the other [material] should be used, because that is prescribed for it there; furthermore, both are connected as subordinate elements (*aṅga*). (Jaimini 12.2.30)

In the animal sacrifices (paśusavanīya), there would be an option if the rite were a modification (vaikṛta), because both [the archetypal and modified forms] are not explicitly heard in the scripture. Or rather, the animal sacrifice should take place [at its own time], because it has a specific traditional injunction; otherwise, that injunction would be rendered meaningless in the event of an option. Furthermore, there is a displacement of the animal sacrifice due to its being prescribed in the middle of the ritual complex (tantra). Jaimini 12.2.31–33.

And if the *tantra* is common to the archetype, the *apūrva* [element] would be useless because of its non-permanence; for it would be purposeless. (Jaimini 12.2.34) Furthermore, an additional quality may be included in a shared [performance] without contradiction, even if it is not primary, just as in the case of "eating from a bronze vessel" (*kāṃsyabhoji*). (Jaimini 12.2.35) However, by the performance of that [additional element], there should be a restriction of the *tantra*, just as the animal sacrifice is restricted by the *sūktavāka*. (Jaimini 12.2.36)
Not so, because there is no contradiction;

and because it is not characterized by the scriptures. In the Viśvajit sacrifice, [the cloth] should be that of a calf's skin because of its specific name; otherwise, due to the predominance of the ritual framework (*tantra*), it would be unwashed (*ahata*).
Or rather, the calf-skin is an upper garment that is not in conflict [with the rule].

(Jaimini 12.3.2) In the case of the subsequent offerings (*anunirvāpyas*), there should be a restriction of the *tantra* (common procedure) because of their greater number, and also because of the observation of the *śviṣṭakṛt* offering.

(Jaimini 12.3.3) Or rather, because they are adventitious (*āgantuka*), they should follow their own specific rules due to a particular scriptural statement; furthermore, the other [the original sacrifice] is primary. (Jaimini 12.3.4)
And because it is its own place [Jaimini 12.3.5].
If it is argued that there is no modification because of the cooking for the Sviṣṭakṛt, [we reply] it is a modification like the Pavamāna [Jaimini 12.3.6].
Or rather, there is no modification, because with respect to the injunction it is like the archetype, and because of its existence [Jaimini 12.3.7].
Jaimini 12.3.8: Since the subordinate elements (guṇas) are prescribed for a single action, all [the subordinate elements] should belong to every action.
Jaimini 12.3.9: But those having a single purpose should be alternatives (vikalpa), for if there were a combination (samuccaya), there would be repetition (āvṛtti) of the principal (pradhāna).
Jaimini 12.3.10: If it is argued that one should repeat [the subordinate element] because of its meaningfulness (arthavattva).
For it is not because [the result] has not been heard; rather, as with a conceptual construction, it shows that there would be efficacy at a later time.

(Jaimini 12.3.11) And because they serve a single purpose among the expiations, there is a connection with what has already been accomplished; therefore, there is the removal of everything. (Jaimini 12.3.12) But their combination is for the sake of the defects. (Jaimini 12.3.13)

The application of mantras should be through their connection with ritual acts, performed according to their own specific nature, because dharma has that as its cause. (Jaimini 12.3.14) Alternatively, the application may be the cause of everything by virtue of the injunction regarding knowledge, because the application exists for the sake of the ritual act. (Jaimini 12.3.15) Because the accents are taught as they are in the original language, there is a prohibition against applying them according to common usage. (Jaimini 12.3.16)
Either there is no instruction regarding the mantra for one who speaks [it], because it arises from habitual practice; or there is the hearing of the spoken word due to habitual practice.
(Jaimini 12.3.17) There is a modification when the cause is not perceived, because that is the logical principle; and this is likewise even when [the cause] is perceived.
(Jaimini 12.3.18) Or rather, it is due to its production [from that], because its characteristic is defined by its oral transmission. (Jaimini 12.3.19)

Because mantras serve the purpose of performance, the commencement of the ritual act should coincide with the end of the mantra, since the entire mantra has the purpose of expressing [the action]. (Jaimini 12.3.20) Because of the expression of continuity, there is a connection with the beginning in the case of a continuous stream. (Jaimini 12.3.21) Or rather, it is a continuous performance of the act, because the acts are distinct and the other [interpretation] would be impossible. (Jaimini 12.3.22)
And because the pouring of the *āghāra* libation is performed with a long stream;
[Jaimini 12.3.23] since the mantras are directly applied (*saṃnipātin*) and serve a single purpose, there would be an option (*vikalpa*) between them.
[Jaimini 12.3.24] In the case of those prescribed by number, there is a combination (*samuccaya*), because they are not directly applied. [Jaimini 12.3.25]

And because, in the cases prescribed by the Brāhmaṇas, all [elements] are taught as being numerically distinct; likewise, there is the observation of the combination of the *yājyā* and the *vaṣaṭkāra*. Or rather, there is an option, because their combination is not explicitly stated in the scripture.
Because the instruction is for the sake of the qualities [of the sacrifice].

(Jaimini 12.3.29) In the case of the *vaṣaṭ*-call, because there is a plurality of purposes, there is a combination; however, the *hautra* recitations would be optional, as they serve a single purpose. (Jaimini 12.3.30) Or rather, because they are descriptive of what is being performed, there is a combination of the *hautra* recitations. (Jaimini 12.3.31)
And it shows that there is a combination [of mantras]. Jaimini 12.3.32:

"The *japas* not connected with ritual acts, as well as those consisting of praise and benediction among the *yājamāna* [mantras], should be combined because the benedictions are distinct. Jaimini 12.4.1:
And it shows that there is a combination. Jaimini 12.4.2.

In the case of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses, however, there should be an option (*vikalpa*), because they serve the purpose of indicating the deity; and this is also because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*). In the case of the purchases (*kraya*), there should be an option, because they serve a single purpose.
Or rather, there is a combination [of the substances], because they are inherent in the substance used for the performance; Jaimini 12.4.6.
And it shows a combination; Jaimini 12.4.7.
And in the case of a consecration, because that [substance] is the primary element; Jaimini 12.4.8.
But there should be an option regarding the numbers, because of the prohibition of what is heard [in scripture].

(Jaimini 12.4.9) However, due to the modification of the substance, it should be a primary act (*arthakarma*) as before; for by that option, there is a predominance of restriction. (Jaimini 12.4.10) Even though they are substances, there is a combination, because the substance is produced through the action; since there is a distinction of acts for each animal, this being so, it follows the original model. (Jaimini 12.4.11)
If it is argued that the same applies to the skull as well, [we reply]:
No, because the ritual action is for the sake of another;
however, its disposal is due to its being a subordinate element.

Even when [the milk] has been boiled, it should be as before. (Jaimini 12.4.15) It is to be treated as an option because the primary focus is on the restriction of the action according to its purpose; furthermore, because in the remaining case there is a connection with the ritual function, therefore it must be a purposeful action (*arthakarma*). (Jaimini 12.4.16) In the case of the *ukhā* (fire-pan), there is a combination of the optional and the obligatory, because desire is observed in the injunction. (Jaimini 12.4.17)
And if the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) did not exist, there would be ritual action;
for that [action] is for the sake of the deity. Or rather, it is a modification (*vikāra*) of the permanent fire, because of the reason stated for the optional rite.
On account of the scriptural statement, there would be an action regarding the unconditioned;
and even in the case of conjunction, there would be a fault.

(Jaimini 12.4.20) If it is argued that this is due to the scriptural statement, then in the other case, there is no acceptance of the general rule because the action has already been performed. (Jaimini 12.4.21–22)

That [fire] should be the Āhavanīya, because of its connection with the oblation (Jaimini 12.4.23). Or rather, it is another [fire], because of being brought after having been carried away; in that case, the purificatory rites are prescribed for it (Jaimini 12.4.24).
But by virtue of its position, they would be omitted (Jaimini 12.4.25).

There is an option regarding constant wearing; for the prohibition could not be without cause. Or rather, the prohibition applies to one whose prosperity has departed because of the requirement of constant wearing.
In the case of the *sattra* and *ahīna* sacrifices, as in the case of one who acts for another, there is no restriction among the group of sacrificers, since there is no distinction.

Or rather, the *gṛhapati* is the primary [officiant], because there is no prohibition; in the *sattra*, he is not connected [with the other roles] like the *hautra*, and because of the scriptural statement. Or rather, it belongs to all [the participants], because it is for their sake.
In case of conflict, the latter prevails. (Jaimini 12.4.32) In the *hautra* [ritual], [the former prevails] because it is for the sake of another.
(Jaimini 12.4.33) A direct statement [of the latter] prevails. (Jaimini 12.4.34)
The office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*) should belong to all social classes (*varṇa*) because of their sovereignty;
or rather, it should belong to Brāhmaṇas alone on account of the traditional law (*smṛti*);
for the others, however, [the office is excluded] because of the injunction regarding the fruit-cup (*phalacamasavidhāna*).
In the case of the *sānnāyya* offering as well, there is likewise a prohibition, because it is the cause for the consumption of Soma;
also because of the specific mention in the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*);
and because it is observed in the case of the *anvāhārya* rice-offering. (Jaimini 12.4.38–40)
